The answer to "idhā" [when] is omitted, its estimated form being "tub'athūn" [you will be resurrected], and it was omitted because what follows indicates it. According to the majority, the governing element of "idhā" is what follows it. Al-Zajjaj said this, and he also said, together with al-Nahhas, that the governing element is ﴿muzziqtum﴾ [you are torn apart]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an error and a corruption of the meaning. It is not an error, nor a corruption of the meaning. The conditional "idhā" is one whose governing element is disputed, and I have shown in my commentary on Sharh al-Tashil [Commentary on al-Tashil] that the correct view is that the verb of the condition governs it, like the rest of the conditional particles. The conditional clause may be governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, since it has the sense of "says to you": ﴿When you are completely torn apart﴾, then he emphasized this with his saying: ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾. It may also be that ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾ is governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, and ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ takes two objects. Were it not for the lām in the predicate of inna, it would be open (fatḥah), and the clause would stand in place of the two objects. On this reading the conditional clause is a parenthetical (i'tirāḍ) clause. Some people prohibited the suspension (ta'līq) in the verbs of knowing, such as i'lam, but the correct view is that it is permissible. The poet said:

*Beware, for you have been informed that you are the one*
*Who will be repaid for what you strive, and will be happy or wretched.*

[p. 260] "Muzzaq" [torn] is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came in the pattern of the passive participle, according to the analogy of the verbal noun of every verb of more than three letters, as in his saying:

*Do you not know that I release the rhymes (musarrāḥī al-qawāfī),*
*Without incapacity regarding them, nor forced?*

That is: my releasing (tasrīḥī) the rhymes. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an adverb of place, meaning: "when you are torn apart in a place of the graves, the bellies of birds and beasts, and what the floods carried off in every direction, and what the winds scattered and cast to every place." End of quotation. "Jadīd" [new] according to the Basrans has the sense of the active participle, as you say: "jadda, fa-huwa jādd wa-jadīd" [he was new, so he is new]. According to the Kufans it has the sense of the passive participle, from "jaddahu" [he cut it] when he cut it.

The apparent meaning is that his saying ﴿Has he invented against God a lie﴾ is from some of them to others, meaning: he is a fabricator ﴿against God a lie﴾ concerning what is attributed to Him regarding the matter of resurrection. ﴿Or is there madness in him﴾, which makes him imagine that and cast it upon his tongue? They placed invention and madness in equal balance, because this statement, in their view, could only come from one of these two: if he believed the opposite of what he brought, he is a fabricator; and if he does not believe it, he is mad. It may also be that it is from the words of the hearer who answered the one who said ﴿Shall we direct you﴾; he wavered between the two matters and did not affirm either, since he permitted this and permitted that, and did not affirm that it was pure fabrication. This was to avoid attributing a lie definitively to a rational person, since a rational person, even a disbeliever, does not accept lying, neither from himself nor from others. God, exalted is He, turned away from their statement. The meaning: the Messenger is not as you attribute to him at all; rather, you are in the torment of the Fire, or in the torment of this world through what you suffer from the nullification of the law, which is true, and the extinguishing of the light of God, which He will complete.

Since the discourse concerned resurrection, He said: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, thus arranging the torment upon the denial of resurrection. The description of error with "distance" (al-bu'd) was mentioned earlier, and it is among the attributes of places; it was borrowed for the meaning. The meaning of "ba'd" here is that its report, which is associated with it, does not end.

﴿Have they not seen﴾, that is, these disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter, ﴿to what is before them﴾, that is: wherever they turn, for the heaven and the earth have surrounded them, and they cannot pass beyond their extremities or go out from the dominion of God in them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They were blinded, so they did not look." He placed between the fā' and the hamzah a verb to which the conjunction could be connected. This differs from what the grammarians hold, namely that there is no omitted element between them, and that the fā' is a conjunction to what precedes the interrogative hamzah, and that the estimated form is "fa-a-lam," but since the interrogative hamzah has the right of initial position, it was placed first. Al-Zamakhshari returned to the view of the grammarians on this matter, and we have refuted this view in what we wrote in Sharh al-Tashil. God, exalted is He, made them stand before His overwhelming power and warned them that it encompasses them, as a means of destroying them. There was a omitted circumstantial clause (ḥāl) here, meaning: "Do they not see to what surrounds them of heaven and earth, subdued under Our power, which We dispose of as We wish?" ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾, as We did with Qarun, ﴿or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾, as We did with the people of the Shade (ash-Shadhah). Or: ﴿Have they not seen to what is before them and what is behind them﴾, encompassing them, while they are subdued under Our power? ﴿Indeed in that﴾, the looking at the heaven and the earth, the reflecting upon them, and what they indicate of God's power, ﴿is a sign (la-āyah), a clear indication and evidence, ﴿for every servant who turns back (munīb)﴾, who returns to his Lord and obeys Him. Mujahid said: "humbled (mukhbit)." Al-Dahhak said: "upright (mustaqīm)." Abu Rawq said: "sincere in monotheism (mukhliṣ fī al-tawḥīd)." Qatada said: "turning to his Lord with his heart (muqbil)," because the one who turns back does not fail to reflect upon God's signs, that He is capable of everything, including resurrection and His punishment of whoever disbelieves in Him.

The majority read ﴿in nashā' nakhsif﴾ [if We will, We shall cause to swallow] and ﴿nusqit﴾ [cause to fall] with nūn in all three. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, al-A'mash, and Ibn Mutarrif read them with yā' in all three. Al-Kisa'i assimilated the fā' into the bā' in "nakhsif bihim" [We cause them to be swallowed]. Abu 'Ali said: this is not permissible, because the bā' is weaker in sound than the fā', so the fā' is not assimilated into it, although the bā' may be assimilated into the fā', as in "ḍaraba Fulānan" [he struck so-and-so]. This is also where the bā' is assimilated into the mīm, as in your saying "iḍrib Mālikan" [strike Malik], but the mīm is not assimilated into the bā', as in your saying "iḍmum bik" [gather with you], because the bā' is lowered from the mīm by the lack of the nasalization (ghunnah) that is in the mīm.

[p. 261] Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Kisa'i read 'nakhsif bihim' with assimilation, but it is not strong." End of quotation. The recitation is a practice transmitted from the Prophet's Companions and followers (sunnah muttaba'ah), and in it there is what is eloquent and what is more eloquent, and all of that is from God's facilitation of the Qur'an for remembrance. So no attention is given to the saying of Abu 'Ali or of al-Zamakhshari.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 34, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2)**

(Surat Saba' has fifty-four verses and is Makki.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to whom praise belongs in the Hereafter. He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. He is the Most Merciful, the Most Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you, the Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight is hidden in the heavens or on the earth, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Book."﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds. For those there is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿But those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, for them is a painful punishment of wretched kind.﴾ ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Shall we show you a man who will tell you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation?" ﴾ ﴿Has he fabricated a lie against God, or is there madness in him?" Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the sky and the earth? If We willed, We could cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them. Surely in that is a sign for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾

(p. 257) This surah: al-Tahrir says it is Makki by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is Makki except for His words, ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾. A group said it is Madani concerning those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like. End of quote. The occasion of its revelation is that Abu Sufyan said to the disbelievers of Makkah, when they heard ﴿That God may punish the hypocrite men and women and the polytheist men and women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]: "Muhammad threatens us with punishment after we die, and frightens us with resurrection. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the Hour will never come to us, and we will not be raised." Then God said: "Say, O Muhammad, ﴿Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected﴾" [al-Taghabun: 7]. This is related by Muqatil. The rest of the surah is a warning and threat to them. Whoever mentions this occasion of revelation shows the connection between this surah and the one before it.

﴿All praise is due to God﴾: it encompasses all kinds of praise.

﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾: its apparent meaning is comprehensiveness. Since the blessing of the Hereafter is something reported, not seen by us in this world, He mentioned it so that its blessings may be measured by the blessings of this world, by analogy of the unseen to the seen, even though they differ in excellence and permanence. It is also said that the "al-" (the definite article) is for a known reference, pointing to His words: ﴿And their last prayer will be, "All praise is due to God"﴾ [Yunus: 10], or to His words: ﴿And they will say, "All praise is due to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Al-Zamakhshari said: The difference between the two praises is that praise is obligatory in this world, because He is the one who bestows His blessings, and it is the way to attaining the blessing of the Hereafter, which is reward. The praise of the Hereafter is not obligatory, because it is for a blessing whose connection to its deserving recipient is obligatory; it is rather the completion of the joy of the believers and the fulfilment of their delight, which they enjoy. End of quote, with some summarising.

﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾: of water. Al-Kalbi said: of the dead and of buried treasures.

﴿And what comes out of it﴾: of plants. Al-Kalbi said: of the precious substances of minerals.

﴿And what descends from the sky﴾: of rain, snow, hail, lightning, provision, and angels.

﴿And what ascends into it﴾: of the deeds of creatures. Al-Kalbi said: and what descends of the angels. It is also said: of decrees, states, supplications, and deeds. It is also said: of livestock and gifts. 'Ali and al-Sulami read: ﴿wa ma yunzalu﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn and a shadda on the zāy, meaning: God, exalted is He.

(Bala) is an answer to the earlier negation in their words ﴿The Hour will not come to us﴾, meaning: Yes, it will surely come to you. The majority read ﴿la-ta'tiyannakum﴾ with the feminine tā' (ta'tiyannakum), meaning: the Hour whose coming you denied. Talq, from his shaykhs, read it with the masculine yā' of the third person (la-ya'tiyannakum), meaning: the Resurrection will surely come to you, because their intended denial of the Hour was that they would not be raised. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it refers to the Hour, meaning "the Day," or it is attributed to God, meaning: the command of the Knower of the unseen will surely come to you, as in His words: ﴿Or your Lord comes﴾ [al-An'am: 158], meaning: His command. It is unlikely that the pronoun refers to the Hour, because it is treated as masculine, which is only found in poetry, such as the verse:

"Nor a land more sprouting in its growth..."

Then He emphasised the answer with an oath concerning the Resurrection, and followed the oath with His words ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ and what follows, so that it is known that the growing of plants is from the unseen which He alone possesses. The oath with His words ﴿by my Lord﴾ is attributed to the Messenger ﷺ, to indicate the intensity of the oath, since He did not use the shared name that both He and those who denied the Hour have in common, which is the word "God."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ruways, Salam, al-Jahdari and Qa'nab read ﴿'Ālimu﴾ with a ḍamma, as a nominative by supposing a pronoun, "huwa." Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿does not escape﴾. Al-Hawfi said: or its predicate is omitted, meaning: the Knower of the unseen is He. The remaining seven read ﴿'Ālimi﴾ with a kasra as a genitive. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' said: this is in apposition (badal). Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be an adjective (sifa), meaning that ('Ālim al-Ghayb) may be definite, and similarly everything that is attached to a definite noun, which in itself does not become definite by that means, may become definite through the genitive construction, except the adjectival noun (al-sifa al-mushabbaha), which does not become definite through an annexation. Sibawayh mentioned this in his book, and few know it.

Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿'Allāmi﴾ as an intensive form with a kasra. The reading of ﴿yaʿzubu﴾ was discussed in Yunus.

The majority read ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾ with a ḍamma on both rā's, and it is possible that it is coordinated with ﴿mithqāl﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], or that it is a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾. According to the first possibility, ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾ is an emphasis for what the negation in ﴿does not escape﴾ contains, and its implied sense is: but it is in a clear Book. This is a metaphor for the controlling and safeguarding of a thing, as if it were in a book, though there is no literal book. According to the second analysis, the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Al-A'mash and Qatada read the rā's with a fatḥa. Ibn 'Atiyya said: coordinated with (dharra), an atom. It is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr, and he attributed it also to Nafi'. What Ibn 'Atiyya said is not necessarily the only possibility: rather, "lā" may be for the negation of the genus, and the subject is the whole of "lā" with what is constructed with it according to the view of Sibawayh, and the predicate is ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾. This is coordination of sentences, not coordination of single words, as Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Al-Zamakhshari said, answering the question of one who asks: Is it permissible to coordinate ﴿nor anything smaller﴾ with ﴿mithqal﴾, and to coordinate ﴿nor anything smaller﴾ with (dharra)? I say: the particle of exception refuses that, unless you make the pronoun in ("'anhu") refer to the unseen, and make the unseen a noun for the hidden things before they are written in the Tablet, because their being recorded on the Tablet is a kind of emergence from concealment, in the sense that nothing separates from the unseen or departs from it except as written in the Tablet. End of quote. This interpretation is not needed if we take the Clear Book to be something other than the Preserved Tablet. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾ with a kasra on the two rā's, as if he intended an omitted genitive complement, the implied meaning being: nor smaller than it, nor greater than it. ("Min dhālika") is not connected to the elative (af'al), but is an explanatory element, because when the genitive complement is omitted, the word becomes ambiguous, so it is clarified by "min dhālika," meaning: "in respect of that." "Min" has come with an elative (af'al al-tafdil) that is annexed, in the verse of the poet:

"We, in planting the young palms, are more knowledgeable of us
than we are in the racing of the horses in the darkness."

This was interpreted as meaning "knowledge concerning us," where he annexed while intending to drop the annexed noun. So Zayd's reading admits this other interpretation: that when he annexed the elatives smaller and greater according to their case endings during annexation. All of this is an interpretation of irregularity (shudhudh). What suits the description of Him as "Knower of the unseen" is that nothing of the hidden things escapes His knowledge, so the time of the coming of the Hour is included in that, and this becomes evidence for the truth of what He swore to, because whoever knows all things entirely and in their parts, and whose power is established, is able to restore what has perished of all spirits and bodies. It is said: His words ﴿not an atom's weight in the heavens﴾ indicate His knowledge of the spirits, and ﴿nor on the earth﴾ indicates His knowledge of things. Just as He brought them both from non-existence into existence at first, so He will restore them a second time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the oath, in the sense of an oath, be an appropriate justification for what they denied? I say: this would be so if He had confined Himself to the oath and not followed it with the decisive argument, which is His words ﴿that He may reward﴾. God has placed in intellects and fixed in natures the necessity of recompense: the doer of good must have a reward, and the doer of evil must have a punishment. End of quote. The question contains some abbreviation, and there is in it a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

The apparent sense is that His words ﴿that He may reward﴾ are connected to ﴿does not escape﴾. It is also said that they are connected to ﴿will surely come to you﴾, and it is also said that they are connected to the operative element in ﴿in a clear Book﴾, meaning: except as established in a clear Book so that He may reward.

The majority read ﴿mu'jizīn﴾ (with a light form), and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Jahdari and Abu al-Simak read it with a doubled ʿayn (mu'ajjizīn), which was discussed in al-Hajj. The meaning: making God's power unable in their assumption. Ibn al-Zubayr said: its meaning is discouraging those who wish to believe from belief, making them incapable of enthusiasm for it, and this is their striving against the signs, meaning: concerning the matter of the signs. Qatada said: competing, supposing that they will outstrip us. Ikrima said: opposing. Ibn Zayd said: striving to nullify them.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿painful﴾ here and in al-Jathiyah with a ḍamma as an adjective of the punishment (al-'adhab), and the remaining seven with a kasra as an adjective of the wretched kind (al-rijz). Al-rijz means the evil punishment. The apparent sense is that His words ﴿And those who strove﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is in the second clause, which is ﴿those﴾ (ula'ika). It is also said that it is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿those who believed﴾, meaning: and that He may reward those who strove. It is possible that the two clauses introduced by ﴿those﴾ are the very reward and punishment. It is also possible that they are resumptive clauses, and the reward and punishment are what they contain of what is greater, such as God's eternal pleasure with the believer and His eternal wrath with the sinner.

Al-'Utbi said: The apparent sense is that His words ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ is a resumptive statement about those who were given knowledge, who know that the Qur'an sent down to you is the truth. It is also said: ﴿and see﴾ is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿that He may reward﴾, as said by al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi. The disagreement concerning ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ in that place where this surah was revealed has been discussed. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning, and that those possessing knowledge may know, at the coming of the Hour, that it is the truth, with a knowledge that cannot be increased upon by agreement, and they may argue with it against those who disbelieved and turned away. It is also permissible that he means: and that whoever among the righteous did not believe may know that it is the truth, so that his grief and distress increase. End of quote. He said "at the coming of the Hour" because he connected ﴿that He may reward﴾ to ﴿you will surely come﴾, so he based the interpretation on that.

The majority read ﴿al-Haqqa﴾ (the truth) with a fatḥa, as a second object of "yarā" (see), and the intervening pronoun is a separator (fasl). Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a ḍamma, making (huwa) a subject and (al-haqq) its predicate, and the clause is in the position of the second object of "yarā." This is the dialect of the Tamim, who make what is a separator for others into a subject, as said by Abu 'Umar al-Jarmi.

The apparent sense is that the subject of "yahdi" (guides) is the pronoun referring to ﴿what has been sent down﴾, which is the Qur'an, and this is a resumptive statement. It is said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the implied "wa huwa yahdi" (and He guides). It is possible that it is coordinated with ﴿al-haqq﴾, the verb being coordinated with the noun, as in His words ﴿ṣāffātin wa yaqbiḍna﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning: spreading and gripping. Likewise the noun is coordinated with the verb in the words of the poet:

"Then I found him one day destroying his enemy,
and a sea of giving, overwhelming the crossings."

Here "wa bahra 'aṭā'in" (and a sea of giving) is coordinated with "yubīru" (destroys). It is also said: the subject of "yahdi" is a pronoun referring to God, and this is far-fetched.

And those who disbelieved said: they are the Quraysh. Some of them said to others, in a manner of wonder and mockery, as a man says to someone he wants to amaze: "Shall I tell you of a strange and rare story?" Since resurrection was impossible in their view, they placed the one who reports its occurrence among those who are wondered at. They used his name, peace be upon him, in its indefinite form in the words: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man?﴾ His name was the most famous proper name among the Quraysh, and indeed in the world, and his report of resurrection was the most famous report. They presented this in the manner of mockery and of amusing themselves with some riddles made for diversion and obscuring, so they made his name indefinite for this reason.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ [will inform you] with a hamzah. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it by replacing the hamzah with a pure yā'. Al-Zamakhshari related from him: "yunbi'ukum," with a hamzah, from anba'a. The answer to "idhā" [when] is omitted, its estimated form being "tub'athūn" [you will be resurrected], and it was omitted because what follows indicates it. According to the majority, the governing element of "idhā" is what follows it. Al-Zajjaj said this, and he also said, together with al-Nahhas, that the governing element is ﴿muzziqtum﴾ [you are torn apart]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an error and a corruption of the meaning. It is not an error, nor a corruption of the meaning. The conditional "idhā" is one whose governing element is disputed, and I have shown in my commentary on Sharh al-Tashil [Commentary on al-Tashil] that the correct view is that the verb of the condition governs it, like the rest of the conditional particles. The conditional clause may be governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, since it has the sense of "says to you": ﴿When you are completely torn apart﴾, then he emphasized this with his saying: ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾. It may also be that ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾ is governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, and ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ takes two objects. Were it not for the lām in the predicate of inna, it would be open (fatḥah), and the clause would stand in place of the two objects. On this reading the conditional clause is a parenthetical (i'tirāḍ) clause. Some people prohibited the suspension (ta'līq) in the verbs of knowing, such as i'lam, but the correct view is that it is permissible. The poet said:

*Beware, for you have been informed that you are the one*
*Who will be repaid for what you strive, and will be happy or wretched.*

[p. 260] "Muzzaq" [torn] is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came in the pattern of the passive participle, according to the analogy of the verbal noun of every verb of more than three letters, as in his saying:

*Do you not know that I release the rhymes (musarrāḥī al-qawāfī),*
*Without incapacity regarding them, nor forced?*

That is: my releasing (tasrīḥī) the rhymes. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an adverb of place, meaning: "when you are torn apart in a place of the graves, the bellies of birds and beasts, and what the floods carried off in every direction, and what the winds scattered and cast to every place." End of quotation. "Jadīd" [new] according to the Basrans has the sense of the active participle, as you say: "jadda, fa-huwa jādd wa-jadīd" [he was new, so he is new]. According to the Kufans it has the sense of the passive participle, from "jaddahu" [he cut it] when he cut it.

The apparent meaning is that his saying ﴿Has he invented against God a lie﴾ is from some of them to others, meaning: he is a fabricator ﴿against God a lie﴾ concerning what is attributed to Him regarding the matter of resurrection. ﴿Or is there madness in him﴾, which makes him imagine that and cast it upon his tongue? They placed invention and madness in equal balance, because this statement, in their view, could only come from one of these two: if he believed the opposite of what he brought, he is a fabricator; and if he does not believe it, he is mad. It may also be that it is from the words of the hearer who answered the one who said ﴿Shall we direct you﴾; he wavered between the two matters and did not affirm either, since he permitted this and permitted that, and did not affirm that it was pure fabrication. This was to avoid attributing a lie definitively to a rational person, since a rational person, even a disbeliever, does not accept lying, neither from himself nor from others. God, exalted is He, turned away from their statement. The meaning: the Messenger is not as you attribute to him at all; rather, you are in the torment of the Fire, or in the torment of this world through what you suffer from the nullification of the law, which is true, and the extinguishing of the light of God, which He will complete.

Since the discourse concerned resurrection, He said: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, thus arranging the torment upon the denial of resurrection. The description of error with "distance" (al-bu'd) was mentioned earlier, and it is among the attributes of places; it was borrowed for the meaning. The meaning of "ba'd" here is that its report, which is associated with it, does not end.

﴿Have they not seen﴾, that is, these disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter, ﴿to what is before them﴾, that is: wherever they turn, for the heaven and the earth have surrounded them, and they cannot pass beyond their extremities or go out from the dominion of God in them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They were blinded, so they did not look." He placed between the fā' and the hamzah a verb to which the conjunction could be connected. This differs from what the grammarians hold, namely that there is no omitted element between them, and that the fā' is a conjunction to what precedes the interrogative hamzah, and that the estimated form is "fa-a-lam," but since the interrogative hamzah has the right of initial position, it was placed first. Al-Zamakhshari returned to the view of the grammarians on this matter, and we have refuted this view in what we wrote in Sharh al-Tashil. God, exalted is He, made them stand before His overwhelming power and warned them that it encompasses them, as a means of destroying them. There was a omitted circumstantial clause (ḥāl) here, meaning: "Do they not see to what surrounds them of heaven and earth, subdued under Our power, which We dispose of as We wish?" ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾, as We did with Qarun, ﴿or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾, as We did with the people of the Shade (ash-Shadhah). Or: ﴿Have they not seen to what is before them and what is behind them﴾, encompassing them, while they are subdued under Our power? ﴿Indeed in that﴾, the looking at the heaven and the earth, the reflecting upon them, and what they indicate of God's power, ﴿is a sign (la-āyah), a clear indication and evidence, ﴿for every servant who turns back (munīb)﴾, who returns to his Lord and obeys Him. Mujahid said: "humbled (mukhbit)." Al-Dahhak said: "upright (mustaqīm)." Abu Rawq said: "sincere in monotheism (mukhliṣ fī al-tawḥīd)." Qatada said: "turning to his Lord with his heart (muqbil)," because the one who turns back does not fail to reflect upon God's signs, that He is capable of everything, including resurrection and His punishment of whoever disbelieves in Him.

The majority read ﴿in nashā' nakhsif﴾ [if We will, We shall cause to swallow] and ﴿nusqit﴾ [cause to fall] with nūn in all three. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, al-A'mash, and Ibn Mutarrif read them with yā' in all three. Al-Kisa'i assimilated the fā' into the bā' in "nakhsif bihim" [We cause them to be swallowed]. Abu 'Ali said: this is not permissible, because the bā' is weaker in sound than the fā', so the fā' is not assimilated into it, although the bā' may be assimilated into the fā', as in "ḍaraba Fulānan" [he struck so-and-so]. This is also where the bā' is assimilated into the mīm, as in your saying "iḍrib Mālikan" [strike Malik], but the mīm is not assimilated into the bā', as in your saying "iḍmum bik" [gather with you], because the bā' is lowered from the mīm by the lack of the nasalization (ghunnah) that is in the mīm.

[p. 261] Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Kisa'i read 'nakhsif bihim' with assimilation, but it is not strong." End of quotation. The recitation is a practice transmitted from the Prophet's Companions and followers (sunnah muttaba'ah), and in it there is what is eloquent and what is more eloquent, and all of that is from God's facilitation of the Qur'an for remembrance. So no attention is given to the saying of Abu 'Ali or of al-Zamakhshari.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 34, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2)**

(Surat Saba' has fifty-four verses and is Makki.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to whom praise belongs in the Hereafter. He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. He is the Most Merciful, the Most Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you, the Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight is hidden in the heavens or on the earth, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Book."﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds. For those there is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿But those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, for them is a painful punishment of wretched kind.﴾ ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Shall we show you a man who will tell you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation?" ﴾ ﴿Has he fabricated a lie against God, or is there madness in him?" Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the sky and the earth? If We willed, We could cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them. Surely in that is a sign for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾

(p. 257) This surah: al-Tahrir says it is Makki by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is Makki except for His words, ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾. A group said it is Madani concerning those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like. End of quote. The occasion of its revelation is that Abu Sufyan said to the disbelievers of Makkah, when they heard ﴿That God may punish the hypocrite men and women and the polytheist men and women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]: "Muhammad threatens us with punishment after we die, and frightens us with resurrection. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the Hour will never come to us, and we will not be raised." Then God said: "Say, O Muhammad, ﴿Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected﴾" [al-Taghabun: 7]. This is related by Muqatil. The rest of the surah is a warning and threat to them. Whoever mentions this occasion of revelation shows the connection between this surah and the one before it.

﴿All praise is due to God﴾: it encompasses all kinds of praise.

﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾: its apparent meaning is comprehensiveness. Since the blessing of the Hereafter is something reported, not seen by us in this world, He mentioned it so that its blessings may be measured by the blessings of this world, by analogy of the unseen to the seen, even though they differ in excellence and permanence. It is also said that the "al-" (the definite article) is for a known reference, pointing to His words: ﴿And their last prayer will be, "All praise is due to God"﴾ [Yunus: 10], or to His words: ﴿And they will say, "All praise is due to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Al-Zamakhshari said: The difference between the two praises is that praise is obligatory in this world, because He is the one who bestows His blessings, and it is the way to attaining the blessing of the Hereafter, which is reward. The praise of the Hereafter is not obligatory, because it is for a blessing whose connection to its deserving recipient is obligatory; it is rather the completion of the joy of the believers and the fulfilment of their delight, which they enjoy. End of quote, with some summarising.

﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾: of water. Al-Kalbi said: of the dead and of buried treasures.

﴿And what comes out of it﴾: of plants. Al-Kalbi said: of the precious substances of minerals.

﴿And what descends from the sky﴾: of rain, snow, hail, lightning, provision, and angels.

﴿And what ascends into it﴾: of the deeds of creatures. Al-Kalbi said: and what descends of the angels. It is also said: of decrees, states, supplications, and deeds. It is also said: of livestock and gifts. 'Ali and al-Sulami read: ﴿wa ma yunzalu﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn and a shadda on the zāy, meaning: God, exalted is He.

(Bala) is an answer to the earlier negation in their words ﴿The Hour will not come to us﴾, meaning: Yes, it will surely come to you. The majority read ﴿la-ta'tiyannakum﴾ with the feminine tā' (ta'tiyannakum), meaning: the Hour whose coming you denied. Talq, from his shaykhs, read it with the masculine yā' of the third person (la-ya'tiyannakum), meaning: the Resurrection will surely come to you, because their intended denial of the Hour was that they would not be raised. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it refers to the Hour, meaning "the Day," or it is attributed to God, meaning: the command of the Knower of the unseen will surely come to you, as in His words: ﴿Or your Lord comes﴾ [al-An'am: 158], meaning: His command. It is unlikely that the pronoun refers to the Hour, because it is treated as masculine, which is only found in poetry, such as the verse:

"Nor a land more sprouting in its growth..."

Then He emphasised the answer with an oath concerning the Resurrection, and followed the oath with His words ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ and what follows, so that it is known that the growing of plants is from the unseen which He alone possesses. The oath with His words ﴿by my Lord﴾ is attributed to the Messenger ﷺ, to indicate the intensity of the oath, since He did not use the shared name that both He and those who denied the Hour have in common, which is the word "God."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ruways, Salam, al-Jahdari and Qa'nab read ﴿'Ālimu﴾ with a ḍamma, as a nominative by supposing a pronoun, "huwa." Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿does not escape﴾. Al-Hawfi said: or its predicate is omitted, meaning: the Knower of the unseen is He. The remaining seven read ﴿'Ālimi﴾ with a kasra as a genitive. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' said: this is in apposition (badal). Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be an adjective (sifa), meaning that ('Ālim al-Ghayb) may be definite, and similarly everything that is attached to a definite noun, which in itself does not become definite by that means, may become definite through the genitive construction, except the adjectival noun (al-sifa al-mushabbaha), which does not become definite through an annexation. Sibawayh mentioned this in his book, and few know it.

Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿'Allāmi﴾ as an intensive form with a kasra. The reading of ﴿yaʿzubu﴾ was discussed in Yunus.

The majority read ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾ with a ḍamma on both rā's, and it is possible that it is coordinated with ﴿mithqāl﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], or that it is a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾. According to the first possibility, ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾ is an emphasis for what the negation in ﴿does not escape﴾ contains, and its implied sense is: but it is in a clear Book. This is a metaphor for the controlling and safeguarding of a thing, as if it were in a book, though there is no literal book. According to the second analysis, the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Al-A'mash and Qatada read the rā's with a fatḥa. Ibn 'Atiyya said: coordinated with (dharra), an atom. It is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr, and he attributed it also to Nafi'. What Ibn 'Atiyya said is not necessarily the only possibility: rather, "lā" may be for the negation of the genus, and the subject is the whole of "lā" with what is constructed with it according to the view of Sibawayh, and the predicate is ﴿but it is in a clear Book﴾. This is coordination of sentences, not coordination of single words, as Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Al-Zamakhshari said, answering the question of one who asks: Is it permissible to coordinate ﴿nor anything smaller﴾ with ﴿mithqal﴾, and to coordinate ﴿nor anything smaller﴾ with (dharra)? I say: the particle of exception refuses that, unless you make the pronoun in ("'anhu") refer to the unseen, and make the unseen a noun for the hidden things before they are written in the Tablet, because their being recorded on the Tablet is a kind of emergence from concealment, in the sense that nothing separates from the unseen or departs from it except as written in the Tablet. End of quote. This interpretation is not needed if we take the Clear Book to be something other than the Preserved Tablet. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾ with a kasra on the two rā's, as if he intended an omitted genitive complement, the implied meaning being: nor smaller than it, nor greater than it. ("Min dhālika") is not connected to the elative (af'al), but is an explanatory element, because when the genitive complement is omitted, the word becomes ambiguous, so it is clarified by "min dhālika," meaning: "in respect of that." "Min" has come with an elative (af'al al-tafdil) that is annexed, in the verse of the poet:

"We, in planting the young palms, are more knowledgeable of us
than we are in the racing of the horses in the darkness."

This was interpreted as meaning "knowledge concerning us," where he annexed while intending to drop the annexed noun. So Zayd's reading admits this other interpretation: that when he annexed the elatives smaller and greater according to their case endings during annexation. All of this is an interpretation of irregularity (shudhudh). What suits the description of Him as "Knower of the unseen" is that nothing of the hidden things escapes His knowledge, so the time of the coming of the Hour is included in that, and this becomes evidence for the truth of what He swore to, because whoever knows all things entirely and in their parts, and whose power is established, is able to restore what has perished of all spirits and bodies. It is said: His words ﴿not an atom's weight in the heavens﴾ indicate His knowledge of the spirits, and ﴿nor on the earth﴾ indicates His knowledge of things. Just as He brought them both from non-existence into existence at first, so He will restore them a second time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the oath, in the sense of an oath, be an appropriate justification for what they denied? I say: this would be so if He had confined Himself to the oath and not followed it with the decisive argument, which is His words ﴿that He may reward﴾. God has placed in intellects and fixed in natures the necessity of recompense: the doer of good must have a reward, and the doer of evil must have a punishment. End of quote. The question contains some abbreviation, and there is in it a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

The apparent sense is that His words ﴿that He may reward﴾ are connected to ﴿does not escape﴾. It is also said that they are connected to ﴿will surely come to you﴾, and it is also said that they are connected to the operative element in ﴿in a clear Book﴾, meaning: except as established in a clear Book so that He may reward.

The majority read ﴿mu'jizīn﴾ (with a light form), and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Jahdari and Abu al-Simak read it with a doubled ʿayn (mu'ajjizīn), which was discussed in al-Hajj. The meaning: making God's power unable in their assumption. Ibn al-Zubayr said: its meaning is discouraging those who wish to believe from belief, making them incapable of enthusiasm for it, and this is their striving against the signs, meaning: concerning the matter of the signs. Qatada said: competing, supposing that they will outstrip us. Ikrima said: opposing. Ibn Zayd said: striving to nullify them.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿painful﴾ here and in al-Jathiyah with a ḍamma as an adjective of the punishment (al-'adhab), and the remaining seven with a kasra as an adjective of the wretched kind (al-rijz). Al-rijz means the evil punishment. The apparent sense is that His words ﴿And those who strove﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is in the second clause, which is ﴿those﴾ (ula'ika). It is also said that it is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿those who believed﴾, meaning: and that He may reward those who strove. It is possible that the two clauses introduced by ﴿those﴾ are the very reward and punishment. It is also possible that they are resumptive clauses, and the reward and punishment are what they contain of what is greater, such as God's eternal pleasure with the believer and His eternal wrath with the sinner.

Al-'Utbi said: The apparent sense is that His words ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ is a resumptive statement about those who were given knowledge, who know that the Qur'an sent down to you is the truth. It is also said: ﴿and see﴾ is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿that He may reward﴾, as said by al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi. The disagreement concerning ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ in that place where this surah was revealed has been discussed. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning, and that those possessing knowledge may know, at the coming of the Hour, that it is the truth, with a knowledge that cannot be increased upon by agreement, and they may argue with it against those who disbelieved and turned away. It is also permissible that he means: and that whoever among the righteous did not believe may know that it is the truth, so that his grief and distress increase. End of quote. He said "at the coming of the Hour" because he connected ﴿that He may reward﴾ to ﴿you will surely come﴾, so he based the interpretation on that.

The majority read ﴿al-Haqqa﴾ (the truth) with a fatḥa, as a second object of "yarā" (see), and the intervening pronoun is a separator (fasl). Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a ḍamma, making (huwa) a subject and (al-haqq) its predicate, and the clause is in the position of the second object of "yarā." This is the dialect of the Tamim, who make what is a separator for others into a subject, as said by Abu 'Umar al-Jarmi.

The apparent sense is that the subject of "yahdi" (guides) is the pronoun referring to ﴿what has been sent down﴾, which is the Qur'an, and this is a resumptive statement. It is said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the implied "wa huwa yahdi" (and He guides). It is possible that it is coordinated with ﴿al-haqq﴾, the verb being coordinated with the noun, as in His words ﴿ṣāffātin wa yaqbiḍna﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning: spreading and gripping. Likewise the noun is coordinated with the verb in the words of the poet:

"Then I found him one day destroying his enemy,
and a sea of giving, overwhelming the crossings."

Here "wa bahra 'aṭā'in" (and a sea of giving) is coordinated with "yubīru" (destroys). It is also said: the subject of "yahdi" is a pronoun referring to God, and this is far-fetched.

And those who disbelieved said: they are the Quraysh. Some of them said to others, in a manner of wonder and mockery, as a man says to someone he wants to amaze: "Shall I tell you of a strange and rare story?" Since resurrection was impossible in their view, they placed the one who reports its occurrence among those who are wondered at. They used his name, peace be upon him, in its indefinite form in the words: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man?﴾ His name was the most famous proper name among the Quraysh, and indeed in the world, and his report of resurrection was the most famous report. They presented this in the manner of mockery and of amusing themselves with some riddles made for diversion and obscuring, so they made his name indefinite for this reason.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ [will inform you] with a hamzah. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it by replacing the hamzah with a pure yā'. Al-Zamakhshari related from him: "yunbi'ukum," with a hamzah, from anba'a. The answer to "idhā" [when] is omitted, its estimated form being "tub'athūn" [you will be resurrected], and it was omitted because what follows indicates it. According to the majority, the governing element of "idhā" is what follows it. Al-Zajjaj said this, and he also said, together with al-Nahhas, that the governing element is ﴿muzziqtum﴾ [you are torn apart]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an error and a corruption of the meaning. It is not an error, nor a corruption of the meaning. The conditional "idhā" is one whose governing element is disputed, and I have shown in my commentary on Sharh al-Tashil [Commentary on al-Tashil] that the correct view is that the verb of the condition governs it, like the rest of the conditional particles. The conditional clause may be governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, since it has the sense of "says to you": ﴿When you are completely torn apart﴾, then he emphasized this with his saying: ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾. It may also be that ﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾ is governed by ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾, and ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ takes two objects. Were it not for the lām in the predicate of inna, it would be open (fatḥah), and the clause would stand in place of the two objects. On this reading the conditional clause is a parenthetical (i'tirāḍ) clause. Some people prohibited the suspension (ta'līq) in the verbs of knowing, such as i'lam, but the correct view is that it is permissible. The poet said:

*Beware, for you have been informed that you are the one*
*Who will be repaid for what you strive, and will be happy or wretched.*

[p. 260] "Muzzaq" [torn] is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came in the pattern of the passive participle, according to the analogy of the verbal noun of every verb of more than three letters, as in his saying:

*Do you not know that I release the rhymes (musarrāḥī al-qawāfī),*
*Without incapacity regarding them, nor forced?*

That is: my releasing (tasrīḥī) the rhymes. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an adverb of place, meaning: "when you are torn apart in a place of the graves, the bellies of birds and beasts, and what the floods carried off in every direction, and what the winds scattered and cast to every place." End of quotation. "Jadīd" [new] according to the Basrans has the sense of the active participle, as you say: "jadda, fa-huwa jādd wa-jadīd" [he was new, so he is new]. According to the Kufans it has the sense of the passive participle, from "jaddahu" [he cut it] when he cut it.

The apparent meaning is that his saying ﴿Has he invented against God a lie﴾ is from some of them to others, meaning: he is a fabricator ﴿against God a lie﴾ concerning what is attributed to Him regarding the matter of resurrection. ﴿Or is there madness in him﴾, which makes him imagine that and cast it upon his tongue? They placed invention and madness in equal balance, because this statement, in their view, could only come from one of these two: if he believed the opposite of what he brought, he is a fabricator; and if he does not believe it, he is mad. It may also be that it is from the words of the hearer who answered the one who said ﴿Shall we direct you﴾; he wavered between the two matters and did not affirm either, since he permitted this and permitted that, and did not affirm that it was pure fabrication. This was to avoid attributing a lie definitively to a rational person, since a rational person, even a disbeliever, does not accept lying, neither from himself nor from others. God, exalted is He, turned away from their statement. The meaning: the Messenger is not as you attribute to him at all; rather, you are in the torment of the Fire, or in the torment of this world through what you suffer from the nullification of the law, which is true, and the extinguishing of the light of God, which He will complete.

Since the discourse concerned resurrection, He said: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, thus arranging the torment upon the denial of resurrection. The description of error with "distance" (al-bu'd) was mentioned earlier, and it is among the attributes of places; it was borrowed for the meaning. The meaning of "ba'd" here is that its report, which is associated with it, does not end.

﴿Have they not seen﴾, that is, these disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter, ﴿to what is before them﴾, that is: wherever they turn, for the heaven and the earth have surrounded them, and they cannot pass beyond their extremities or go out from the dominion of God in them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They were blinded, so they did not look." He placed between the fā' and the hamzah a verb to which the conjunction could be connected. This differs from what the grammarians hold, namely that there is no omitted element between them, and that the fā' is a conjunction to what precedes the interrogative hamzah, and that the estimated form is "fa-a-lam," but since the interrogative hamzah has the right of initial position, it was placed first. Al-Zamakhshari returned to the view of the grammarians on this matter, and we have refuted this view in what we wrote in Sharh al-Tashil. God, exalted is He, made them stand before His overwhelming power and warned them that it encompasses them, as a means of destroying them. There was a omitted circumstantial clause (ḥāl) here, meaning: "Do they not see to what surrounds them of heaven and earth, subdued under Our power, which We dispose of as We wish?" ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾, as We did with Qarun, ﴿or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾, as We did with the people of the Shade (ash-Shadhah). Or: ﴿Have they not seen to what is before them and what is behind them﴾, encompassing them, while they are subdued under Our power? ﴿Indeed in that﴾, the looking at the heaven and the earth, the reflecting upon them, and what they indicate of God's power, ﴿is a sign (la-āyah), a clear indication and evidence, ﴿for every servant who turns back (munīb)﴾, who returns to his Lord and obeys Him. Mujahid said: "humbled (mukhbit)." Al-Dahhak said: "upright (mustaqīm)." Abu Rawq said: "sincere in monotheism (mukhliṣ fī al-tawḥīd)." Qatada said: "turning to his Lord with his heart (muqbil)," because the one who turns back does not fail to reflect upon God's signs, that He is capable of everything, including resurrection and His punishment of whoever disbelieves in Him.

The majority read ﴿in nashā' nakhsif﴾ [if We will, We shall cause to swallow] and ﴿nusqit﴾ [cause to fall] with nūn in all three. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, al-A'mash, and Ibn Mutarrif read them with yā' in all three. Al-Kisa'i assimilated the fā' into the bā' in "nakhsif bihim" [We cause them to be swallowed]. Abu 'Ali said: this is not permissible, because the bā' is weaker in sound than the fā', so the fā' is not assimilated into it, although the bā' may be assimilated into the fā', as in "ḍaraba Fulānan" [he struck so-and-so]. This is also where the bā' is assimilated into the mīm, as in your saying "iḍrib Mālikan" [strike Malik], but the mīm is not assimilated into the bā', as in your saying "iḍmum bik" [gather with you], because the bā' is lowered from the mīm by the lack of the nasalization (ghunnah) that is in the mīm.

[p. 261] Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Kisa'i read 'nakhsif bihim' with assimilation, but it is not strong." End of quotation. The recitation is a practice transmitted from the Prophet's Companions and followers (sunnah muttaba'ah), and in it there is what is eloquent and what is more eloquent, and all of that is from God's facilitation of the Qur'an for remembrance. So no attention is given to the saying of Abu 'Ali or of al-Zamakhshari.

**[p. 262]** The connection between the story of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and what precedes it is this: those disbelievers denied the Resurrection because they deemed it impossible. So they were informed of the occurrence of something that is customarily impossible and that they cannot deny, since reports of some of it had spread among them, and their poets mentioned it, as will be mentioned, God willing: the mountains and birds returning in praise with Dawud, the softening of iron, which is the hardest substance, the subjection of the wind to Sulayman, the melting of copper for him, just as He softened iron for his father, and the subjection of the jinn to him for hard labours of his choosing. It has been said: when He mentioned those of His servants who turn back to Him in repentance, He mentioned Dawud among them, as He said: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, and fell down bowing, and turned penitently﴾ [Sad: 24], and He explained what He gave him in return for his repentance, so He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Dawud grace from Us﴾. It has also been said: He mentioned His favour upon Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as an argument concerning what He bestowed upon Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: do not consider this far-fetched, for We have previously favoured Our servants with such and such. When the illustration for Muhammad, peace be upon him, was finished, the illustration returned to them with the case of Saba' and their destruction through disbelief and arrogance. End. The grace that was given to Dawud: the Psalms (al-Zabur), justice in judgment, trust in God, the subjection of the mountains and birds, and the softening of iron, are the opinions given.

﴿Ya jibal﴾ is an implied saying (idmar li-l-qawl). It may be a verbal noun, meaning "We said, O mountains," in which case it is a substitute (badal) for (fadlan). It may be a verb, meaning "We said," in which case it is a substitute for (atayna). It may be a fresh sentence, meaning "We said, O mountains." He treated the mountains as rational beings who obey and submit when commanded, and respond when called, indicating that there is no living thing, inanimate object, speaking or silent, but that it is subject to His will and not resistant to His desire, and as evidence of the might of Lordship and the majesty of Divinity, in that He called the mountains and commanded them.

The majority read ﴿awwibi﴾, from the doubled form of ʾaba yaʾubu, and its meaning is: glorify with him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Muwarrij and Abu Maysara said: awwibi means glorify, in the language of Abyssinia, meaning that he glorifies and it repeats the glorification with him, that is, it echoes the remembrance. The verb was doubled for emphasis, said Ibn ʿAtiyyah. It appears, however, that the doubling is for transitivity, not for emphasis, since the root ʾaba is intransitive, meaning "return," and it was made transitive by doubling, as they explained it by saying: make it return the glorification with him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of the mountains' glorification is that God creates glorification in them, as He created speech in the tree, so that from them is heard what is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for Dawud. It has been said: he used to lament over his sin with a melodic and sorrowful chant, and the mountains would help him in his lament with their echoes, and the birds with their voices. End. His saying, "as He created speech in the tree," means that what Moses heard is something God created in the tree of speech, not that it is God's speech in reality, and this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. As for his saying that the mountains help him in his lament with their echoes, this is nothing, because the echo is not the voice of the mountains in reality, and God called the mountains and commanded them to return with him, whereas the mountains are not commanded to produce an echo, since it is not their act; rather it is one of the effects of the speaker's voice, as the proof establishes.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿awwibi maʿahu﴾ is: travel with him wherever he travels. Ta'wib means travelling in the day. A person would travel by night and then return to travel by day, that is, repeat it. Tamim ibn Muqbil said:

*We overtook a tribe that travelled in the day, after we had raised the sun's rays while the glance was inclining.*

Another said:

*Two days: a day of stopping and gatherings, and a day of journeying to the enemies, returning to it.*

It has been said: awwibi means: move about with him as he moves about. Thus, when he recited the Psalms, the mountains echoed with him, and the birds listened to him, as though they did what he did.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿uwibi﴾, as an imperative from awaba, meaning: make it return with him in the glorification, or in the journeying, according to the two views. The command to the mountains is like the command to a single feminine entity, because the plural of non-rational things permits this, as in: "O horses of God, mount!" and "O Lord, another [time]!" This has also come with all feminine rational beings, as the poet said:

*We left the horses and the cherished camels, and said to the women: stay with them.*

But this is rare. The majority read ﴿wal-tayr﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the place of ﴿ya jibal﴾. Sibawayh said: and Abu ʿAmr said: by supposing a verb implied, the estimate being: and We subjected the birds to him. Al-Kisa'i said: as a conjunction with (fadlan), that is, and the glorification of the birds. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is because it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿahu, the "object with" construction). End. This is not permissible, because before it is maʿahu, and the verb does not take two objects of accompaniment except by substitution or conjunction; just as one cannot say "Zayd came with ʿAmr with Zaynab" except by conjunction, so this is the same.

As-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz, Abu Yahya, Abu Nawfal, Yaʿqub, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, a group of the people of Madinah, and ʿAsim in one narration read ﴿wal-tayru﴾ in the nominative, as a conjunction with the wording of ﴿ya jibal﴾. It has also been said: as a conjunction with the pronoun in ﴿awwibi﴾, and the separation by the adverbial phrase made it permissible. It has also been said: nominative as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, meaning: and the birds return in praise.

As for the softening of iron, Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: it became like wax. Al-Hasan said: like dough, and he would work it without fire. Al-Suddi said: like wet clay, dough and wax, which he shaped as he wished without fire or hammering. It has been said: he was given a power by which iron softens. Muqatil said: he used to finish a coat of mail in part of a day or part of a night, its price being a thousand dirhams. Dawud would disguise himself and ask the people about his condition. An angel came to him in the form of a man and asked him, and he said: an excellent servant, were it not for one defect in him. He said: and what is it? The angel said: he takes his provision from the public treasury; if he ate from the work of his hands, his virtues would be complete. So he prayed to God to teach him a craft and make it easy for him, and He taught him the craft of making coats of mail and softened iron for him, so he prospered, and he would spend a third of his wealth on the interests of the Muslims.

The ﴿an﴾ in ﴿an iʿmal﴾ is verbal (maṣdariyyah, introducing a verbal noun), and it is with the preposition dropped, meaning: We softened it for the work of ﴿sabighat﴾ (full coats of mail). Al-Hawfi and others permitted that it be explanatory (mufassirah), but this is not valid, because a condition of it is that a meaning of saying precede it, and there is no meaning of saying here. Some supposed an implied verb before it so that it could be explanatory, the estimate being: and We commanded him that ʿmal, i.e., work, but there is no necessity that calls for this omitted element. It was also read ﴿sabighat﴾ with the ṣād instead of the sīn, and it has been mentioned that this is a dialectal form, in the verse ﴿and He completed His favours upon you﴾ (wa-asbagha ʿalaykum niʿamahu).

﴿And measure well in the links﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the size of the ring, meaning: do not make them small so that they become weak, and the coat does not hold in defence, nor large so that the wearer is reached through its gaps. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the rivet, which should be neither so thin that it breaks, nor so thick that it splits, with the letters fa' and qaf. Qatadah said: coats of mail were previously plates which were heavy, and he was the first to make the coat of mail of rings.

The apparent meaning of the command in ﴿Work, O family of Dawud﴾ is addressed to the family of Dawud, even though they have not previously been mentioned. It is also permissible that it be a command to Dawud, which God honoured by addressing him with the plural form.

﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind﴾. Al-Hasan said: Sulayman slaughtered the horses because they distracted him from the afternoon prayer, so God replaced them with something better, and made the wind swift, running by his command. The majority read ﴿al-rīḥa﴾ in the accusative, meaning: and to Sulayman We subjected the wind. Abu Bakr read it in the nominative as a beginning, with the predicate in the prepositional phrase, and the noun ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ would be by omission of a modifier, meaning: the subjection of the wind, or by implying the predicate, meaning: the wind is subjected. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywah and Khalid ibn Ilyas read ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ in the nominative as a plural. Qatadah said: in the morning, it would cover from dawn until near noon a distance of a month's journey, and in the afternoon, from after noon until sunset, a distance of a month's journey. Al-Hasan said: he would leave his place of residence in Syria, intending Tadmur, which the jinn had built with stone slabs and columns, and he would take a noon rest in Istakhr and an evening rest from there, and would spend the night in Kabul in the land of Khurasan. The ghuduww is not the month; rather, there is an omitted modifier, meaning: its morning course, that is, its running in the morning, a distance of a month, and its evening course, that is, its running in the evening, a distance of a month. Here he informed about the evening in relation to the morning by a time period, which is a month, meaning one complete month. The accusative of "shahr" is permissible, but it was not read so, as far as I know. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ghadwatuha wa-rawhatuha on the pattern fa'lah, which denotes a single instance from ghada and raha. Wahb said: Sulayman's residence was at Tadmur, which the jinn had built for him with stone slabs, columns, white and red marble, and in it the poet al-Nabighah says:

*Except Sulayman, to whom God said: "Stand in the wilderness and mark it off from the desert."*
*And the host of the jinn, that I have permitted them to build Tadmur with stone slabs and columns.*

I found verses carved on a rock in the land of Yashkur, bearing witness to one of Sulayman's companions, peace be upon him, and they are:

*We, and there is no power save in God, travel from the lands, from the land of Tadmur.*
*When we travel, our rest is a month's journey, and the morning and evening of another.*
*People whom God honoured with their souls willingly, through the victory of the son of Dawud, the pure prophet.*
*They have in the meanings of religion merit and elevation, and if they are ever described, it is of the best of folk.*
*And if they ride the obedient wind, it hastens, eager, not falling short through its ease.*
*Birds in ranks shade them, and whenever it flutters above them, it does not spread out.*

End of what Wahb related.

﴿And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him﴾. The apparent meaning is that He made for him a spring in its mine flowing like springs of water, as a proof of his prophethood. Qatadah said: he would use it for whatever he wished. From Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi: it was made to flow for him for three days and their nights, and it was in the land of Yemen. Mujahid said: it flowed from Sanaʾa, and copper did not melt for anyone before him, as is narrated, and it used not to melt. A group said: the meaning is that We melted copper for him in the manner that iron softened for Dawud, peace be upon him.

They said: The works were produced by him while he was cold, without fire, and (ʿayn) here means the essence. Others said: No one had melted it before him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by it the copper mine, a spring for him, just as He softened iron for Dawud, so it gushed forth as water gushes from a spring. For this reason He named it "the spring of molten copper" (ʿayn al-qiṭr) after what it became, as in ﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. End of quotation.

﴿Whoever works﴾ may be in the accusative position, meaning: "And We subjected to him from among the jinn whoever works." It may also be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding prepositional phrase, ﴿by the permission of his Lord﴾, in accordance with His saying ﴿and whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yazigh," the imperfect of zāgha, meaning: "and whoever turns away from Our command, which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman." It was also read "yuzigh" with a dammah on the yā' from azāgha, meaning: "and whoever inclines and diverts himself from Our command." ("The punishment of the blaze") is the punishment of the Hereafter, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suddi said: With him was an angel holding a whip of fire, which he would strike him with whenever he disobeyed him, from a place the jinni could not see.

Some of the Batiniyya (esotericists), or those resembling them, have distorted these sentences. They claim that the glorification of the mountains is of the same type as His saying ﴿there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44]; that the subjugation of the wind means that he tamed horses, which are like the wind; and that ﴿its morning journey is a month﴾ means a farsakh (a unit of distance), because one who goes out for pleasure generally does not travel more than a farsakh. The softening of iron and the flowing of molten copper, they say, means extracting their melt by fire and using tools made from them. (These are ta'wilat (allegorical interpretations) that are corrupt.)

﴿And of the jinn﴾: they are men of the children of Adam who were strong, and were likened to them in their strength. This is a corrupt interpretation and a complete departure from what the people of tafsir say concerning the verse, and it is an attempt to limit Divine power. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

"The maḥārīb" (sanctuaries/prayer niches): Mujahid said they are the places of worship (mashāhid), named after one part of them by way of metonymy. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the palaces. Qatada said: both of them. Ibn Zayd said: dwellings. It was also said: what is ascended to by stairs, like upper rooms.

"And statues": images. They were of things other than living beings. Al-Dahhak said: they were statues of living beings, and making them was permissible in that law (sharʿ, the earlier revealed law). Al-Zamakhshari said: they were images of angels, prophets, and righteous people, which were made in the mosques of copper, brass, glass, and marble, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. This is among the matters on which the sharīʿas (revealed laws) may differ, since it is not among the reprehensible acts, like injustice and lying. From Abu al-ʿĀliya: making images was not forbidden at that time, or they were images with their heads removed. End of quotation. In it there is some omission.

It was also said: the statues were talismans (ṭalsamāt, magical charms); he would make a statue of a crocodile, or of a fly, or of a mosquito, and command that the thing represented not exceed that representation, so long as that statue and image are forbidden in our law. The severe warnings against image-makers have been transmitted, and some scholars have an exception for some of them. In the hadith of Sahl ibn Ḥunayf: "Allah has cursed the image-makers," and he (ﷺ) did not make an exception for it.

Makki reported in al-Hidaya (The Guidance) that a people permitted image-making, and al-Nahhas reported it from a people who argued with His saying ﴿and statues﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this. But I do not know of any of the leading scholars of knowledge who permits it.

Another reading: ﴿like cisterns﴾ without the yā', which is the original form, using the kasrah as a sufficient marker and treating the alif and lām as functioning like what replaces them, which is tanwīn (nunation). Just as it is omitted with tanwīn, it is omitted with what replaces it, which is the alif-lām. "Al-rāsiyāt" (the fixed ones) are the ones firmly set upon the cooking stones (athāfī, tripods), so they are not moved or carried because of their size.

The sanctuaries were mentioned before the statues because carvings are typically found in buildings. The large bowls (jifān) were mentioned before the cooking pots (qudūr), because the pots are the instrument of cooking, while the bowls are the instrument of eating, and cooking comes before eating, owing to the arrangement of royal buildings. He intended to show the magnificence of the spread that is laid out in those dwellings. He pointed to the bowls because they are the ones that hold food; the pots are not brought there and are not present there, and for this reason He said ﴿fixed﴾. When He described the bowls, the mind moved to the grandeur of what is cooked in them, so He mentioned the pots for the sake of coherence. Regarding Dawud, He mentioned his occupation with the instruments of war, because he needed to fight enemies; regarding Sulayman, He mentioned the sanctuaries and statues, because he was a king, son of a king, whose father had firmly established his kingdom for him, so his condition was one of peace, since no one could fight against him.

After His saying ﴿that make full coats of mail﴾, and ﴿work, O family of Dawud﴾, and after what the jinn do, He said ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾, indicating that a person should not become absorbed in this world nor turn toward its adornments, and that he must do righteous deeds: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud.﴾

It was also said: the object of "work" is omitted, meaning: "Work the acts of obedience and persist in them as gratitude to your Lord for what He has bestowed upon you." It was said that "gratitude" (shukran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was said it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause), or an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) governed by "work," meaning: "Work a deed which is gratitude," just as the prayer, the fasting, and all acts of worship in themselves are gratitude when they fill its place. It was also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), by implying (taḍmīn, conjugation of meaning) in "work" the sense of "give thanks": "Give thanks to Allah through deeds, in gratitude."

It is reported that the prayer place of the family of Dawud was never empty of someone standing in prayer by night and day, and they would take turns at it. Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to eat barley, and feed his family coarse bread (khushkār) and the poor fine bread (darmak), and he never ate his fill. When he was asked about that, he said: "I fear that if I am satisfied, I will forget the hungry."

"Al-Shakūr" (the very grateful) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha), and it is intended as a genus. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The very grateful" is one who gives thanks for all his states. Al-Suddi said: one who gives thanks for gratitude itself. It was also said: one who sees his inability to give thanks.

This sentence may be addressed to the family of Dawud, which is the apparent meaning, and it may be addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). In it is an admonition and an encouragement to gratitude.

**[p. 262]** The connection between the story of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and what precedes it is this: those disbelievers denied the Resurrection because they deemed it impossible. So they were informed of the occurrence of something that is customarily impossible and that they cannot deny, since reports of some of it had spread among them, and their poets mentioned it, as will be mentioned, God willing: the mountains and birds returning in praise with Dawud, the softening of iron, which is the hardest substance, the subjection of the wind to Sulayman, the melting of copper for him, just as He softened iron for his father, and the subjection of the jinn to him for hard labours of his choosing. It has been said: when He mentioned those of His servants who turn back to Him in repentance, He mentioned Dawud among them, as He said: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, and fell down bowing, and turned penitently﴾ [Sad: 24], and He explained what He gave him in return for his repentance, so He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Dawud grace from Us﴾. It has also been said: He mentioned His favour upon Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as an argument concerning what He bestowed upon Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: do not consider this far-fetched, for We have previously favoured Our servants with such and such. When the illustration for Muhammad, peace be upon him, was finished, the illustration returned to them with the case of Saba' and their destruction through disbelief and arrogance. End. The grace that was given to Dawud: the Psalms (al-Zabur), justice in judgment, trust in God, the subjection of the mountains and birds, and the softening of iron, are the opinions given.

﴿Ya jibal﴾ is an implied saying (idmar li-l-qawl). It may be a verbal noun, meaning "We said, O mountains," in which case it is a substitute (badal) for (fadlan). It may be a verb, meaning "We said," in which case it is a substitute for (atayna). It may be a fresh sentence, meaning "We said, O mountains." He treated the mountains as rational beings who obey and submit when commanded, and respond when called, indicating that there is no living thing, inanimate object, speaking or silent, but that it is subject to His will and not resistant to His desire, and as evidence of the might of Lordship and the majesty of Divinity, in that He called the mountains and commanded them.

The majority read ﴿awwibi﴾, from the doubled form of ʾaba yaʾubu, and its meaning is: glorify with him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Muwarrij and Abu Maysara said: awwibi means glorify, in the language of Abyssinia, meaning that he glorifies and it repeats the glorification with him, that is, it echoes the remembrance. The verb was doubled for emphasis, said Ibn ʿAtiyyah. It appears, however, that the doubling is for transitivity, not for emphasis, since the root ʾaba is intransitive, meaning "return," and it was made transitive by doubling, as they explained it by saying: make it return the glorification with him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of the mountains' glorification is that God creates glorification in them, as He created speech in the tree, so that from them is heard what is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for Dawud. It has been said: he used to lament over his sin with a melodic and sorrowful chant, and the mountains would help him in his lament with their echoes, and the birds with their voices. End. His saying, "as He created speech in the tree," means that what Moses heard is something God created in the tree of speech, not that it is God's speech in reality, and this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. As for his saying that the mountains help him in his lament with their echoes, this is nothing, because the echo is not the voice of the mountains in reality, and God called the mountains and commanded them to return with him, whereas the mountains are not commanded to produce an echo, since it is not their act; rather it is one of the effects of the speaker's voice, as the proof establishes.
