Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿awwibi maʿahu﴾ is: travel with him wherever he travels. Ta'wib means travelling in the day. A person would travel by night and then return to travel by day, that is, repeat it. Tamim ibn Muqbil said:

*We overtook a tribe that travelled in the day, after we had raised the sun's rays while the glance was inclining.*

Another said:

*Two days: a day of stopping and gatherings, and a day of journeying to the enemies, returning to it.*

It has been said: awwibi means: move about with him as he moves about. Thus, when he recited the Psalms, the mountains echoed with him, and the birds listened to him, as though they did what he did.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿uwibi﴾, as an imperative from awaba, meaning: make it return with him in the glorification, or in the journeying, according to the two views. The command to the mountains is like the command to a single feminine entity, because the plural of non-rational things permits this, as in: "O horses of God, mount!" and "O Lord, another [time]!" This has also come with all feminine rational beings, as the poet said:

*We left the horses and the cherished camels, and said to the women: stay with them.*

But this is rare. The majority read ﴿wal-tayr﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the place of ﴿ya jibal﴾. Sibawayh said: and Abu ʿAmr said: by supposing a verb implied, the estimate being: and We subjected the birds to him. Al-Kisa'i said: as a conjunction with (fadlan), that is, and the glorification of the birds. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is because it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿahu, the "object with" construction). End. This is not permissible, because before it is maʿahu, and the verb does not take two objects of accompaniment except by substitution or conjunction; just as one cannot say "Zayd came with ʿAmr with Zaynab" except by conjunction, so this is the same.

As-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz, Abu Yahya, Abu Nawfal, Yaʿqub, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, a group of the people of Madinah, and ʿAsim in one narration read ﴿wal-tayru﴾ in the nominative, as a conjunction with the wording of ﴿ya jibal﴾. It has also been said: as a conjunction with the pronoun in ﴿awwibi﴾, and the separation by the adverbial phrase made it permissible. It has also been said: nominative as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, meaning: and the birds return in praise.

As for the softening of iron, Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: it became like wax. Al-Hasan said: like dough, and he would work it without fire. Al-Suddi said: like wet clay, dough and wax, which he shaped as he wished without fire or hammering. It has been said: he was given a power by which iron softens. Muqatil said: he used to finish a coat of mail in part of a day or part of a night, its price being a thousand dirhams. Dawud would disguise himself and ask the people about his condition. An angel came to him in the form of a man and asked him, and he said: an excellent servant, were it not for one defect in him. He said: and what is it? The angel said: he takes his provision from the public treasury; if he ate from the work of his hands, his virtues would be complete. So he prayed to God to teach him a craft and make it easy for him, and He taught him the craft of making coats of mail and softened iron for him, so he prospered, and he would spend a third of his wealth on the interests of the Muslims.

The ﴿an﴾ in ﴿an iʿmal﴾ is verbal (maṣdariyyah, introducing a verbal noun), and it is with the preposition dropped, meaning: We softened it for the work of ﴿sabighat﴾ (full coats of mail). Al-Hawfi and others permitted that it be explanatory (mufassirah), but this is not valid, because a condition of it is that a meaning of saying precede it, and there is no meaning of saying here. Some supposed an implied verb before it so that it could be explanatory, the estimate being: and We commanded him that ʿmal, i.e., work, but there is no necessity that calls for this omitted element. It was also read ﴿sabighat﴾ with the ṣād instead of the sīn, and it has been mentioned that this is a dialectal form, in the verse ﴿and He completed His favours upon you﴾ (wa-asbagha ʿalaykum niʿamahu).

﴿And measure well in the links﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the size of the ring, meaning: do not make them small so that they become weak, and the coat does not hold in defence, nor large so that the wearer is reached through its gaps. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the rivet, which should be neither so thin that it breaks, nor so thick that it splits, with the letters fa' and qaf. Qatadah said: coats of mail were previously plates which were heavy, and he was the first to make the coat of mail of rings.

The apparent meaning of the command in ﴿Work, O family of Dawud﴾ is addressed to the family of Dawud, even though they have not previously been mentioned. It is also permissible that it be a command to Dawud, which God honoured by addressing him with the plural form.

﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind﴾. Al-Hasan said: Sulayman slaughtered the horses because they distracted him from the afternoon prayer, so God replaced them with something better, and made the wind swift, running by his command. *Except Sulayman, to whom God said: "Stand in the wilderness and mark it off from the desert."*
*And the host of the jinn, that I have permitted them to build Tadmur with stone slabs and columns.*

I found verses carved on a rock in the land of Yashkur, bearing witness to one of Sulayman's companions, peace be upon him, and they are:

*We, and there is no power save in God, travel from the lands, from the land of Tadmur.*
*When we travel, our rest is a month's journey, and the morning and evening of another.*

*And if they ride the obedient wind, it hastens, eager, not falling short through its ease.*
*Birds in ranks shade them, and whenever it flutters above them, it does not spread out.*

End of what Wahb related.

Regarding Dawud, He mentioned his occupation with the instruments of war, because he needed to fight enemies; regarding Sulayman, He mentioned the sanctuaries and statues, because he was a king, son of a king, whose father had firmly established his kingdom for him, so his condition was one of peace, since no one could fight against him.

After His saying ﴿that make full coats of mail﴾, and ﴿work, O family of Dawud﴾, and after what the jinn do, He said ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾, indicating that a person should not become absorbed in this world nor turn toward its adornments, and that he must do righteous deeds: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud.﴾

It was also said: the object of "work" is omitted, meaning: "Work the acts of obedience and persist in them as gratitude to your Lord for what He has bestowed upon you." It was said that "gratitude" (shukran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was said it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause), or an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) governed by "work," meaning: "Work a deed which is gratitude," just as the prayer, the fasting, and all acts of worship in themselves are gratitude when they fill its place. It was also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), by implying (taḍmīn, conjugation of meaning) in "work" the sense of "give thanks": "Give thanks to Allah through deeds, in gratitude."

It is reported that the prayer place of the family of Dawud was never empty of someone standing in prayer by night and day, and they would take turns at it. Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to eat barley, and feed his family coarse bread (khushkār) and the poor fine bread (darmak), and he never ate his fill. When he was asked about that, he said: "I fear that if I am satisfied, I will forget the hungry."

"Al-Shakūr" (the very grateful) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha), and it is intended as a genus. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The very grateful" is one who gives thanks for all his states. Al-Suddi said: one who gives thanks for gratitude itself. It was also said: one who sees his inability to give thanks.

This sentence may be addressed to the family of Dawud, which is the apparent meaning, and it may be addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). In it is an admonition and an encouragement to gratitude.

**[p. 262]** The connection between the story of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and what precedes it is this: those disbelievers denied the Resurrection because they deemed it impossible. So they were informed of the occurrence of something that is customarily impossible and that they cannot deny, since reports of some of it had spread among them, and their poets mentioned it, as will be mentioned, God willing: the mountains and birds returning in praise with Dawud, the softening of iron, which is the hardest substance, the subjection of the wind to Sulayman, the melting of copper for him, just as He softened iron for his father, and the subjection of the jinn to him for hard labours of his choosing. It has been said: when He mentioned those of His servants who turn back to Him in repentance, He mentioned Dawud among them, as He said: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, and fell down bowing, and turned penitently﴾ [Sad: 24], and He explained what He gave him in return for his repentance, so He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Dawud grace from Us﴾. It has also been said: He mentioned His favour upon Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as an argument concerning what He bestowed upon Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: do not consider this far-fetched, for We have previously favoured Our servants with such and such. When the illustration for Muhammad, peace be upon him, was finished, the illustration returned to them with the case of Saba' and their destruction through disbelief and arrogance. End. The grace that was given to Dawud: the Psalms (al-Zabur), justice in judgment, trust in God, the subjection of the mountains and birds, and the softening of iron, are the opinions given.

﴿Ya jibal﴾ is an implied saying (idmar li-l-qawl). It may be a verbal noun, meaning "We said, O mountains," in which case it is a substitute (badal) for (fadlan). It may be a verb, meaning "We said," in which case it is a substitute for (atayna). It may be a fresh sentence, meaning "We said, O mountains." He treated the mountains as rational beings who obey and submit when commanded, and respond when called, indicating that there is no living thing, inanimate object, speaking or silent, but that it is subject to His will and not resistant to His desire, and as evidence of the might of Lordship and the majesty of Divinity, in that He called the mountains and commanded them.

The majority read ﴿awwibi﴾, from the doubled form of ʾaba yaʾubu, and its meaning is: glorify with him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Muwarrij and Abu Maysara said: awwibi means glorify, in the language of Abyssinia, meaning that he glorifies and it repeats the glorification with him, that is, it echoes the remembrance. The verb was doubled for emphasis, said Ibn ʿAtiyyah. It appears, however, that the doubling is for transitivity, not for emphasis, since the root ʾaba is intransitive, meaning "return," and it was made transitive by doubling, as they explained it by saying: make it return the glorification with him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of the mountains' glorification is that God creates glorification in them, as He created speech in the tree, so that from them is heard what is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for Dawud. It has been said: he used to lament over his sin with a melodic and sorrowful chant, and the mountains would help him in his lament with their echoes, and the birds with their voices. End. His saying, "as He created speech in the tree," means that what Moses heard is something God created in the tree of speech, not that it is God's speech in reality, and this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. As for his saying that the mountains help him in his lament with their echoes, this is nothing, because the echo is not the voice of the mountains in reality, and God called the mountains and commanded them to return with him, whereas the mountains are not commanded to produce an echo, since it is not their act; rather it is one of the effects of the speaker's voice, as the proof establishes.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿awwibi maʿahu﴾ is: travel with him wherever he travels. Ta'wib means travelling in the day. A person would travel by night and then return to travel by day, that is, repeat it. Tamim ibn Muqbil said:

*We overtook a tribe that travelled in the day, after we had raised the sun's rays while the glance was inclining.*

Another said:

*Two days: a day of stopping and gatherings, and a day of journeying to the enemies, returning to it.*

It has been said: awwibi means: move about with him as he moves about. Thus, when he recited the Psalms, the mountains echoed with him, and the birds listened to him, as though they did what he did.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿uwibi﴾, as an imperative from awaba, meaning: make it return with him in the glorification, or in the journeying, according to the two views. The command to the mountains is like the command to a single feminine entity, because the plural of non-rational things permits this, as in: "O horses of God, mount!" and "O Lord, another [time]!" This has also come with all feminine rational beings, as the poet said:

*We left the horses and the cherished camels, and said to the women: stay with them.*

But this is rare. The majority read ﴿wal-tayr﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the place of ﴿ya jibal﴾. Sibawayh said: and Abu ʿAmr said: by supposing a verb implied, the estimate being: and We subjected the birds to him. Al-Kisa'i said: as a conjunction with (fadlan), that is, and the glorification of the birds. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is because it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿahu, the "object with" construction). End. This is not permissible, because before it is maʿahu, and the verb does not take two objects of accompaniment except by substitution or conjunction; just as one cannot say "Zayd came with ʿAmr with Zaynab" except by conjunction, so this is the same.

As-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz, Abu Yahya, Abu Nawfal, Yaʿqub, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, a group of the people of Madinah, and ʿAsim in one narration read ﴿wal-tayru﴾ in the nominative, as a conjunction with the wording of ﴿ya jibal﴾. It has also been said: as a conjunction with the pronoun in ﴿awwibi﴾, and the separation by the adverbial phrase made it permissible. It has also been said: nominative as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, meaning: and the birds return in praise.

As for the softening of iron, Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: it became like wax. Al-Hasan said: like dough, and he would work it without fire. Al-Suddi said: like wet clay, dough and wax, which he shaped as he wished without fire or hammering. It has been said: he was given a power by which iron softens. Muqatil said: he used to finish a coat of mail in part of a day or part of a night, its price being a thousand dirhams. Dawud would disguise himself and ask the people about his condition. An angel came to him in the form of a man and asked him, and he said: an excellent servant, were it not for one defect in him. He said: and what is it? The angel said: he takes his provision from the public treasury; if he ate from the work of his hands, his virtues would be complete. So he prayed to God to teach him a craft and make it easy for him, and He taught him the craft of making coats of mail and softened iron for him, so he prospered, and he would spend a third of his wealth on the interests of the Muslims.

The ﴿an﴾ in ﴿an iʿmal﴾ is verbal (maṣdariyyah, introducing a verbal noun), and it is with the preposition dropped, meaning: We softened it for the work of ﴿sabighat﴾ (full coats of mail). Al-Hawfi and others permitted that it be explanatory (mufassirah), but this is not valid, because a condition of it is that a meaning of saying precede it, and there is no meaning of saying here. Some supposed an implied verb before it so that it could be explanatory, the estimate being: and We commanded him that ʿmal, i.e., work, but there is no necessity that calls for this omitted element. It was also read ﴿sabighat﴾ with the ṣād instead of the sīn, and it has been mentioned that this is a dialectal form, in the verse ﴿and He completed His favours upon you﴾ (wa-asbagha ʿalaykum niʿamahu).

﴿And measure well in the links﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the size of the ring, meaning: do not make them small so that they become weak, and the coat does not hold in defence, nor large so that the wearer is reached through its gaps. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the rivet, which should be neither so thin that it breaks, nor so thick that it splits, with the letters fa' and qaf. Qatadah said: coats of mail were previously plates which were heavy, and he was the first to make the coat of mail of rings.

The apparent meaning of the command in ﴿Work, O family of Dawud﴾ is addressed to the family of Dawud, even though they have not previously been mentioned. It is also permissible that it be a command to Dawud, which God honoured by addressing him with the plural form.

﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind﴾. Al-Hasan said: Sulayman slaughtered the horses because they distracted him from the afternoon prayer, so God replaced them with something better, and made the wind swift, running by his command. The majority read ﴿al-rīḥa﴾ in the accusative, meaning: and to Sulayman We subjected the wind. Abu Bakr read it in the nominative as a beginning, with the predicate in the prepositional phrase, and the noun ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ would be by omission of a modifier, meaning: the subjection of the wind, or by implying the predicate, meaning: the wind is subjected. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywah and Khalid ibn Ilyas read ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ in the nominative as a plural. Qatadah said: in the morning, it would cover from dawn until near noon a distance of a month's journey, and in the afternoon, from after noon until sunset, a distance of a month's journey. Al-Hasan said: he would leave his place of residence in Syria, intending Tadmur, which the jinn had built with stone slabs and columns, and he would take a noon rest in Istakhr and an evening rest from there, and would spend the night in Kabul in the land of Khurasan. The ghuduww is not the month; rather, there is an omitted modifier, meaning: its morning course, that is, its running in the morning, a distance of a month, and its evening course, that is, its running in the evening, a distance of a month. Here he informed about the evening in relation to the morning by a time period, which is a month, meaning one complete month. The accusative of "shahr" is permissible, but it was not read so, as far as I know. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ghadwatuha wa-rawhatuha on the pattern fa'lah, which denotes a single instance from ghada and raha. Wahb said: Sulayman's residence was at Tadmur, which the jinn had built for him with stone slabs, columns, white and red marble, and in it the poet al-Nabighah says:

*Except Sulayman, to whom God said: "Stand in the wilderness and mark it off from the desert."*
*And the host of the jinn, that I have permitted them to build Tadmur with stone slabs and columns.*

I found verses carved on a rock in the land of Yashkur, bearing witness to one of Sulayman's companions, peace be upon him, and they are:

*We, and there is no power save in God, travel from the lands, from the land of Tadmur.*
*When we travel, our rest is a month's journey, and the morning and evening of another.*
*People whom God honoured with their souls willingly, through the victory of the son of Dawud, the pure prophet.*
*They have in the meanings of religion merit and elevation, and if they are ever described, it is of the best of folk.*
*And if they ride the obedient wind, it hastens, eager, not falling short through its ease.*
*Birds in ranks shade them, and whenever it flutters above them, it does not spread out.*

End of what Wahb related.

﴿And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him﴾. The apparent meaning is that He made for him a spring in its mine flowing like springs of water, as a proof of his prophethood. Qatadah said: he would use it for whatever he wished. From Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi: it was made to flow for him for three days and their nights, and it was in the land of Yemen. Mujahid said: it flowed from Sanaʾa, and copper did not melt for anyone before him, as is narrated, and it used not to melt. A group said: the meaning is that We melted copper for him in the manner that iron softened for Dawud, peace be upon him.

They said: The works were produced by him while he was cold, without fire, and (ʿayn) here means the essence. Others said: No one had melted it before him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by it the copper mine, a spring for him, just as He softened iron for Dawud, so it gushed forth as water gushes from a spring. For this reason He named it "the spring of molten copper" (ʿayn al-qiṭr) after what it became, as in ﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. End of quotation.

﴿Whoever works﴾ may be in the accusative position, meaning: "And We subjected to him from among the jinn whoever works." It may also be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding prepositional phrase, ﴿by the permission of his Lord﴾, in accordance with His saying ﴿and whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yazigh," the imperfect of zāgha, meaning: "and whoever turns away from Our command, which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman." It was also read "yuzigh" with a dammah on the yā' from azāgha, meaning: "and whoever inclines and diverts himself from Our command." ("The punishment of the blaze") is the punishment of the Hereafter, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suddi said: With him was an angel holding a whip of fire, which he would strike him with whenever he disobeyed him, from a place the jinni could not see.

Some of the Batiniyya (esotericists), or those resembling them, have distorted these sentences. They claim that the glorification of the mountains is of the same type as His saying ﴿there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44]; that the subjugation of the wind means that he tamed horses, which are like the wind; and that ﴿its morning journey is a month﴾ means a farsakh (a unit of distance), because one who goes out for pleasure generally does not travel more than a farsakh. The softening of iron and the flowing of molten copper, they say, means extracting their melt by fire and using tools made from them. (These are ta'wilat (allegorical interpretations) that are corrupt.)

﴿And of the jinn﴾: they are men of the children of Adam who were strong, and were likened to them in their strength. This is a corrupt interpretation and a complete departure from what the people of tafsir say concerning the verse, and it is an attempt to limit Divine power. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

"The maḥārīb" (sanctuaries/prayer niches): Mujahid said they are the places of worship (mashāhid), named after one part of them by way of metonymy. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the palaces. Qatada said: both of them. Ibn Zayd said: dwellings. It was also said: what is ascended to by stairs, like upper rooms.

"And statues": images. They were of things other than living beings. Al-Dahhak said: they were statues of living beings, and making them was permissible in that law (sharʿ, the earlier revealed law). Al-Zamakhshari said: they were images of angels, prophets, and righteous people, which were made in the mosques of copper, brass, glass, and marble, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. This is among the matters on which the sharīʿas (revealed laws) may differ, since it is not among the reprehensible acts, like injustice and lying. From Abu al-ʿĀliya: making images was not forbidden at that time, or they were images with their heads removed. End of quotation. In it there is some omission.

It was also said: the statues were talismans (ṭalsamāt, magical charms); he would make a statue of a crocodile, or of a fly, or of a mosquito, and command that the thing represented not exceed that representation, so long as that statue and image are forbidden in our law. The severe warnings against image-makers have been transmitted, and some scholars have an exception for some of them. In the hadith of Sahl ibn Ḥunayf: "Allah has cursed the image-makers," and he (ﷺ) did not make an exception for it.

Makki reported in al-Hidaya (The Guidance) that a people permitted image-making, and al-Nahhas reported it from a people who argued with His saying ﴿and statues﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this. But I do not know of any of the leading scholars of knowledge who permits it.

Another reading: ﴿like cisterns﴾ without the yā', which is the original form, using the kasrah as a sufficient marker and treating the alif and lām as functioning like what replaces them, which is tanwīn (nunation). Just as it is omitted with tanwīn, it is omitted with what replaces it, which is the alif-lām. "Al-rāsiyāt" (the fixed ones) are the ones firmly set upon the cooking stones (athāfī, tripods), so they are not moved or carried because of their size.

The sanctuaries were mentioned before the statues because carvings are typically found in buildings. The large bowls (jifān) were mentioned before the cooking pots (qudūr), because the pots are the instrument of cooking, while the bowls are the instrument of eating, and cooking comes before eating, owing to the arrangement of royal buildings. He intended to show the magnificence of the spread that is laid out in those dwellings. He pointed to the bowls because they are the ones that hold food; the pots are not brought there and are not present there, and for this reason He said ﴿fixed﴾. When He described the bowls, the mind moved to the grandeur of what is cooked in them, so He mentioned the pots for the sake of coherence. Regarding Dawud, He mentioned his occupation with the instruments of war, because he needed to fight enemies; regarding Sulayman, He mentioned the sanctuaries and statues, because he was a king, son of a king, whose father had firmly established his kingdom for him, so his condition was one of peace, since no one could fight against him.

An angel came to him in the form of a man and asked him, and he said: an excellent servant, were it not for one defect in him. He said: and what is it? The angel said: he takes his provision from the public treasury; if he ate from the work of his hands, his virtues would be complete. So he prayed to God to teach him a craft and make it easy for him, and He taught him the craft of making coats of mail and softened iron for him, so he prospered, and he would spend a third of his wealth on the interests of the Muslims.

The ﴿an﴾ in ﴿an iʿmal﴾ is verbal (maṣdariyyah, introducing a verbal noun), and it is with the preposition dropped, meaning: We softened it for the work of ﴿sabighat﴾ (full coats of mail). Al-Hawfi and others permitted that it be explanatory (mufassirah), but this is not valid, because a condition of it is that a meaning of saying precede it, and there is no meaning of saying here. Some supposed an implied verb before it so that it could be explanatory, the estimate being: and We commanded him that ʿmal, i.e., work, but there is no necessity that calls for this omitted element. It was also read ﴿sabighat﴾ with the ṣād instead of the sīn, and it has been mentioned that this is a dialectal form, in the verse ﴿and He completed His favours upon you﴾ (wa-asbagha ʿalaykum niʿamahu).

﴿And measure well in the links﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the size of the ring, meaning: do not make them small so that they become weak, and the coat does not hold in defence, nor large so that the wearer is reached through its gaps. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the rivet, which should be neither so thin that it breaks, nor so thick that it splits, with the letters fa' and qaf. Qatadah said: coats of mail were previously plates which were heavy, and he was the first to make the coat of mail of rings.

The apparent meaning of the command in ﴿Work, O family of Dawud﴾ is addressed to the family of Dawud, even though they have not previously been mentioned. It is also permissible that it be a command to Dawud, which God honoured by addressing him with the plural form.

﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind﴾. Al-Hasan said: Sulayman slaughtered the horses because they distracted him from the afternoon prayer, so God replaced them with something better, and made the wind swift, running by his command. The majority read ﴿al-rīḥa﴾ in the accusative, meaning: and to Sulayman We subjected the wind. Abu Bakr read it in the nominative as a beginning, with the predicate in the prepositional phrase, and the noun ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ would be by omission of a modifier, meaning: the subjection of the wind, or by implying the predicate, meaning: the wind is subjected. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywah and Khalid ibn Ilyas read ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ in the nominative as a plural. Qatadah said: in the morning, it would cover from dawn until near noon a distance of a month's journey, and in the afternoon, from after noon until sunset, a distance of a month's journey. Al-Hasan said: he would leave his place of residence in Syria, intending Tadmur, which the jinn had built with stone slabs and columns, and he would take a noon rest in Istakhr and an evening rest from there, and would spend the night in Kabul in the land of Khurasan. The ghuduww is not the month; rather, there is an omitted modifier, meaning: its morning course, that is, its running in the morning, a distance of a month, and its evening course, that is, its running in the evening, a distance of a month. Here he informed about the evening in relation to the morning by a time period, which is a month, meaning one complete month. The accusative of "shahr" is permissible, but it was not read so, as far as I know. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ghadwatuha wa-rawhatuha on the pattern fa'lah, which denotes a single instance from ghada and raha. Wahb said: Sulayman's residence was at Tadmur, which the jinn had built for him with stone slabs, columns, white and red marble, and in it the poet al-Nabighah says:

*Except Sulayman, to whom God said: "Stand in the wilderness and mark it off from the desert."*
*And the host of the jinn, that I have permitted them to build Tadmur with stone slabs and columns.*

I found verses carved on a rock in the land of Yashkur, bearing witness to one of Sulayman's companions, peace be upon him, and they are:

*We, and there is no power save in God, travel from the lands, from the land of Tadmur.*
*When we travel, our rest is a month's journey, and the morning and evening of another.*
*People whom God honoured with their souls willingly, through the victory of the son of Dawud, the pure prophet.*
*They have in the meanings of religion merit and elevation, and if they are ever described, it is of the best of folk.*
*And if they ride the obedient wind, it hastens, eager, not falling short through its ease.*
*Birds in ranks shade them, and whenever it flutters above them, it does not spread out.*

End of what Wahb related.

﴿And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him﴾. The apparent meaning is that He made for him a spring in its mine flowing like springs of water, as a proof of his prophethood. Qatadah said: he would use it for whatever he wished. From Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi: it was made to flow for him for three days and their nights, and it was in the land of Yemen. Mujahid said: it flowed from Sanaʾa, and copper did not melt for anyone before him, as is narrated, and it used not to melt. A group said: the meaning is that We melted copper for him in the manner that iron softened for Dawud, peace be upon him.

They said: The works were produced by him while he was cold, without fire, and (ʿayn) here means the essence. Others said: No one had melted it before him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by it the copper mine, a spring for him, just as He softened iron for Dawud, so it gushed forth as water gushes from a spring. For this reason He named it "the spring of molten copper" (ʿayn al-qiṭr) after what it became, as in ﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. End of quotation.

﴿Whoever works﴾ may be in the accusative position, meaning: "And We subjected to him from among the jinn whoever works." It may also be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding prepositional phrase, ﴿by the permission of his Lord﴾, in accordance with His saying ﴿and whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yazigh," the imperfect of zāgha, meaning: "and whoever turns away from Our command, which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman." It was also read "yuzigh" with a dammah on the yā' from azāgha, meaning: "and whoever inclines and diverts himself from Our command." ("The punishment of the blaze") is the punishment of the Hereafter, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suddi said: With him was an angel holding a whip of fire, which he would strike him with whenever he disobeyed him, from a place the jinni could not see.

Some of the Batiniyya (esotericists), or those resembling them, have distorted these sentences. They claim that the glorification of the mountains is of the same type as His saying ﴿there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44]; that the subjugation of the wind means that he tamed horses, which are like the wind; and that ﴿its morning journey is a month﴾ means a farsakh (a unit of distance), because one who goes out for pleasure generally does not travel more than a farsakh. The softening of iron and the flowing of molten copper, they say, means extracting their melt by fire and using tools made from them. (These are ta'wilat (allegorical interpretations) that are corrupt.)

﴿And of the jinn﴾: they are men of the children of Adam who were strong, and were likened to them in their strength. This is a corrupt interpretation and a complete departure from what the people of tafsir say concerning the verse, and it is an attempt to limit Divine power. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

"The maḥārīb" (sanctuaries/prayer niches): Mujahid said they are the places of worship (mashāhid), named after one part of them by way of metonymy. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the palaces. Qatada said: both of them. Ibn Zayd said: dwellings. It was also said: what is ascended to by stairs, like upper rooms.

"And statues": images. They were of things other than living beings. Al-Dahhak said: they were statues of living beings, and making them was permissible in that law (sharʿ, the earlier revealed law). Al-Zamakhshari said: they were images of angels, prophets, and righteous people, which were made in the mosques of copper, brass, glass, and marble, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. This is among the matters on which the sharīʿas (revealed laws) may differ, since it is not among the reprehensible acts, like injustice and lying. From Abu al-ʿĀliya: making images was not forbidden at that time, or they were images with their heads removed. End of quotation. In it there is some omission.

It was also said: the statues were talismans (ṭalsamāt, magical charms); he would make a statue of a crocodile, or of a fly, or of a mosquito, and command that the thing represented not exceed that representation, so long as that statue and image are forbidden in our law. The severe warnings against image-makers have been transmitted, and some scholars have an exception for some of them. In the hadith of Sahl ibn Ḥunayf: "Allah has cursed the image-makers," and he (ﷺ) did not make an exception for it.

Makki reported in al-Hidaya (The Guidance) that a people permitted image-making, and al-Nahhas reported it from a people who argued with His saying ﴿and statues﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this. But I do not know of any of the leading scholars of knowledge who permits it.

Another reading: ﴿like cisterns﴾ without the yā', which is the original form, using the kasrah as a sufficient marker and treating the alif and lām as functioning like what replaces them, which is tanwīn (nunation). Just as it is omitted with tanwīn, it is omitted with what replaces it, which is the alif-lām. "Al-rāsiyāt" (the fixed ones) are the ones firmly set upon the cooking stones (athāfī, tripods), so they are not moved or carried because of their size.

The sanctuaries were mentioned before the statues because carvings are typically found in buildings. The large bowls (jifān) were mentioned before the cooking pots (qudūr), because the pots are the instrument of cooking, while the bowls are the instrument of eating, and cooking comes before eating, owing to the arrangement of royal buildings. He intended to show the magnificence of the spread that is laid out in those dwellings. He pointed to the bowls because they are the ones that hold food; the pots are not brought there and are not present there, and for this reason He said ﴿fixed﴾. When He described the bowls, the mind moved to the grandeur of what is cooked in them, so He mentioned the pots for the sake of coherence. Regarding Dawud, He mentioned his occupation with the instruments of war, because he needed to fight enemies; regarding Sulayman, He mentioned the sanctuaries and statues, because he was a king, son of a king, whose father had firmly established his kingdom for him, so his condition was one of peace, since no one could fight against him.

After His saying ﴿that make full coats of mail﴾, and ﴿work, O family of Dawud﴾, and after what the jinn do, He said ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾, indicating that a person should not become absorbed in this world nor turn toward its adornments, and that he must do righteous deeds: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud.﴾

It was also said: the object of "work" is omitted, meaning: "Work the acts of obedience and persist in them as gratitude to your Lord for what He has bestowed upon you." It was said that "gratitude" (shukran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was said it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause), or an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) governed by "work," meaning: "Work a deed which is gratitude," just as the prayer, the fasting, and all acts of worship in themselves are gratitude when they fill its place. It was also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), by implying (taḍmīn, conjugation of meaning) in "work" the sense of "give thanks": "Give thanks to Allah through deeds, in gratitude."

It is reported that the prayer place of the family of Dawud was never empty of someone standing in prayer by night and day, and they would take turns at it. Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to eat barley, and feed his family coarse bread (khushkār) and the poor fine bread (darmak), and he never ate his fill. When he was asked about that, he said: "I fear that if I am satisfied, I will forget the hungry."

"Al-Shakūr" (the very grateful) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha), and it is intended as a genus. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The very grateful" is one who gives thanks for all his states. Al-Suddi said: one who gives thanks for gratitude itself. It was also said: one who sees his inability to give thanks.

This sentence may be addressed to the family of Dawud, which is the apparent meaning, and it may be addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). In it is an admonition and an encouragement to gratitude.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verse 14:

﴿Then when We decreed death for him﴾: that is, We carried out upon him what We had decreed for him from eternity of death, and brought him forth into the realm of existence. The answer to *lamma* (when) is the affirmative negation (*al-nafy al-mujab*), and this shows that *lamma* is a particle (*harf*), not an adverb of time (*zarf*), contrary to those who claimed otherwise. For if it were an adverb, the answer would be the governing verb together with what it governs, and that verb is negative, and a governing element before it does not govern what comes after it. A parallel to this has already passed for us in Surat Yusuf, in His words ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them anything against God﴾ [Yusuf: 68]. The pronoun in ﴿showed them﴾ refers to the jinn who used to work for him. Solomon had commanded the jinn to build a palace (*sarh*) for him, and they built it for him. He entered it in seclusion, so that for one day of his life he might be free of troubles. A young man came in upon him and said to him: "How did you enter upon me without permission?" He said: "I entered with permission." He said: "And who gave you permission?" He said: "The Lord of this palace." Then he knew that he was the Angel of Death, who had come to seize his soul. He said: "Glory be to God! This is the day in which I sought tranquility (*al-safa*)." The angel said to him: "You sought what has not been created." So he leaned firmly upon his staff, and the angel seized his soul, while the jinn continued working as usual.

Solomon had intended to conceal his death, because a year's work remained to complete the building of the mosque. So he asked God to complete it through the hands of humans and jinn. He would seclude himself for two or three months, and they would say: "He is engaged in devotional seclusion (*yatahannath*)." It is also said that the Angel of Death had informed him that one hour of his life remained. So he summoned the devils, who built the palace for him, and he stood praying while leaning upon his staff, and the angel seized his soul while he was leaning on it. The devils used to gather around his prayer niche (*mihrab*), and none of them could look at him during his prayer without being burned. One of them passed by and did not hear his voice; then he returned and still did not hear it, so he looked and found that he had fallen dead. His age was fifty-three years. He became king after the death of his father when he was thirteen years old. His father had laid the foundations of the building of the mosque on the site of the carpet of Moses, but died before completing it, and he bequeathed it to his son, so he commanded the devils to complete it, and he himself died before its completion.

﴿A creature of the earth eating﴾ is the woodworm (*sus al-khashab*), and it is the termite (*al-arada*). It is also said that it is not the woodworm, because the woodworm is not one of the creatures of the earth; rather, this is an animal of the earth whose nature is to eat wood, and that exists. A group, among them Abu Hatim, said: "*Al-ard* here is a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *aradat al-abwab wal-khashab* (the doors and the wood were eaten by termites), so it is as if he said: the creature of the eating which is in that form." When *al-ard* is a verbal noun, its verb is *aradat al-dabbah al-khashab ta'ruduhu aradan*, and the form is *arida* with a kasra on the *ra*, like *jada'tu anfahu fajida'*. It is said that it is a verbal noun of a verb with a fatha on the middle radical. The reading of Ibn Abbas and al-Abbas ibn al-Fadl is *al-aradu* with a fatha on the *ra*, because the verbal noun of the intransitive form (*fa'ala* in its *mutawa'a* sense) of a verb is on the pattern *fa'al*, like *jada'a anfuhu jad'an* and *akalat al-asnan akalan*, the intransitive of *akaltu*. It is also said that *al-arad* with a fatha on the *ra* is the plural of *aradah*, and this is an instance of the general being attributed to the specific, since "creature" (*dabbah*) is more general than "earth" (*ard*). The reading of the majority is with a sukun on the *ra*, so the obvious meaning is that it is the known earth, though it has previously been mentioned that it is a verbal noun of *aradat al-dabbah al-khashab*. The clause ﴿eating﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning it ate his staff, and it is a concomitant circumstance (*hal musahiba*). It has been mentioned that *minsa'ah* is the staff. It is reported that it was made of carob wood, because he used to worship in Bayt al-Maqdis, and every year a tree would grow for him in his prayer niche, which would inform him of its benefits. He would command that it be uprooted and dispose of its benefits, and it would be planted again so that it might propagate. When his death drew near, a tree grew, and he asked it, and it said: "I am the carob tree. I came out for the ruin of your kingdom." So he knew that his term had come, and he prepared himself, took a staff from it, and called for provisions for a year, while the jinn imagined that he was taking nourishment at night. It is reported that Solomon was in a dome, and he instructed some of his family to conceal his death from humans and jinn for a year, so that the building that had begun in the time of David might be completed. When a year had passed since his death, he fell from the staff. The amount that the termite would eat in one day was examined and measured against it, and it was known that the termite had eaten the staff from him for a year.

Nafi', Abu Amr, and a group read *minsa'atuhu* with an *alif*, and its original form is *minsa'atuhu*, in which the *hamzah* was changed to an *alif* as a non-analogical substitution (*badal ghayr qiyasi*). Abu Amr said: "As for me, I do not pronounce it with *hamzah*, because I do not know a derivation for it. If it is one that is not pronounced with *hamzah*, then I have been cautious, and if it is one that is pronounced with *hamzah*, then it may be permissible for me to omit the *hamzah* in what is pronounced with it." Ibn Dhakwan and a group among them Bakkar, al-Walidan ibn Utbah, and Ibn Muslim read *minsa'atuhu* with a silent *hamzah*, and this is from the removal of motion for lightness (*taskin al-tahrik takhfifan*), and it is not analogical. The grammarians considered this reading weak, because it would require that what precedes the feminine marker be silent, other than the *fa'*. It is said that the analogical form of it is lightening between-between (*takhfif bayn bayn*), and the transmitter did not record it accurately. Harun ibn Musa al-Akhfash al-Dimashqi recited as evidence for the silence of this reading the verse of the rajaz poet:

*A man fallen from wine who rose from his drunkenness, like the standing of an old man on his staff.*

The rest of the Seven read with *hamzah*, with a fatha. It was also read with a fatha on the *mim* and a lightening of the *hamzah* by transposition and deletion, and on the pattern *mafala'ah*: *mansa'ah*. A group, among them Umar ibn Thabit from Ibn Jubayr, read it as a separated preposition and *sa'atihi* with the *ta'* in the genitive, and it is said its meaning is "from his staff." It is called *sa'at al-qaws* (the bow's limb) and *sayatuhu* together, and it is its upper and lower limb. The staff was called *sa'at al-qaws* by way of metaphor, especially if the transmission is sound that he had made it from carob wood before his death, so that when he leaned upon it, and it was as when it was cut from a green tree, it had bent until it became like a bow. Do you not see that when you lean on a green branch, how it bends until its two ends almost meet? It has two dialectal forms: *sa'ah* and *siyah*, as one says *qihah* and *qahah*, and what is omitted from *sa'ah* and *siyah*.

﴿Then when he fell﴾: that is, he fell dead from the staff. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *kharra* refers to Solomon. It is said that he did not die until he was found lying down on a journey, but he was in a building constructed around him, and the termite ate the threshold of the door until the door collapsed, and thus his death was known. Ibn Abbas said: "He died in his place of worship on his bed, having locked the door upon himself, and the termite ate the staff, that is, the threshold of the door, so when he fell, that is, the door." End of quotation.

This has a weakness, because if *minsa'ah* were the threshold, and the pronoun returned to it, the construction would have been *fa-lamma kharrat* with the feminine *ta'*, and the omission of such a *ta'* does not occur except in poetic necessity, and it would not be a case of mentioning the meaning in terms of the return to the meaning, because that is rare. The majority read *tabayyanat* as active, so it may be from *tabayyana* in the sense of *bana* (became manifest), meaning the jinn became manifest, with *al-jinn* as the subject, and *an* and what follows it as a substitution (*badal*) for *al-jinn*. As you say *tabayyana Zayd jahlahu*, meaning the ignorance of Zayd became manifest, so the meaning is: the ignorance of the jinn regarding knowledge of the unseen became manifest to the people, and that what they claimed in that regard is not correct. It may also be from *tabayyana* in the sense of *alima* (knew) and *adraka* (perceived), and the jinn here are the servants of the jinn and their weaklings (*ḍu'afa'uhum*), ﴿that had they known﴾, that is, had their chiefs and great ones known the unseen, as said by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or those who claimed knowledge of the unseen among them came to know their incapacity and that they do not know the unseen, even if they were knowing of their own condition before that. The intention by them is mockery, as one mocks the claimant of falsehood when his argument is refuted and his invalidity becomes clear, as in your saying: Have you come to know that you are a wrongdoer, while you do not know that he has always been manifest in that?" End of quotation. *Tabayyana* comes intransitively in the sense of *bana* and *zahara* (became apparent), and transitively in the sense of *alima*, as is attested in Arabic speech. The poet said:

*It became clear to me that lowliness is humiliation, and that the honor of men is in their tallness.*

Another said:

*O Fatimah, indeed I am dying, so know this, and do not grieve, for all people die.*

That is: so know that, that is, be aware of it. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Sibawayh held that *an* has no place in the grammatical structure; rather, it is merely a measured particle, like *anna* that takes the place of an oath with the verb that means certainty and conviction, because these verbs, namely *tahaqqaqa* (came to be certain), *tayaqqana* (became certain), *alima* (knew), and what is similar to them, take the place of the oath. Therefore *fa-ma labithu* is the answer of the oath, not the answer of *law* (if). According to the first opinions, it is the answer of *law*." In the book of al-Nahhas there is an indication that he reads ﴿tabayyanat al-jinn﴾ with a fatha on *al-jinn*, that is, *tabayyanat al-ins al-jinn* (the humans knew the jinn), and the meaning is that if the jinn knew the unseen, his death would not have been hidden from them, that is, the death of Solomon. It is evident that it was hidden from them by their continuing in service and humble labor while he was dead. Ibn Abbas, as mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh and Ya'qub with a variant from him, read *tubayyinat* as passive, and from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Ali ibn al-Husayn, and al-Dahhak there is a reading at this place that differs from the written text of the Mushaf and from what is transmitted from them, which the exegetes mentioned. We set aside mention of it, following our custom of omitting the transmission of anomalous readings that greatly contradict the written text.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 15–21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There was indeed for Saba' in their dwelling a sign: two gardens on the right and on the left. "Eat from the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him. A good land and a Forgiving Lord."﴾ ﴿But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote-trees.﴾ ﴿That is how We recompensed them for their disbelief. And do We recompense any but the ungrateful?﴾ ﴿And We placed between them and the cities that We had blessed visible cities, and We determined the travel between them: "Travel between them by night and by day in security."﴾ ﴿But they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys longer," and they wronged themselves. So We made them into tales, and We scattered them completely. Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is patient and grateful.﴾ ﴿And Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a group of the believers.﴾ ﴿He had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it. Your Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾

Abu Hayyan said: When the Exalted mentioned the state of those who give thanks for His blessings through the mention of Dawud and Sulayman, He explained the state of those who disbelieve in His blessings through the story of Saba', as an admonition and warning to Quraysh and an alert to what befell those who disbelieved the blessings of Allah. The discussion of Saba' has already occurred in Surat al-Naml. When Bilqis became ruler, her people fought over the water of their valley. So she gave up her kingdom and settled in her palace. They pressed her to return, but she refused. They said, "You must return, or we will kill you." She said to them, "You have no intellect, and you do not obey me." They said, "We will obey you." So she returned to their valley. Whenever they were rained upon, the flood came to them from a distance of three days' journey. So she ordered that it be blocked, and the space between the two mountains was sealed with a dam (masa'a) of rock and bitumen (qar). She held the water back behind the dam and made for it gates, some above others. Behind it she built a basin with twelve outlets, according to the number of their rivers, and the water flowed out for them in equal shares, until what happened between her and Sulayman, peace be upon him, which has been mentioned in Surat al-Naml. It is said that the one who built the dam for them was Himyar, the ancestor of the Yemeni tribes. It is reported from al-Dahhak that they lived in the fatra (interval) between 'Isa and Muhammad. It is said that they had a chief called "the Donkey," who lived in the fatra. When his son died, he raised his head to the sky, spat, and disbelieved. Hence the proverb: "More disbelieving than a donkey," and it is said: "the basin of the belly of a donkey," meaning like the valley of a donkey, when the flood overwhelmed them.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿فِي مَساكِنِهِمْ﴾ (fi masakinihim, "in their dwellings") in the plural. al-Nakha'i, Hamza and Hafs read it in the singular with a fatha on the kaf (maskanihim). al-Kisa'i read it in the singular with a kasra on the kaf (maskinihim), which is also the reading of al-A'mash and 'Alqama. Abu al-Hasan said: the kasra on the kaf is a widespread dialect, the dialect of people today, while the fatha is the dialect of the Hijaz, and it is now rare. al-Farra' said: it is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. Whoever reads the plural, the meaning is clear, since each person has a dwelling. Whoever reads the singular should take it as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "in their living," so that it is not a singular used to mean the plural, since Sibawayh considered that a necessity (darura), as in: "Eat in part of your belly, you will be spared," meaning "your bellies." And the verse of the poet:

"Their necks have been bitten by the hides of buffaloes,"

meaning "hides."

(Ayah) means: a sign, a clear indication of Allah, His power, His bounty, and the obligation to give thanks to Him. Or the story of its people became a sign for themselves, since its inhabitants turned away from giving thanks to Allah for it, so He ruined them and replaced their gardens for them with bitter fruit, tamarisk and athl, as their produce. ﴿جَنَّتانِ﴾ (two gardens) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is two gardens," as al-Zajjaj said; or it is an apposition (badal), as al-Farra' said, saying: it is in the nominative because it explains "sign." Makki and others said this, and Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it without mentioning the basis of his weakening. And some said ﴿جَنَّتانِ﴾ is a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is in His words ﴿عَنْ يَمِينٍ وشِمالٍ﴾ (on the right and on the left), and that is the end of his statement. This is not evident, because it is indefinite, and there is no justification for beginning with it, unless one believes that there is an omitted qualifier, meaning "two gardens belonging to them," or "great two gardens belonging to them, on the right and on the left." On this assumption the sentence is disconnected from what precedes it.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾ in the accusative, with "sign" (ayah) as the subject of "was" and "two gardens" as the predicate. It is said that the reason the two gardens are a sign is the growth of bitter fruit, athl and lote-trees in place of the fruit-bearing trees. Qatada said: their orchards had trees and fruits that delighted people with their shade, and it did not mean two gardens only, but meant on both sides, to the right and to the left. End of quote. al-Zamakhshari said: he meant a group of orchards on the right of their town and another on its left, and each of the two groups, in its closeness and density, is like one garden, as the populated countryside and its orchards are. Or he meant: each man's orchard was on the right and left of his dwelling, as He said: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapes﴾ (Al-Kahf 32). End of quote. Ibn Zayd said: there were no fleas, mosquitoes, or scorpions in it; their clothes were not infested with lice, and their animals did not tire. A woman would walk under the trees with a basket on her head, and it would fill with fruit without her reaching out her hand for anything. Something similar is reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord﴾ is the saying of Allah to them through the tongues of the prophets sent to them. It is reported that this was with faith in Allah. Or it is the saying of the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal) to them, as they saw many blessings and spread-out provisions. This also indicates the completion of the blessing upon them, since no fear or illness prevented them from eating its fruits.

﴿And give thanks to Him﴾ for what He has bestowed upon you. ﴿A good land﴾: that is, of noble soil, pleasant air, abundant in blessings, free from vermin and harms. ﴿And a Forgiving Lord﴾: there is no punishment for enjoying His blessings in this world, and no torment in the Hereafter. This is a complete pleasure, free from immediate and ultimate corruptions. Ruways read ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ وَرَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ with the four words in the accusative. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: "Dwell in a good land and worship a forgiving Lord." al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative as praise (madh).

Since the Exalted mentioned what came from His side of goodness toward them, He mentioned what came from their side in return, saying ﴿فَأعْرَضُوا﴾ (But they turned away), that is, from what their prophets brought to them. They were thirteen prophets, who called them to Allah the Exalted and reminded them of His blessings, but they denied them and said: "We do not know of any blessing from Allah." So He explained how vengeance was taken upon them, as He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed We will take vengeance upon the criminals﴾ (al-Sajda 22). So Allah sent upon them the jurrad, a blind mouse that bred in it and is called the mole (khuld), and it gnawed through the dam bit by bit. He sent a flood into that valley, which carried away that dam. It is reported that it was so great, and the water so abundant, that it filled the space between the two mountains, and it carried away the gardens and many of the people who could not flee. It is reported that when it broke the dam, that was the cause of the gardens drying up, and they were destroyed in this way.

al-Mughira ibn Hakim and Abu Maysara said: al-'Arim in the language of Yemen is the plural of 'arima, which is everything built or raised to hold back water. Ibn Jubayr said: al-'Arim means the embankment (musanna'a) in the language of Abyssinia. al-Akhfash said: it is Arabic, and that structure is called in the language of the Hijaz al-musanna'a, as if they were the dikes and dams. From this meaning is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And in that is an example for the one who takes warning: the ruins of Ma'arib, which al-'Arim has effaced.
A stone dam which Himyar built for them: when its defense surged, it did not shake.
It made the crops and trees grow, with its water abundant, when it was divided.
Then they became scattered; they could not get from it even a drink for a weaned child."

Another poet said:

"And from Saba', for those present, are the ruins, when they built, besides it, the flood of al-'Arim."

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak said: al-'Irim is a name, and that water itself is the one with which the dam was built. End of quote. It is possible that the valley was called by that name because of its proximity to that structure, so it became its proper name. Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-'Arim means "the strong," so it is possible that it is an adjective of the flood, with the noun added to its adjective, and the implied meaning is "the strong flood." Or it is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "the flood of the strong rain from which the flood came," or "the flood of the strong mouse," so al-'Arim is an adjective of the mouse. It is said: al-'Arim is the name of the mouse, and the flood is attributed to it because it was the cause of the ruin of the dam, which the flood carried away, and attribution can occur on the basis of even the slightest connection. 'Urwa ibn al-Ward read, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, al-'Arm, with the ra' sukun, as a lightened form of al-'Arim, like their saying "al-kabd" for "al-kabid" in "fi al-kabid."

When whoever drowned drowned and whoever was saved was saved, they scattered and dispersed until the Arabs made them a proverb, saying: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'," and "the hands of Saba'." It is said: al-Aws and al-Khazraj are among them. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the flood of that valley reached Makka and benefited it, and the flood of al-'Arim was in the possession of Dhu al-Adh'ar ibn Hassan, in the fatra between 'Isa and our Prophet. End of quote.

The letter ba' entered in ﴿بِجَنَّتَيْهِمْ﴾ (for their two gardens) on what is passing away (al-zail), and what was the substitute is put in the accusative, which is ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾ (two gardens), according to the common usage of the Arabic language, although for one who is attributed to knowledge, it is frequent that he understands the reverse, so much so that some said: "If one substituted the letter ḍād for ẓā', his prayer would not be valid." That is an error in the Arabic language. If one substituted ẓā' for ḍād, we have already discussed that in al-Baqara in His words ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ (al-Baqara 108). He called this replacement "two gardens" by way of contrast, because what had bitter fruit, athl and tamarisk is not called a garden, since they are trees from which one hardly benefits. The dual of dhāt came in the sound form, according to the more correct view, when restoring its original radical in the dual, so He said ﴿dhawātā ukul﴾ (two of bearing produce), as He said ﴿dhawātā afnān﴾ (two of many branches) (al-Rahman 48). It is permissible that one does not restore the radical, and says "dhātā" with such-and-such on the form of "dhāt." The disagreement about vowelling the kaf of ukul, with damma or sukun, has already been mentioned.

al-Jumhur read ﴿أُكُلٍ﴾ (ukulin) with tanwin. The ukul is the edible fruit. al-Zamakhshari analysed it as having an omitted modifier, meaning "ukul of khamt," or the ukul was described by khamt, as if it were said "dhawātā ukulin shabaʿin" (two of produce, satisfying). End of quote. Describing with nouns is not a regular pattern, although something of it has come, such as their saying: "I passed by a plain of 'arfaj all of it." Abu 'Ali said: substitution (badal) in this is not good, because khamt is not the same as ukul itself. End of quote. This is permissible according to what al-Zamakhshari said, because a substitute in reality is that omitted noun; when it is omitted, what replaces it takes its case. Abu 'Ali said: the adjective is also like that, meaning not as an adjective of "two gardens", because khamt is a noun, not an adjective. The best view regarding it is that it is an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), as if it clarified that the ukul is this tree and from it. End of quote. This is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, since the condition for explanatory apposition is that it be definite and what precedes it is definite, and they do not permit that in the indefinite from the indefinite except the Kufans; the Basrans refused to take up their view in this matter. Abu 'Amr read ﴿أُكُلِ خَمْطٍ﴾ (ukuli khamtin) with the genitive construction (idafa), meaning "the fruit of khamt." It was read ﴿وَأَثْلًا وَشَيْئًا﴾ with the accusative, transmitted by al-Fadl ibn Ibrahim, as coordinated with ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾. ﴿قَلِيلٍ﴾ (qalil, "few") is an adjective of ﴿سِدْرٍ﴾ (lote-tree). He described it as few because it was the best and most noble of its trees, as al-Hasan said. That refers to what He imposed upon them of destroying their lands, drowning most of them, scattering them throughout the lands, and replacing them with many trees of tasty and delightful fruits by the bitter fruit, athl and lote-trees. Then He mentioned the cause of that, which is their disbelief in Allah and their denial of His blessings.

﴿And do We recompense﴾ with this punishment ﴿any but the ungrateful﴾: that is, the extreme in disbelief. He is recompensed with the like of his deed in measure for measure. As for the believer, his reward is with increase and multiplication. al-Jumhur read it with a damma on the ya' and fatha on the zay, al-Kafur in the nominative. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the nun and kasra on the zay, al-Kafura in the accusative. Muslim ibn Jundub read yujazā in the passive, al-Kafuru in the nominative. The word jaza' is most often used for good, and mujazat for evil, but in their specification each of the two may occupy the position of the other.

(p-272) The phrase ﴿And We made between them and the towns which We had blessed visible towns﴾ comes after His words ﴿and We replaced them﴾. When He mentioned the blessings He had bestowed on them, namely their two gardens, and mentioned their replacement with *al-khamt* (tamarisk), *al-athl* (tamarisk-like trees) and *al-sidr* (lote-trees), He also mentioned the blessing of their connected towns and the replacement of these with deserts and wastelands. His words ﴿And We made﴾ describe their condition before the flood came. Along with the two gardens and the special blessing they had, He had set right the lands adjacent to them, populated them, made them their owners, and arranged travel by bringing the towns close to one another. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "So much so that a traveller from Ma'rib to Syria would spend the night in one town and take his midday rest in another, and would not need to carry provisions."

*Al-qura* (the towns) are cities. The word is also used for a small gathering, which is also called *qarya*. The towns which were blessed are, by the consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of scholars) of the commentators, the lands of Syria. The visible towns are those between Syria and Ma'rib, and they are the small settlements that are the open countryside. End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words. What he mentioned, that the blessed towns are the towns of Syria by consensus, is not as he stated. Mujahid said: they are al-Sarawa. Wahb said: the towns of San'a'. Ibn Jubayr said: the towns of Ma'rib. Ibn 'Abbas said: the towns of Bayt al-Maqdis. Their blessing is the abundance of their trees or their fruits.

As for describing the towns as ﴿visible﴾, Qatadah said: they were connected along the road; they would set out in the morning and rest at midday in one town, and set out in the afternoon and spend the night in another. It was said: every mile had a town with a market, and this was the reason the road was safe. Al-Mubarrad said: *zahira* means elevated, i.e. on the hills and mounds, and this is the most noble of towns. It was also said: *zahira* means that when you left one, the next one became visible to you. It was said: *zahira* means well-known, as one says "this is a *zahir* matter", meaning well-known. It was also said: *zahira* means populated. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: what appears to me is that the meaning of *zahira* is "outside the (main) boundary", so it refers to the small towns that lie on the outskirts of cities; as if by this description he distinguished the small towns from the general towns, which are the cities. The outskirts of cities are what lies outside them in the open wilderness and plains. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "We alighted at the outskirts of a desert", i.e. outside it. His words ﴿visible﴾ mean that they are apparent; people call them by the names *al-badiya* (the desert) and *al-dahiya* (the outlying area). From this is the poet's saying:

"Had a band of Quraysh witnessed me,
Quraysh of al-Bitah, not Quraysh of the outskirts."

He means: those who came out from the valley of Makkah. In a hadith: "And the people of the outskirts came and dwelt in the upper rooms."

﴿And We determined therein the travel﴾. It has been mentioned that the one who set out in the morning would rest at midday in one town, and the one who set out in the afternoon would spend the night in another, until he reached his destination safe from enemies, hunger, thirst and the calamities of travellers. Al-Dahhak said: the measures of the stages were such that the towns were according to their measures. Al-Kalbi said: the measures of the midday rest and the night's stay. Al-Qutaybi said: between every town and the next there was one fixed measure. It was also said: between every two towns was half a day's journey. These sayings are close to one another. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿Travel﴾ are a literal command, spoken through their prophets. Al-Zamakhshari said: there was no speech there, but when they were enabled to travel and its means were made easy for them, it was as if they had been commanded to do so and given permission for it. End of his words. The insertion of the particle *fa* in his words *fa-ka'annahum* is not permissible; the correct form is *ka'annahum*, since it is the predicate of *lakinnahum*. Qatadah said: they would travel a distance of four months in security; even if a man found the killer of his son, he would not harm him; and the traveller would not take provisions or a water-skin, because of the blessings which God had spread out for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Travel therein﴾: if you wish, by night, and if you wish, by day, for the security there does not vary with the changing of times; or, travel therein secure and without fear, even if your journeys there are prolonged and extend over days and nights; or, travel therein your nights and your days for the duration of your lives, for at every moment and time you will encounter nothing there but security. End of his words. He mentioned the nights first, because they are the time when fear is most expected, as if to say: He granted them security by night, so that night would be equal to day in this.

When the period of blessing grew long for them, they became insolent and grew weary of well-being, and they sought to exchange what is lower for what is better, as the Children of Israel had done. They said: if the picking of our fruits were farther away, it would be more appealing and more valuable. So they wished that God would place between them and Syria deserts, so that they might ride their mounts through them and take provisions for the journey. They said ﴿Our Lord, make the distances of our journeys far﴾.

The majority of the Seven Readers read *rabbana* with the accusative (*nasb*) as a vocative, and *ba'id* as an imperative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read the same, except that they doubled the 'ayn. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read *Rabbuna* with the nominative (*raf'*), following a past-tense verb with a doubled 'ayn. Ibn 'Abbas also, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Abu Hatim, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ibn Ya'mar also, Abu Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Salam, and Abu Haywah read it the same way, except that they have an *alif* between the *ba'* and the 'ayn. Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan, brother of al-Husayn, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also, Sufyan ibn Husayn, and Ibn al-Sami'fa' read *rabbana* with the accusative, *Ba'uda* with a *damma* on the 'ayn as a past-tense verb, and *bayna* with the accusative, except Sa'id among them, who put a *damma* on the *nun* of *bayna* and made it the subject. For those who read it with the accusative, the subject is a pronoun referring to the journey, i.e. "let the journey be far between our journeys." Whoever reads *rabbana* as a vocative, if an imperative follows it, that is a sign of their insolence and arrogance; if a past-tense verb follows it, that is a complaint about what had befallen them from the distance of the journeys they had earlier requested. Whoever reads *rabbana* with the nominative, the verb can only be in the past tense, and it is a declarative sentence containing one group's complaint to another about what had befallen them from the distance of the journeys. Whoever reads *ba'id* or *ba''id* with the *alif* and the doubling, then *bayna* is the direct object, because both are transitive verbs, and *bayna* is not an adverb of place. Do you not see how the one who read it in the nominative made it a noun? So likewise when it is in the accusative, and when it is read as *bu'ida* in the passive. Ibn Ya'mar read *bayna safarina* in the singular; the majority read it in the plural.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they said﴾. Al-Kalbi said: it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while they had wronged themselves by denying the messengers.

﴿So We made them into tales﴾, i.e. admonitions and lessons which are spoken of and used as examples. It was also said: nothing of them remained but the tale; had a group of them remained, they would not have become tales.

﴿And We scattered them completely﴾, i.e. a dispersal, which people have made a proverb. Kuthayyir said:

"O Azza, the bounties of Saba', how I was after you,
Since your departure no sight has pleased the eyes."

Qatadah said: We scattered them by distance. Ibn Sallam said: We made them dust which the winds scatter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ghassan in Syria, Anmar in Yathrib, Judham in Tihamah, and al-Azd in Oman. In *al-Tahrir*, it is stated that among them Quda'ah settled in Makkah, Asad in Bahrain, and Khuza'ah in Tihamah. In a hadith it is said that Saba' was the father of ten tribes. When the flood came upon Ma'rib, which was the name of their land, six tribes went off to the right, i.e. they dispersed into the lands of Yemen: Kindah, al-Azd, al-Sifr, Mudhhij, and Anmar, from whom were Bajilah and Khath'am, and a group called Hujayr, which retained the name of the first father. Four tribes went off to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan and Khuza'ah. From these "left-hand" tribes were the sons of Qutaylah, namely the Aws and the Khazraj, and from them also 'Amilah and others.

﴿Indeed, in that are signs﴾, i.e. in the stories of these people there is indeed a sign, i.e. a lesson.

﴿For every patient one, grateful﴾: patient in refraining from sins and steadfast in acts of obedience, grateful for blessings. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the people of Saba' mentioned before. It was said that it refers to the children of Adam. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Talhah, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and the Kufans read ﴿ṣaddaqa﴾ with the doubled *dal*, and *ẓannahu* is in the accusative as the direct object of *ṣaddaqa*, the meaning being: he found his assumption true, i.e. he assumed something and what he assumed came to pass. The rest of the Seven read it with the single *dal*, so *ẓannahu* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: he assumed an assumption; or by dropping the preposition, meaning: in his assumption; or as a direct object, like the saying "I was wrong in my assumption" and "I was right in my assumption". This assumption of his occurred when he said ﴿I will surely mislead them and I will surely lead them astray﴾, and this is something he said as an assumption of his own, so that assumption came true. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Zuhri, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Abu al-Jahjah al-A'rabi, one of the eloquent Arabs, and Bilal ibn Abi Barzah read *Iblisa* in the accusative and *ẓannahu* in the nominative. He ascribed the verb to his assumption, because it was an assumption which became, among the people, a true one, as if his assumption had told the truth and had not been contradicted. 'Abd al-Warith, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read *wa-Iblisu ẓannuhu* with both in the nominative, so *ẓannuhu* is a substitute for *Iblisu*, a substitution of part (*badal ishtimal*).

﴿So they followed him﴾, i.e. in disbelief.

﴿except a group﴾: they are the believers. The *min* is explanatory of the kind, and it cannot be partitive, because that would imply that a group of believers followed Iblis. His words ﴿except a group﴾ indicate a small number, since believers are few compared to disbelievers, as He said: ﴿I will surely take control of his descendants, except a few﴾. ﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e. Iblis had no power over them, i.e. no domination or control through whispering and enticement, and no proof, except the wisdom in distinguishing the believer in the Hereafter from the one who doubts it. He explained the domination by knowledge, and what is meant is what knowledge has related to, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿except that We may know﴾ means "existing", since knowledge precedes everything. End of his words. Ibn Qutaybah said the same, saying: "that We may know" means "as it occurs", as We knew it before its occurrence. Qatadah said: that God may know by it the believer from the unbeliever, as a general and manifest matter by which one deserves punishment or reward. It was said: that Our allies and our party may know. Al-Hasan said: By God, he had no whip and no sword, but he enticed them, and they inclined by his adornment. End of his words, as He said about him: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾ (Ibrahim: 22). Al-Zuhri read *illa liyu'lama* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *lam*, in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: *illa liyu'lama man yu'minu*, with the *ya'*.

﴿And your Lord is, over all things, Guardian﴾. Either it is for emphasis, He used it instead of *hafiz* (guardian), or it means *muhafiz*, like *jalis* and *khalil*. Guarding includes knowledge and power, because whoever does not know a thing and is unable cannot guard it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 15–21 (part 1 of 2):
