End of his words. He mentioned the nights first, because they are the time when fear is most expected, as if to say: He granted them security by night, so that night would be equal to day in this.

When the period of blessing grew long for them, they became insolent and grew weary of well-being, and they sought to exchange what is lower for what is better, as the Children of Israel had done. They said: if the picking of our fruits were farther away, it would be more appealing and more valuable. So they wished that God would place between them and Syria deserts, so that they might ride their mounts through them and take provisions for the journey. They said ﴿Our Lord, make the distances of our journeys far﴾.

The majority of the Seven Readers read *rabbana* with the accusative (*nasb*) as a vocative, and *ba'id* as an imperative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read the same, except that they doubled the 'ayn. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read *Rabbuna* with the nominative (*raf'*), following a past-tense verb with a doubled 'ayn. Ibn 'Abbas also, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Abu Hatim, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ibn Ya'mar also, Abu Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Salam, and Abu Haywah read it the same way, except that they have an *alif* between the *ba'* and the 'ayn. Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan, brother of al-Husayn, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also, Sufyan ibn Husayn, and Ibn al-Sami'fa' read *rabbana* with the accusative, *Ba'uda* with a *damma* on the 'ayn as a past-tense verb, and *bayna* with the accusative, except Sa'id among them, who put a *damma* on the *nun* of *bayna* and made it the subject. For those who read it with the accusative, the subject is a pronoun referring to the journey, i.e. "let the journey be far between our journeys." Whoever reads *rabbana* as a vocative, if an imperative follows it, that is a sign of their insolence and arrogance; if a past-tense verb follows it, that is a complaint about what had befallen them from the distance of the journeys they had earlier requested. Whoever reads *rabbana* with the nominative, the verb can only be in the past tense, and it is a declarative sentence containing one group's complaint to another about what had befallen them from the distance of the journeys. Whoever reads *ba'id* or *ba''id* with the *alif* and the doubling, then *bayna* is the direct object, because both are transitive verbs, and *bayna* is not an adverb of place. Do you not see how the one who read it in the nominative made it a noun? So likewise when it is in the accusative, and when it is read as *bu'ida* in the passive. Ibn Ya'mar read *bayna safarina* in the singular; the majority read it in the plural.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they said﴾. Al-Kalbi said: it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while they had wronged themselves by denying the messengers.

﴿So We made them into tales﴾, i.e. admonitions and lessons which are spoken of and used as examples. It was also said: nothing of them remained but the tale; had a group of them remained, they would not have become tales.

﴿And We scattered them completely﴾, i.e. a dispersal, which people have made a proverb. Kuthayyir said:

"O Azza, the bounties of Saba', how I was after you,
Since your departure no sight has pleased the eyes."

Qatadah said: We scattered them by distance. Ibn Sallam said: We made them dust which the winds scatter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ghassan in Syria, Anmar in Yathrib, Judham in Tihamah, and al-Azd in Oman. In *al-Tahrir*, it is stated that among them Quda'ah settled in Makkah, Asad in Bahrain, and Khuza'ah in Tihamah. In a hadith it is said that Saba' was the father of ten tribes. When the flood came upon Ma'rib, which was the name of their land, six tribes went off to the right, i.e. they dispersed into the lands of Yemen: Kindah, al-Azd, al-Sifr, Mudhhij, and Anmar, from whom were Bajilah and Khath'am, and a group called Hujayr, which retained the name of the first father. Four tribes went off to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan and Khuza'ah. From these "left-hand" tribes were the sons of Qutaylah, namely the Aws and the Khazraj, and from them also 'Amilah and others.

﴿Indeed, in that are signs﴾, i.e. in the stories of these people there is indeed a sign, i.e. a lesson.

﴿For every patient one, grateful﴾: patient in refraining from sins and steadfast in acts of obedience, grateful for blessings. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the people of Saba' mentioned before. It was said that it refers to the children of Adam. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Talhah, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and the Kufans read ﴿ṣaddaqa﴾ with the doubled *dal*, and *ẓannahu* is in the accusative as the direct object of *ṣaddaqa*, the meaning being: he found his assumption true, i.e. he assumed something and what he assumed came to pass. The rest of the Seven read it with the single *dal*, so *ẓannahu* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: he assumed an assumption; or by dropping the preposition, meaning: in his assumption; or as a direct object, like the saying "I was wrong in my assumption" and "I was right in my assumption". This assumption of his occurred when he said ﴿I will surely mislead them and I will surely lead them astray﴾, and this is something he said as an assumption of his own, so that assumption came true. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Zuhri, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Abu al-Jahjah al-A'rabi, one of the eloquent Arabs, and Bilal ibn Abi Barzah read *Iblisa* in the accusative and *ẓannahu* in the nominative. He ascribed the verb to his assumption, because it was an assumption which became, among the people, a true one, as if his assumption had told the truth and had not been contradicted. 'Abd al-Warith, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read *wa-Iblisu ẓannuhu* with both in the nominative, so *ẓannuhu* is a substitute for *Iblisu*, a substitution of part (*badal ishtimal*).

﴿So they followed him﴾, i.e. in disbelief.

﴿except a group﴾: they are the believers. The *min* is explanatory of the kind, and it cannot be partitive, because that would imply that a group of believers followed Iblis. His words ﴿except a group﴾ indicate a small number, since believers are few compared to disbelievers, as He said: ﴿I will surely take control of his descendants, except a few﴾. ﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e. Iblis had no power over them, i.e. no domination or control through whispering and enticement, and no proof, except the wisdom in distinguishing the believer in the Hereafter from the one who doubts it. He explained the domination by knowledge, and what is meant is what knowledge has related to, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿except that We may know﴾ means "existing", since knowledge precedes everything. End of his words. Ibn Qutaybah said the same, saying: "that We may know" means "as it occurs", as We knew it before its occurrence. Qatadah said: that God may know by it the believer from the unbeliever, as a general and manifest matter by which one deserves punishment or reward. It was said: that Our allies and our party may know. Al-Hasan said: By God, he had no whip and no sword, but he enticed them, and they inclined by his adornment. End of his words, as He said about him: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾ (Ibrahim: 22). Al-Zuhri read *illa liyu'lama* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *lam*, in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: *illa liyu'lama man yu'minu*, with the *ya'*.

﴿And your Lord is, over all things, Guardian﴾. Either it is for emphasis, He used it instead of *hafiz* (guardian), or it means *muhafiz*, like *jalis* and *khalil*. Guarding includes knowledge and power, because whoever does not know a thing and is unable cannot guard it.

[p. 275] When he had described the state of the grateful and the state of the disbelievers, and had mentioned Quraysh and those who did not believe among earlier peoples, he returned to addressing them, saying: ﴿Say﴾ (O Muhammad) to the polytheists to whom the example was given through the story of Sheba (Saba'), which is well known among them through transmission in their reports and poetry: ﴿Call upon those you claimed﴾, meaning their objects of worship from among the angels and idols. This is a command to supplicate which is a challenge (ta'jiz) and an establishment of proof (iqamat al-hujjah). It is narrated that this was revealed at the time of the famine that struck Quraysh, meaning: call upon them so that they may remove from you what has befallen you, and turn to them in whatever matter confronts you.

"Zaʿama" (claimed) is one of the verbs that take two objects when it denotes belief (i'tiqadiyyah). The first object is the omitted pronoun referring to "those," and the second is also omitted because the meaning indicates it, and its attribute has taken its place. The estimate is: "those whom you claimed to be gods besides Him." The omission of the second object is made acceptable by the presence of its attribute in its place; were it not for this, it would not be acceptable, since the omission of one of the two objects of ẓanna (to think) and its sisters for brevity (ikhtisar) is disputed. Ibn Malakut prohibited it, while the majority permitted it, though it is rare even so. The second object cannot be "min dunihi" (besides Him), because it is not a complete statement: if you said "they are besides Him," it would not be correct, nor would the clause "they do not possess an atom's weight" (from His words) be acceptable as the second object, because if this attribution were a claim made by them, they would be confessing the truth and speaking it, whereas the intended meaning is that this would be a monotheism from them, and that their gods and objects of worship do not possess anything by their own admission.

Then He informed about their gods that they do not possess an atom's weight, and that is the most insignificant of things; and when ownership of the most insignificant is negated from them, ownership of the greatest is all the more negated. Then He mentioned the place of that atom's weight, which is the heavens and the earth. Then He informed that they have no share (shirk) in the heavens or the earth, thereby negating both kinds of ownership: independent ownership (istibdad) and partnership. Then He negated any assistance from them to Him, exalted is He, in anything He created, by His words: ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Thus He made clear the incapacity of their objects of worship from every direction.

Since there were among the Arabs those who worshipped the angels so that they would intercede for them, He negated that their intercession benefits. The negation extends to intercession itself, meaning: there is no intercession from them that would benefit; the meaning is not that they intercede and their intercession does not benefit, meaning that no intercession at all occurs from their objects of worship. And because their worshippers are disbelievers, if the objects of worship were idols or disbelievers, such as Pharaoh, the negation of intercession from them is evident. If they were angels or others who were worshipped, such as Jesus (peace be upon him), then their intercession, when it occurs, is for a believer.

﴿Except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ is an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent (istithna' mufarragh, i.e., an exception in which the excluded noun is omitted), so the excluded element is omitted, its estimate being: "intercession benefits no one, except for him to whom He has given permission." The phrase "for anyone" may mean the one interceded for, which is the apparent meaning, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean the one interceded for, for whose sake He gave permission that intercession be made on his behalf, while the intercessor is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. It may also mean the intercessor, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean: except for an intercessor to whom He has given permission to intercede, while the one interceded for is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. On this possibility, the "lam" in "adhina lahu" (to whom He has given permission) is the lam of communication (lam al-tabligh), not the lam of cause (lam al-'illah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: One says "the intercession is for Zayd," in the sense that he is the intercessor, just as one says "the generosity is for Zayd," and in the sense that he is the one interceded for, just as one says "the standing is for Zayd." So His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be according to either of these two aspects: meaning, intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom He has given permission from among the intercessors, and granted to him; or intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom permission was given, meaning for the sake of its intercessor; or it is the second lam in your saying "he gave permission to Zayd for ʿAmr," meaning for his sake; as if it were said: "except for the one for whose sake permission was given to the intercessor." This is a subtle aspect, and it is the preferred one. And this is a refutation of their saying: "These are our intercessors with God." End of quotation. He thus made ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent in the sense of states (ahwal), and for this reason he estimated it as "except being" (illa ka'inah); whereas according to what we have established, it is an exception from entities (dhawat).

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The doctrines that lead to polytheism are four. One who says: God created the heavens and made the earth and the earthly things subject to their rule, and we are among the earthly things, so we worship the stars and the celestial angels, and they are our god, and God is their god. This is refuted by His words ﴿they do not possess﴾ ﴿in the heavens﴾, as you admitted, ﴿nor in the earth﴾, contrary to what you claimed. Another says: the heavens are from God in independent authority, and the earthly things are from Him through the mediation of the stars, for He, exalted is He, created the elements and the compounds within them through conjunctions, movements, and risings, so they made partners with God in the earth; and the first group made the earth belong to other than Him. This is refuted by His words ﴿and they have no share in them both﴾, meaning the earth is like the heavens, belonging to God and not to other than Him, and no other has any portion in them both. Another says: compounds and events are from God, but He delegated them to the stars, and the act of one who has been authorized is attributed to the one who gives authority, and withdrawn from the one authorized in it. They made the heavens specific to God, so this is refuted by His words ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Another says: we worship the idols, which are the images of the angels, so that they may intercede for us. This is refuted by His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit﴾, the whole clause.

The "al-" in "al-shafa'ah" (intercession) is apparently for generality, meaning the intercession of all creation. It has been said that it is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning the intercession of the angels whom they claimed to be partners and intercessors. End of quotation, and there is some abridgment in it.

Abu al-Baqa' said: The "lam" in ﴿for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be connected to "intercession," because you say "I interceded for him," and you may connect it to "benefits." End of quotation. This is weak, because the object is placed after the verb, so the entry of the lam upon it is rare.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "udhina" with a dammah on the hamzah; the rest of the seven read it with a fathah, meaning God gave permission to him.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in His words "qulubihim" (their hearts) refers back to what the pronouns of the third person in His words "they do not possess" and "for them" and "for Him from them" refer to, namely the angels whom they took as gods and intercessors. The estimate would then be: "except for him whom He has given permission among them."

[p. 277] "Hatta" (until) indicates a limit (ghayah), but there is no return in the speech indicating that "until" is a limit for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an omission in the speech that the apparent meaning indicates, as if he said: "Nor are they intercessors as you wish, but they are servants or submitters forever," meaning obedient, "until, when fear is removed from their hearts." He said: The reports have been abundantly transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that His words ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ refer only to the angels, when they hear the revelation, meaning Gabriel, and when God commands it they hear it like the dragging of an iron chain over smooth rock, and they are then struck with fear out of reverence and awe. It has also been said: it is fear that the Hour might come; when that fear is removed from their hearts, meaning it is lifted and dispelled from them, some of them say to others, and to Gabriel: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ The ones asked say: He has said ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾. In keeping with this meaning of mentioning the angels at the beginning of the verses, this verse fits the first interpretation; and whoever does not perceive that the angels are referred to from the beginning of His words ﴿those you claimed﴾ will find that this verse is not connected to what precedes it, and therefore the exegetes were confused in interpreting it, to the point that some said, regarding the disbelievers after the arrival of death: "They are struck with fear in their hearts by the loss of life, and they see the reality, and their fear of what is said to them in their lifetime is removed, so they are told at that time: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ and they say: He has said the truth; they confess when confession no longer benefits you." Another group said: the verse concerns the entire world, and His words "until" mean in the Hereafter. The first interpretation regarding the angels is the correct one, and it is the one the reports have abundantly supported, and this (other view) is far-fetched. End of quotation.

If the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ does not refer back to ﴿those you claimed﴾, it refers back to the one to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿and Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20] refers, and the pronoun in "'alayhim" (upon them) refers to all the disbelievers, and "until" is a limit for His words ﴿so they followed him﴾ [Saba': 20]. The striking with fear would then be at the moment of separation from life, or their following of him is made to continue with them until the Day of Resurrection, figuratively.

The clause after His words ﴿Say, call upon﴾ is parenthetical (i'tirad) between the thing limited (al-mughayya) and the limit (al-ghayah). Ibn Zayd said: They acknowledged God when acknowledgment no longer benefited them, so the meaning is: Satan was struck with fear from their hearts, and what he used to seek from them departed from them; ﴿they say: what has your Lord said?﴾. Al-Hasan said: "What has your Lord said?" is said to the polytheists only through the tongues of the prophets, and they acknowledged when it no longer benefited. It has also been said that "until" is a limit connected to His words ﴿you claimed﴾, meaning: you claimed disbelief up to the limit of the striking with fear, then you abandoned what you had claimed and said: "He has said the truth." End of quotation. In that case there is a shift (iltifat) in the speech from the second person in ﴿you claimed﴾ to the third person in ﴿was removed from their hearts﴾.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: When it is proclaimed, they are struck with fear, and their fear continues until the fear is removed from their hearts. Some of the intercessors among the angels say to some of the angels: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ regarding the acceptance of our intercession? Then some answer others: He has said, that is God has said, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning the true word, which is the acceptance of their intercession, if He, exalted is He, has permitted them in that; and He does not grant permission except while He desires the acceptance of the intercession.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what is the saying ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ connected, when there is nothing before it that "until" could be a limit for? I say: it is connected to what is understood from this speech, namely that there is an awaiting of permission, a pause, a delay, and fear on the part of those who hope for intercession and the intercessors: will they be granted permission or not? And that permission is not granted except after a considerable period of time and a long waiting. A similar state is indicated by His words, mighty is He who speaks: [p. 278] ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful; they cannot address Him [with any speech]﴾ [al-Naba': 37], ﴿on the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks; they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is right﴾ [al-Naba': 38]; as if it were said: they wait and pause for a long time, fearful and alarmed.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 22–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Until, when terror is lifted from their hearts﴾, meaning the terror is removed from the hearts of the intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, by a word that the Lord of Might speaks in granting permission. They rejoice at this, and some of them ask others, ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ They reply, ﴿"The truth,"﴾ that is, the true word, which is the permission for intercession for whomever He is pleased with. End of quote.

From this it is concluded that "until" (hatta) indicates a final limit (ghaya), and that this is either:

1. For a stated expression, which is "you claimed" (za'amtum). In this case the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ is an iltifat (a shift from direct address to third person), and it refers to the disbelievers. Or the verb is "they followed him" (fa-ittaba'uhu), and in this there is a consistency of pronouns in the third person singular. The separation by the parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) is also there, and the pronoun likewise refers to the disbelievers. The pronoun in "they said" (qalu) refers to the angels, the pronoun of address in "your Lord" (rabbukum) is addressed to the disbelievers, and the third person in the second "they said" (qalu) refers to the disbelievers.

2. Or it is for an implied element. What Ibn 'Atiyya suggested cannot be correct as a limit, because what follows the limit must be different from what precedes it. They are servants who are always submissive and never depart from that, neither when terror is lifted from their hearts nor when it is not. Applying this to the angels at the time of revelation does not fit the verse. The fact that the Prophet (ﷺ), in the story of the revelation, said, "When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts," does not prove that this verse concerns the angels at the time God speaks the revelation. The hadith was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the dragging of a chain over rock, and they fall down senseless. They remain so until Gabriel, peace be upon him, comes to them. When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts. They say, 'O Gabriel, what has your Lord said?' He says, 'The truth.' Then they call out, 'The truth.'"

What al-Zamakhshari suggested is possible, but in it there is a specification of those whom you claimed besides Him as being the angels, while those who worshipped them include angels and others. There is also a specification of those who were given permission as being the angels, whereas those permitted to intercede include the angels and others. Do you not see what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) related regarding the intercession in His saying, mighty and majestic?

It is also read: ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ with doubled "z", from "fazaʿ" (terror), in the passive voice, meaning the terror is caused to fly away from their hearts. The form "fa''ala" comes with several meanings, among them removal. Here it is like: "qarradtu al-baʿir" (I de-ticked the camel), meaning I removed the ticks from it.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Talha, Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Ibn 'Amir read it in the active voice, also from "fazaʿ". If the pronoun in "from their hearts" refers to the angels, the subject of "fazaʿa" is God. If it refers to the disbelievers, the pronoun refers to those who misled them.

Al-Hasan read ﴿fuziʿa﴾ from "fazaʿ" with a lightened "z", in the passive voice, and ﴿from their hearts﴾ is in the place of a nominative subject for it, like your saying "inṭalaqa Yazid" (Yazid departed).

Al-Hasan also read, as well as Abu al-Mutawakkil, Qatada, and Mujahid: ﴿fazzaʿa﴾ with a doubled "z", in the active voice, from "fazaʿ". Al-Hasan also read the same with a lightened "z". 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan as well, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Qatada also, and Abu Mijlaz read ﴿furrigha﴾ from "faraagh" (emptiness), with doubled "r", in the passive voice.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa read ﴿ifranqa'a﴾ ﴿ʿan qulubihim﴾, meaning it was uncovered from them, and it is said: it dispersed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The word is composed of the letters of separation with the addition of the ʿayn, just as qamtar is composed of the letters of qamt with the addition of the rāʾ." End of quote. If al-Zamakhshari means that the ʿayn is among the letters of augmentation, and likewise the rāʾ, which is the apparent sense of his words, then this is not correct, because the ʿayn and the rāʾ are not among the letters of augmentation. If he means that the word contains letters, and that what they mention as added to those letters, namely the ʿayn and the rāʾ, is like the root of farqaʿa and qamtara, then this is correct. But were it not for the implication of what al-Zamakhshari said about this word, I would not have mentioned this reading, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf).

They also said other things regarding God's saying, ﴿Until, when it is lifted﴾, besides what has preceded. Ka'b said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks, without how, the angels strike their wings and fall down in terror. They say to one another, ﴿'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'The truth.'﴾" It is also said: when Isra'fil calls them from their graves, they reply, saying "What?", and this is from the terror which is the calling and the seeking of help, as Zuhayr said:

*When they are terrified they fly to the one they seek refuge with,*
*tall spears, neither weak nor unarmed.*

(p-279)

It is also said: it is the terror of the angels of the lowest heaven at the descent of the arrangers (al-mudabbirat) to the earth. It is also said: when there was an interval (fatra) between Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ), and God sent Muhammad, God sent Gabriel with the revelation. The angels thought that something of the matter of the Hour had descended, and they were stunned by that. So Gabriel began passing by every heaven, lifting the terror from them and informing them that it was the revelation. This was said by Qatada, Muqatil, and Ibn al-Sa'ib. It is also said: the angels who follow one another (al-muʿaqqibat), who go among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when God sends them down, a loud sound is heard from them, so those below them among the angels think it is something of the matter of the Hour, and they fall prostrate, stunned. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud.

These sayings, and those preceding them, scarcely fit the words of the Qur'an. So I ask God to grant us understanding of His Book. The closest of them to me is that the pronoun in "their hearts" (qulubihim) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "they followed him" (ittaba'uhu) and "upon them" (ʿalayhim) refers, and to some of those who are in doubt about it. The sentence after that is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraD). And the saying "they said" (qalu), that is, the angels, to those followers who are doubtful, asking them a question of reproach: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾, on the tongue of the one who was sent to you after the veil was lifted from their hearts. Then they will acknowledge at that time that what He said, and what His prophets brought, is the truth, not the falsehood in which we were, following Iblis and doubting the resurrection.

"What" (mādhā) may be the object of "said" (qāla), meaning "what thing has your Lord said?" It may also be in the place of a nominative, with "dhā" as a relative pronoun, meaning "what is it that your Lord said?" and "dhā" is its predicate, and the object of "said" is an implied pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿qalu al-ḥaqqu﴾ with "al-ḥaqqu" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: its saying is the truth. ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence and glorification by them.

Then he returned to addressing the disbelievers and asked them about who provides for them, arguing against them that their provider is God, since they cannot say that their gods provide for them, and ask them whether they ﴿possess not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾. He commanded him to take on the task of answering and affirming on their behalf with his saying, ﴿"Say: God"﴾, because they may not answer out of love for obstinacy and preference for polytheism. It is known that there is no answer for them, or for anyone, except to say, "He is God."

﴿"And indeed we"﴾, that is, the monotheists who provide and worship, ﴿"or you"﴾, the polytheists who worship idols and inanimate things.

﴿"Surely we are upon guidance"﴾, that is, a straight path, ﴿"or in clear error"﴾, that is, in obvious and manifest confusion. The meaning is: one of the two parties, us or you, is surely upon one of the two states of guidance or misguidance, and the statement is put in the form of doubt and possibility. It is known that whoever worships God and affirms His oneness is upon guidance, and whoever worships other than Him, whether a stone or something else, is in error. This sentence includes fairness and gentleness in calling to God, and whoever hears it knows that it is a statement of attribution. Refutation by indirect allusion and implication is more eloquent than refutation by explicit statement. Similar to this is the saying of the Arabs: "May God disgrace the liar between me and you," which is said by one who is certain that his companion is the liar. A parallel to it is the saying of the poet:

*So whichever of us and you was the worse, he will be led to humiliation in disgrace.*

And Hassan said:

*Do you satirize him when you are not equal to him? So the worse of you two is the ransom for the better.*

This type is called in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan) istidrāj al-mukhāṭab (drawing the addressee along). One mentions to him a matter which he accepts, even if it is contrary to what is actually the case, until he listens to what is being put to him. For if he began with something he dislikes, he would not listen, and one keeps moving him from state to state until the truth becomes clear to him and he accepts it. Here, when they heard the alternation between him and them, it appeared to them that he was not certain that the truth was with him, so he said to them by way of reasoning: your gods do not possess an atom's weight, and they neither benefit nor harm, because they are inanimate, and you know this. Thus it became certain that the provider for them, and the one who benefits and harms, is God, glorified be He.

It is also said: the meaning of the sentence is to belittle the polytheists and to mock them. They have made clear that their gods provide them with nothing and neither benefit nor harm. So God wanted from His Prophet, and commanded him, to rebuke them, belittle them, and call them liars with a statement that is not explicit, if that is more forceful in belittling them, like your saying: "Surely one of us is a liar," while you know that the person you are addressing is the liar, but you rebuked him with a wording that is not explicit (p-280).

The "or" (aw) here is used in its proper function, to indicate one of two things or several things. The predicate of ﴿"Surely we or you"﴾ is ﴿"upon guidance or in clear error"﴾, and it does not need an omitted element to be posited, since the meaning is: one of us is in one of these two. Like your saying: "Zayd or ʿAmr is in the palace, or in the mosque." This does not need an omitted element to be posited, since its meaning is: one of these two is in one of these two. It is also said: the predicate is omitted. It is said the predicate of "lā" (wa-lahu, a grammatical term) is omitted, and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance or in clear error," so it was omitted because the predicate of what follows indicates it. Thus "upon guidance or in clear error", the affirmed predicate, is a predicate about it (inna), or "you", since it is in the estimate of "we". But because it was omitted, the pronoun was joined. It is also said: it is the predicate of the second, and the estimate is: "Or you, surely upon guidance or in clear error," and it was omitted because the predicate of the first indicates it. This affirmed one is ﴿"surely upon guidance or in clear error"﴾. There is no need for this estimate of omission if what follows "or" is not conjoined by it, as in: "Zayd or ʿAmr is standing." That would need this estimate. And "inna" with what may be a predicate, its subject is conjoined by "or", and the predicate is conjoined by "or", so it does not need it.

Abu ʿUbayda held that "or" has the meaning of "wa" (and), so it is of the category of wrapping and spreading (al-laff wa al-nashr), and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance, and you in clear error," so he informs about each according to what fits it. There is no need to remove "or" from its proper function.

"Upon" (ʿalā) is used with guidance because its holder is one of elevation and firm establishment in what he is upon, acting as he wills. "From" (ʿan) is used with error because he is immersed in confusion, bewildered therein, not knowing where to turn.

[p. 275] When he had described the state of the grateful and the state of the disbelievers, and had mentioned Quraysh and those who did not believe among earlier peoples, he returned to addressing them, saying: ﴿Say﴾ (O Muhammad) to the polytheists to whom the example was given through the story of Sheba (Saba'), which is well known among them through transmission in their reports and poetry: ﴿Call upon those you claimed﴾, meaning their objects of worship from among the angels and idols. This is a command to supplicate which is a challenge (ta'jiz) and an establishment of proof (iqamat al-hujjah). It is narrated that this was revealed at the time of the famine that struck Quraysh, meaning: call upon them so that they may remove from you what has befallen you, and turn to them in whatever matter confronts you.

"Zaʿama" (claimed) is one of the verbs that take two objects when it denotes belief (i'tiqadiyyah). The first object is the omitted pronoun referring to "those," and the second is also omitted because the meaning indicates it, and its attribute has taken its place. The estimate is: "those whom you claimed to be gods besides Him." The omission of the second object is made acceptable by the presence of its attribute in its place; were it not for this, it would not be acceptable, since the omission of one of the two objects of ẓanna (to think) and its sisters for brevity (ikhtisar) is disputed. Ibn Malakut prohibited it, while the majority permitted it, though it is rare even so. The second object cannot be "min dunihi" (besides Him), because it is not a complete statement: if you said "they are besides Him," it would not be correct, nor would the clause "they do not possess an atom's weight" (from His words) be acceptable as the second object, because if this attribution were a claim made by them, they would be confessing the truth and speaking it, whereas the intended meaning is that this would be a monotheism from them, and that their gods and objects of worship do not possess anything by their own admission.

Then He informed about their gods that they do not possess an atom's weight, and that is the most insignificant of things; and when ownership of the most insignificant is negated from them, ownership of the greatest is all the more negated. Then He mentioned the place of that atom's weight, which is the heavens and the earth. Then He informed that they have no share (shirk) in the heavens or the earth, thereby negating both kinds of ownership: independent ownership (istibdad) and partnership. Then He negated any assistance from them to Him, exalted is He, in anything He created, by His words: ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Thus He made clear the incapacity of their objects of worship from every direction.

Since there were among the Arabs those who worshipped the angels so that they would intercede for them, He negated that their intercession benefits. The negation extends to intercession itself, meaning: there is no intercession from them that would benefit; the meaning is not that they intercede and their intercession does not benefit, meaning that no intercession at all occurs from their objects of worship. And because their worshippers are disbelievers, if the objects of worship were idols or disbelievers, such as Pharaoh, the negation of intercession from them is evident. If they were angels or others who were worshipped, such as Jesus (peace be upon him), then their intercession, when it occurs, is for a believer.

﴿Except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ is an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent (istithna' mufarragh, i.e., an exception in which the excluded noun is omitted), so the excluded element is omitted, its estimate being: "intercession benefits no one, except for him to whom He has given permission." The phrase "for anyone" may mean the one interceded for, which is the apparent meaning, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean the one interceded for, for whose sake He gave permission that intercession be made on his behalf, while the intercessor is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. It may also mean the intercessor, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean: except for an intercessor to whom He has given permission to intercede, while the one interceded for is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. On this possibility, the "lam" in "adhina lahu" (to whom He has given permission) is the lam of communication (lam al-tabligh), not the lam of cause (lam al-'illah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: One says "the intercession is for Zayd," in the sense that he is the intercessor, just as one says "the generosity is for Zayd," and in the sense that he is the one interceded for, just as one says "the standing is for Zayd." So His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be according to either of these two aspects: meaning, intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom He has given permission from among the intercessors, and granted to him; or intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom permission was given, meaning for the sake of its intercessor; or it is the second lam in your saying "he gave permission to Zayd for ʿAmr," meaning for his sake; as if it were said: "except for the one for whose sake permission was given to the intercessor." This is a subtle aspect, and it is the preferred one. And this is a refutation of their saying: "These are our intercessors with God." End of quotation. He thus made ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent in the sense of states (ahwal), and for this reason he estimated it as "except being" (illa ka'inah); whereas according to what we have established, it is an exception from entities (dhawat).

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The doctrines that lead to polytheism are four. One who says: God created the heavens and made the earth and the earthly things subject to their rule, and we are among the earthly things, so we worship the stars and the celestial angels, and they are our god, and God is their god. This is refuted by His words ﴿they do not possess﴾ ﴿in the heavens﴾, as you admitted, ﴿nor in the earth﴾, contrary to what you claimed. Another says: the heavens are from God in independent authority, and the earthly things are from Him through the mediation of the stars, for He, exalted is He, created the elements and the compounds within them through conjunctions, movements, and risings, so they made partners with God in the earth; and the first group made the earth belong to other than Him. This is refuted by His words ﴿and they have no share in them both﴾, meaning the earth is like the heavens, belonging to God and not to other than Him, and no other has any portion in them both. Another says: compounds and events are from God, but He delegated them to the stars, and the act of one who has been authorized is attributed to the one who gives authority, and withdrawn from the one authorized in it. They made the heavens specific to God, so this is refuted by His words ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Another says: we worship the idols, which are the images of the angels, so that they may intercede for us. This is refuted by His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit﴾, the whole clause.

The "al-" in "al-shafa'ah" (intercession) is apparently for generality, meaning the intercession of all creation. It has been said that it is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning the intercession of the angels whom they claimed to be partners and intercessors. End of quotation, and there is some abridgment in it.

Abu al-Baqa' said: The "lam" in ﴿for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be connected to "intercession," because you say "I interceded for him," and you may connect it to "benefits." End of quotation. This is weak, because the object is placed after the verb, so the entry of the lam upon it is rare.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "udhina" with a dammah on the hamzah; the rest of the seven read it with a fathah, meaning God gave permission to him.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in His words "qulubihim" (their hearts) refers back to what the pronouns of the third person in His words "they do not possess" and "for them" and "for Him from them" refer to, namely the angels whom they took as gods and intercessors. The estimate would then be: "except for him whom He has given permission among them."

[p. 277] "Hatta" (until) indicates a limit (ghayah), but there is no return in the speech indicating that "until" is a limit for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an omission in the speech that the apparent meaning indicates, as if he said: "Nor are they intercessors as you wish, but they are servants or submitters forever," meaning obedient, "until, when fear is removed from their hearts." He said: The reports have been abundantly transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that His words ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ refer only to the angels, when they hear the revelation, meaning Gabriel, and when God commands it they hear it like the dragging of an iron chain over smooth rock, and they are then struck with fear out of reverence and awe. It has also been said: it is fear that the Hour might come; when that fear is removed from their hearts, meaning it is lifted and dispelled from them, some of them say to others, and to Gabriel: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ The ones asked say: He has said ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾. In keeping with this meaning of mentioning the angels at the beginning of the verses, this verse fits the first interpretation; and whoever does not perceive that the angels are referred to from the beginning of His words ﴿those you claimed﴾ will find that this verse is not connected to what precedes it, and therefore the exegetes were confused in interpreting it, to the point that some said, regarding the disbelievers after the arrival of death: "They are struck with fear in their hearts by the loss of life, and they see the reality, and their fear of what is said to them in their lifetime is removed, so they are told at that time: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ and they say: He has said the truth; they confess when confession no longer benefits you." Another group said: the verse concerns the entire world, and His words "until" mean in the Hereafter. The first interpretation regarding the angels is the correct one, and it is the one the reports have abundantly supported, and this (other view) is far-fetched. End of quotation.

If the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ does not refer back to ﴿those you claimed﴾, it refers back to the one to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿and Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20] refers, and the pronoun in "'alayhim" (upon them) refers to all the disbelievers, and "until" is a limit for His words ﴿so they followed him﴾ [Saba': 20]. The striking with fear would then be at the moment of separation from life, or their following of him is made to continue with them until the Day of Resurrection, figuratively.

The clause after His words ﴿Say, call upon﴾ is parenthetical (i'tirad) between the thing limited (al-mughayya) and the limit (al-ghayah). Ibn Zayd said: They acknowledged God when acknowledgment no longer benefited them, so the meaning is: Satan was struck with fear from their hearts, and what he used to seek from them departed from them; ﴿they say: what has your Lord said?﴾. Al-Hasan said: "What has your Lord said?" is said to the polytheists only through the tongues of the prophets, and they acknowledged when it no longer benefited. It has also been said that "until" is a limit connected to His words ﴿you claimed﴾, meaning: you claimed disbelief up to the limit of the striking with fear, then you abandoned what you had claimed and said: "He has said the truth." End of quotation. In that case there is a shift (iltifat) in the speech from the second person in ﴿you claimed﴾ to the third person in ﴿was removed from their hearts﴾.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: When it is proclaimed, they are struck with fear, and their fear continues until the fear is removed from their hearts. Some of the intercessors among the angels say to some of the angels: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ regarding the acceptance of our intercession? Then some answer others: He has said, that is God has said, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning the true word, which is the acceptance of their intercession, if He, exalted is He, has permitted them in that; and He does not grant permission except while He desires the acceptance of the intercession.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what is the saying ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ connected, when there is nothing before it that "until" could be a limit for? I say: it is connected to what is understood from this speech, namely that there is an awaiting of permission, a pause, a delay, and fear on the part of those who hope for intercession and the intercessors: will they be granted permission or not? And that permission is not granted except after a considerable period of time and a long waiting. A similar state is indicated by His words, mighty is He who speaks: [p. 278] ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful; they cannot address Him [with any speech]﴾ [al-Naba': 37], ﴿on the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks; they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is right﴾ [al-Naba': 38]; as if it were said: they wait and pause for a long time, fearful and alarmed.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 22–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Until, when terror is lifted from their hearts﴾, meaning the terror is removed from the hearts of the intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, by a word that the Lord of Might speaks in granting permission. They rejoice at this, and some of them ask others, ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ They reply, ﴿"The truth,"﴾ that is, the true word, which is the permission for intercession for whomever He is pleased with. End of quote.

From this it is concluded that "until" (hatta) indicates a final limit (ghaya), and that this is either:

1. For a stated expression, which is "you claimed" (za'amtum). In this case the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ is an iltifat (a shift from direct address to third person), and it refers to the disbelievers. Or the verb is "they followed him" (fa-ittaba'uhu), and in this there is a consistency of pronouns in the third person singular. The separation by the parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) is also there, and the pronoun likewise refers to the disbelievers. The pronoun in "they said" (qalu) refers to the angels, the pronoun of address in "your Lord" (rabbukum) is addressed to the disbelievers, and the third person in the second "they said" (qalu) refers to the disbelievers.

2. Or it is for an implied element. What Ibn 'Atiyya suggested cannot be correct as a limit, because what follows the limit must be different from what precedes it. They are servants who are always submissive and never depart from that, neither when terror is lifted from their hearts nor when it is not. Applying this to the angels at the time of revelation does not fit the verse. The fact that the Prophet (ﷺ), in the story of the revelation, said, "When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts," does not prove that this verse concerns the angels at the time God speaks the revelation. The hadith was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the dragging of a chain over rock, and they fall down senseless. They remain so until Gabriel, peace be upon him, comes to them. When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts. They say, 'O Gabriel, what has your Lord said?' He says, 'The truth.' Then they call out, 'The truth.'"

What al-Zamakhshari suggested is possible, but in it there is a specification of those whom you claimed besides Him as being the angels, while those who worshipped them include angels and others. There is also a specification of those who were given permission as being the angels, whereas those permitted to intercede include the angels and others. Do you not see what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) related regarding the intercession in His saying, mighty and majestic?

It is also read: ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ with doubled "z", from "fazaʿ" (terror), in the passive voice, meaning the terror is caused to fly away from their hearts. The form "fa''ala" comes with several meanings, among them removal. Here it is like: "qarradtu al-baʿir" (I de-ticked the camel), meaning I removed the ticks from it.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Talha, Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Ibn 'Amir read it in the active voice, also from "fazaʿ". If the pronoun in "from their hearts" refers to the angels, the subject of "fazaʿa" is God. If it refers to the disbelievers, the pronoun refers to those who misled them.

Al-Hasan read ﴿fuziʿa﴾ from "fazaʿ" with a lightened "z", in the passive voice, and ﴿from their hearts﴾ is in the place of a nominative subject for it, like your saying "inṭalaqa Yazid" (Yazid departed).

Al-Hasan also read, as well as Abu al-Mutawakkil, Qatada, and Mujahid: ﴿fazzaʿa﴾ with a doubled "z", in the active voice, from "fazaʿ". Al-Hasan also read the same with a lightened "z". 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan as well, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Qatada also, and Abu Mijlaz read ﴿furrigha﴾ from "faraagh" (emptiness), with doubled "r", in the passive voice.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa read ﴿ifranqa'a﴾ ﴿ʿan qulubihim﴾, meaning it was uncovered from them, and it is said: it dispersed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The word is composed of the letters of separation with the addition of the ʿayn, just as qamtar is composed of the letters of qamt with the addition of the rāʾ." End of quote. If al-Zamakhshari means that the ʿayn is among the letters of augmentation, and likewise the rāʾ, which is the apparent sense of his words, then this is not correct, because the ʿayn and the rāʾ are not among the letters of augmentation. If he means that the word contains letters, and that what they mention as added to those letters, namely the ʿayn and the rāʾ, is like the root of farqaʿa and qamtara, then this is correct. But were it not for the implication of what al-Zamakhshari said about this word, I would not have mentioned this reading, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf).

They also said other things regarding God's saying, ﴿Until, when it is lifted﴾, besides what has preceded. Ka'b said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks, without how, the angels strike their wings and fall down in terror. They say to one another, ﴿'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'The truth.'﴾" It is also said: when Isra'fil calls them from their graves, they reply, saying "What?", and this is from the terror which is the calling and the seeking of help, as Zuhayr said:

*When they are terrified they fly to the one they seek refuge with,*
*tall spears, neither weak nor unarmed.*

(p-279)

It is also said: it is the terror of the angels of the lowest heaven at the descent of the arrangers (al-mudabbirat) to the earth. It is also said: when there was an interval (fatra) between Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ), and God sent Muhammad, God sent Gabriel with the revelation. The angels thought that something of the matter of the Hour had descended, and they were stunned by that. So Gabriel began passing by every heaven, lifting the terror from them and informing them that it was the revelation. This was said by Qatada, Muqatil, and Ibn al-Sa'ib. It is also said: the angels who follow one another (al-muʿaqqibat), who go among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when God sends them down, a loud sound is heard from them, so those below them among the angels think it is something of the matter of the Hour, and they fall prostrate, stunned. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud.

These sayings, and those preceding them, scarcely fit the words of the Qur'an. So I ask God to grant us understanding of His Book. The closest of them to me is that the pronoun in "their hearts" (qulubihim) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "they followed him" (ittaba'uhu) and "upon them" (ʿalayhim) refers, and to some of those who are in doubt about it. The sentence after that is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraD). And the saying "they said" (qalu), that is, the angels, to those followers who are doubtful, asking them a question of reproach: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾, on the tongue of the one who was sent to you after the veil was lifted from their hearts. Then they will acknowledge at that time that what He said, and what His prophets brought, is the truth, not the falsehood in which we were, following Iblis and doubting the resurrection.

"What" (mādhā) may be the object of "said" (qāla), meaning "what thing has your Lord said?" It may also be in the place of a nominative, with "dhā" as a relative pronoun, meaning "what is it that your Lord said?" and "dhā" is its predicate, and the object of "said" is an implied pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿qalu al-ḥaqqu﴾ with "al-ḥaqqu" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: its saying is the truth. ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence and glorification by them.

Then he returned to addressing the disbelievers and asked them about who provides for them, arguing against them that their provider is God, since they cannot say that their gods provide for them, and ask them whether they ﴿possess not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾. He commanded him to take on the task of answering and affirming on their behalf with his saying, ﴿"Say: God"﴾, because they may not answer out of love for obstinacy and preference for polytheism. It is known that there is no answer for them, or for anyone, except to say, "He is God."

﴿"And indeed we"﴾, that is, the monotheists who provide and worship, ﴿"or you"﴾, the polytheists who worship idols and inanimate things.

﴿"Surely we are upon guidance"﴾, that is, a straight path, ﴿"or in clear error"﴾, that is, in obvious and manifest confusion. The meaning is: one of the two parties, us or you, is surely upon one of the two states of guidance or misguidance, and the statement is put in the form of doubt and possibility. It is known that whoever worships God and affirms His oneness is upon guidance, and whoever worships other than Him, whether a stone or something else, is in error. This sentence includes fairness and gentleness in calling to God, and whoever hears it knows that it is a statement of attribution. Refutation by indirect allusion and implication is more eloquent than refutation by explicit statement. Similar to this is the saying of the Arabs: "May God disgrace the liar between me and you," which is said by one who is certain that his companion is the liar. A parallel to it is the saying of the poet:

*So whichever of us and you was the worse, he will be led to humiliation in disgrace.*

And Hassan said:

*Do you satirize him when you are not equal to him? So the worse of you two is the ransom for the better.*

This type is called in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan) istidrāj al-mukhāṭab (drawing the addressee along). One mentions to him a matter which he accepts, even if it is contrary to what is actually the case, until he listens to what is being put to him. For if he began with something he dislikes, he would not listen, and one keeps moving him from state to state until the truth becomes clear to him and he accepts it. Here, when they heard the alternation between him and them, it appeared to them that he was not certain that the truth was with him, so he said to them by way of reasoning: your gods do not possess an atom's weight, and they neither benefit nor harm, because they are inanimate, and you know this. Thus it became certain that the provider for them, and the one who benefits and harms, is God, glorified be He.

It is also said: the meaning of the sentence is to belittle the polytheists and to mock them. They have made clear that their gods provide them with nothing and neither benefit nor harm. So God wanted from His Prophet, and commanded him, to rebuke them, belittle them, and call them liars with a statement that is not explicit, if that is more forceful in belittling them, like your saying: "Surely one of us is a liar," while you know that the person you are addressing is the liar, but you rebuked him with a wording that is not explicit (p-280).

The "or" (aw) here is used in its proper function, to indicate one of two things or several things. The predicate of ﴿"Surely we or you"﴾ is ﴿"upon guidance or in clear error"﴾, and it does not need an omitted element to be posited, since the meaning is: one of us is in one of these two. Like your saying: "Zayd or ʿAmr is in the palace, or in the mosque." This does not need an omitted element to be posited, since its meaning is: one of these two is in one of these two. It is also said: the predicate is omitted. It is said the predicate of "lā" (wa-lahu, a grammatical term) is omitted, and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance or in clear error," so it was omitted because the predicate of what follows indicates it. Thus "upon guidance or in clear error", the affirmed predicate, is a predicate about it (inna), or "you", since it is in the estimate of "we". But because it was omitted, the pronoun was joined. It is also said: it is the predicate of the second, and the estimate is: "Or you, surely upon guidance or in clear error," and it was omitted because the predicate of the first indicates it. This affirmed one is ﴿"surely upon guidance or in clear error"﴾. There is no need for this estimate of omission if what follows "or" is not conjoined by it, as in: "Zayd or ʿAmr is standing." That would need this estimate. And "inna" with what may be a predicate, its subject is conjoined by "or", and the predicate is conjoined by "or", so it does not need it.

Abu ʿUbayda held that "or" has the meaning of "wa" (and), so it is of the category of wrapping and spreading (al-laff wa al-nashr), and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance, and you in clear error," so he informs about each according to what fits it. There is no need to remove "or" from its proper function.

"Upon" (ʿalā) is used with guidance because its holder is one of elevation and firm establishment in what he is upon, acting as he wills. "From" (ʿan) is used with error because he is immersed in confusion, bewildered therein, not knowing where to turn.

[p. 275] When he had described the state of the grateful and the state of the disbelievers, and had mentioned Quraysh and those who did not believe among earlier peoples, he returned to addressing them, saying: ﴿Say﴾ (O Muhammad) to the polytheists to whom the example was given through the story of Sheba (Saba'), which is well known among them through transmission in their reports and poetry: ﴿Call upon those you claimed﴾, meaning their objects of worship from among the angels and idols. This is a command to supplicate which is a challenge (ta'jiz) and an establishment of proof (iqamat al-hujjah). It is narrated that this was revealed at the time of the famine that struck Quraysh, meaning: call upon them so that they may remove from you what has befallen you, and turn to them in whatever matter confronts you.

"Zaʿama" (claimed) is one of the verbs that take two objects when it denotes belief (i'tiqadiyyah). The first object is the omitted pronoun referring to "those," and the second is also omitted because the meaning indicates it, and its attribute has taken its place. The estimate is: "those whom you claimed to be gods besides Him." The omission of the second object is made acceptable by the presence of its attribute in its place; were it not for this, it would not be acceptable, since the omission of one of the two objects of ẓanna (to think) and its sisters for brevity (ikhtisar) is disputed. Ibn Malakut prohibited it, while the majority permitted it, though it is rare even so. The second object cannot be "min dunihi" (besides Him), because it is not a complete statement: if you said "they are besides Him," it would not be correct, nor would the clause "they do not possess an atom's weight" (from His words) be acceptable as the second object, because if this attribution were a claim made by them, they would be confessing the truth and speaking it, whereas the intended meaning is that this would be a monotheism from them, and that their gods and objects of worship do not possess anything by their own admission.

Then He informed about their gods that they do not possess an atom's weight, and that is the most insignificant of things; and when ownership of the most insignificant is negated from them, ownership of the greatest is all the more negated. Then He mentioned the place of that atom's weight, which is the heavens and the earth. Then He informed that they have no share (shirk) in the heavens or the earth, thereby negating both kinds of ownership: independent ownership (istibdad) and partnership. Then He negated any assistance from them to Him, exalted is He, in anything He created, by His words: ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Thus He made clear the incapacity of their objects of worship from every direction.

Since there were among the Arabs those who worshipped the angels so that they would intercede for them, He negated that their intercession benefits. The negation extends to intercession itself, meaning: there is no intercession from them that would benefit; the meaning is not that they intercede and their intercession does not benefit, meaning that no intercession at all occurs from their objects of worship. And because their worshippers are disbelievers, if the objects of worship were idols or disbelievers, such as Pharaoh, the negation of intercession from them is evident. If they were angels or others who were worshipped, such as Jesus (peace be upon him), then their intercession, when it occurs, is for a believer.

﴿Except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ is an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent (istithna' mufarragh, i.e., an exception in which the excluded noun is omitted), so the excluded element is omitted, its estimate being: "intercession benefits no one, except for him to whom He has given permission." The phrase "for anyone" may mean the one interceded for, which is the apparent meaning, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean the one interceded for, for whose sake He gave permission that intercession be made on his behalf, while the intercessor is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. It may also mean the intercessor, so His words ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ mean: except for an intercessor to whom He has given permission to intercede, while the one interceded for is not mentioned but is indicated by the meaning. On this possibility, the "lam" in "adhina lahu" (to whom He has given permission) is the lam of communication (lam al-tabligh), not the lam of cause (lam al-'illah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: One says "the intercession is for Zayd," in the sense that he is the intercessor, just as one says "the generosity is for Zayd," and in the sense that he is the one interceded for, just as one says "the standing is for Zayd." So His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be according to either of these two aspects: meaning, intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom He has given permission from among the intercessors, and granted to him; or intercession benefits only when it is made for one to whom permission was given, meaning for the sake of its intercessor; or it is the second lam in your saying "he gave permission to Zayd for ʿAmr," meaning for his sake; as if it were said: "except for the one for whose sake permission was given to the intercessor." This is a subtle aspect, and it is the preferred one. And this is a refutation of their saying: "These are our intercessors with God." End of quotation. He thus made ﴿except for him to whom He has given permission﴾ an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent in the sense of states (ahwal), and for this reason he estimated it as "except being" (illa ka'inah); whereas according to what we have established, it is an exception from entities (dhawat).

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The doctrines that lead to polytheism are four. One who says: God created the heavens and made the earth and the earthly things subject to their rule, and we are among the earthly things, so we worship the stars and the celestial angels, and they are our god, and God is their god. This is refuted by His words ﴿they do not possess﴾ ﴿in the heavens﴾, as you admitted, ﴿nor in the earth﴾, contrary to what you claimed. Another says: the heavens are from God in independent authority, and the earthly things are from Him through the mediation of the stars, for He, exalted is He, created the elements and the compounds within them through conjunctions, movements, and risings, so they made partners with God in the earth; and the first group made the earth belong to other than Him. This is refuted by His words ﴿and they have no share in them both﴾, meaning the earth is like the heavens, belonging to God and not to other than Him, and no other has any portion in them both. Another says: compounds and events are from God, but He delegated them to the stars, and the act of one who has been authorized is attributed to the one who gives authority, and withdrawn from the one authorized in it. They made the heavens specific to God, so this is refuted by His words ﴿and He has no supporter among them﴾. Another says: we worship the idols, which are the images of the angels, so that they may intercede for us. This is refuted by His words ﴿and intercession does not benefit﴾, the whole clause.

The "al-" in "al-shafa'ah" (intercession) is apparently for generality, meaning the intercession of all creation. It has been said that it is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning the intercession of the angels whom they claimed to be partners and intercessors. End of quotation, and there is some abridgment in it.

Abu al-Baqa' said: The "lam" in ﴿for him to whom He has given permission﴾ may be connected to "intercession," because you say "I interceded for him," and you may connect it to "benefits." End of quotation. This is weak, because the object is placed after the verb, so the entry of the lam upon it is rare.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "udhina" with a dammah on the hamzah; the rest of the seven read it with a fathah, meaning God gave permission to him.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in His words "qulubihim" (their hearts) refers back to what the pronouns of the third person in His words "they do not possess" and "for them" and "for Him from them" refer to, namely the angels whom they took as gods and intercessors. The estimate would then be: "except for him whom He has given permission among them."

[p. 277] "Hatta" (until) indicates a limit (ghayah), but there is no return in the speech indicating that "until" is a limit for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an omission in the speech that the apparent meaning indicates, as if he said: "Nor are they intercessors as you wish, but they are servants or submitters forever," meaning obedient, "until, when fear is removed from their hearts." He said: The reports have been abundantly transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that His words ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ refer only to the angels, when they hear the revelation, meaning Gabriel, and when God commands it they hear it like the dragging of an iron chain over smooth rock, and they are then struck with fear out of reverence and awe. It has also been said: it is fear that the Hour might come; when that fear is removed from their hearts, meaning it is lifted and dispelled from them, some of them say to others, and to Gabriel: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ The ones asked say: He has said ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾. In keeping with this meaning of mentioning the angels at the beginning of the verses, this verse fits the first interpretation; and whoever does not perceive that the angels are referred to from the beginning of His words ﴿those you claimed﴾ will find that this verse is not connected to what precedes it, and therefore the exegetes were confused in interpreting it, to the point that some said, regarding the disbelievers after the arrival of death: "They are struck with fear in their hearts by the loss of life, and they see the reality, and their fear of what is said to them in their lifetime is removed, so they are told at that time: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ and they say: He has said the truth; they confess when confession no longer benefits you." Another group said: the verse concerns the entire world, and His words "until" mean in the Hereafter. The first interpretation regarding the angels is the correct one, and it is the one the reports have abundantly supported, and this (other view) is far-fetched. End of quotation.

If the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ does not refer back to ﴿those you claimed﴾, it refers back to the one to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿and Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20] refers, and the pronoun in "'alayhim" (upon them) refers to all the disbelievers, and "until" is a limit for His words ﴿so they followed him﴾ [Saba': 20]. The striking with fear would then be at the moment of separation from life, or their following of him is made to continue with them until the Day of Resurrection, figuratively.

The clause after His words ﴿Say, call upon﴾ is parenthetical (i'tirad) between the thing limited (al-mughayya) and the limit (al-ghayah). Ibn Zayd said: They acknowledged God when acknowledgment no longer benefited them, so the meaning is: Satan was struck with fear from their hearts, and what he used to seek from them departed from them; ﴿they say: what has your Lord said?﴾. Al-Hasan said: "What has your Lord said?" is said to the polytheists only through the tongues of the prophets, and they acknowledged when it no longer benefited. It has also been said that "until" is a limit connected to His words ﴿you claimed﴾, meaning: you claimed disbelief up to the limit of the striking with fear, then you abandoned what you had claimed and said: "He has said the truth." End of quotation. In that case there is a shift (iltifat) in the speech from the second person in ﴿you claimed﴾ to the third person in ﴿was removed from their hearts﴾.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: When it is proclaimed, they are struck with fear, and their fear continues until the fear is removed from their hearts. Some of the intercessors among the angels say to some of the angels: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ regarding the acceptance of our intercession? Then some answer others: He has said, that is God has said, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning the true word, which is the acceptance of their intercession, if He, exalted is He, has permitted them in that; and He does not grant permission except while He desires the acceptance of the intercession.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what is the saying ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ connected, when there is nothing before it that "until" could be a limit for? I say: it is connected to what is understood from this speech, namely that there is an awaiting of permission, a pause, a delay, and fear on the part of those who hope for intercession and the intercessors: will they be granted permission or not? And that permission is not granted except after a considerable period of time and a long waiting. A similar state is indicated by His words, mighty is He who speaks: [p. 278] ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful; they cannot address Him [with any speech]﴾ [al-Naba': 37], ﴿on the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks; they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is right﴾ [al-Naba': 38]; as if it were said: they wait and pause for a long time, fearful and alarmed.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 22–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Until, when terror is lifted from their hearts﴾, meaning the terror is removed from the hearts of the intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, by a word that the Lord of Might speaks in granting permission. They rejoice at this, and some of them ask others, ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ They reply, ﴿"The truth,"﴾ that is, the true word, which is the permission for intercession for whomever He is pleased with. End of quote.

From this it is concluded that "until" (hatta) indicates a final limit (ghaya), and that this is either:

1. For a stated expression, which is "you claimed" (za'amtum). In this case the pronoun in ﴿from their hearts﴾ is an iltifat (a shift from direct address to third person), and it refers to the disbelievers. Or the verb is "they followed him" (fa-ittaba'uhu), and in this there is a consistency of pronouns in the third person singular. The separation by the parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) is also there, and the pronoun likewise refers to the disbelievers. The pronoun in "they said" (qalu) refers to the angels, the pronoun of address in "your Lord" (rabbukum) is addressed to the disbelievers, and the third person in the second "they said" (qalu) refers to the disbelievers.

2. Or it is for an implied element. What Ibn 'Atiyya suggested cannot be correct as a limit, because what follows the limit must be different from what precedes it. They are servants who are always submissive and never depart from that, neither when terror is lifted from their hearts nor when it is not. Applying this to the angels at the time of revelation does not fit the verse. The fact that the Prophet (ﷺ), in the story of the revelation, said, "When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts," does not prove that this verse concerns the angels at the time God speaks the revelation. The hadith was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the dragging of a chain over rock, and they fall down senseless. They remain so until Gabriel, peace be upon him, comes to them. When Gabriel comes to them, terror is lifted from their hearts. They say, 'O Gabriel, what has your Lord said?' He says, 'The truth.' Then they call out, 'The truth.'"

What al-Zamakhshari suggested is possible, but in it there is a specification of those whom you claimed besides Him as being the angels, while those who worshipped them include angels and others. There is also a specification of those who were given permission as being the angels, whereas those permitted to intercede include the angels and others. Do you not see what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) related regarding the intercession in His saying, mighty and majestic?

It is also read: ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ with doubled "z", from "fazaʿ" (terror), in the passive voice, meaning the terror is caused to fly away from their hearts. The form "fa''ala" comes with several meanings, among them removal. Here it is like: "qarradtu al-baʿir" (I de-ticked the camel), meaning I removed the ticks from it.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Talha, Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Ibn 'Amir read it in the active voice, also from "fazaʿ". If the pronoun in "from their hearts" refers to the angels, the subject of "fazaʿa" is God. If it refers to the disbelievers, the pronoun refers to those who misled them.

Al-Hasan read ﴿fuziʿa﴾ from "fazaʿ" with a lightened "z", in the passive voice, and ﴿from their hearts﴾ is in the place of a nominative subject for it, like your saying "inṭalaqa Yazid" (Yazid departed).

Al-Hasan also read, as well as Abu al-Mutawakkil, Qatada, and Mujahid: ﴿fazzaʿa﴾ with a doubled "z", in the active voice, from "fazaʿ". Al-Hasan also read the same with a lightened "z". 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan as well, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Qatada also, and Abu Mijlaz read ﴿furrigha﴾ from "faraagh" (emptiness), with doubled "r", in the passive voice.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa read ﴿ifranqa'a﴾ ﴿ʿan qulubihim﴾, meaning it was uncovered from them, and it is said: it dispersed.
