Al-Zamakhshari said: "The word is composed of the letters of separation with the addition of the ʿayn, just as qamtar is composed of the letters of qamt with the addition of the rāʾ." End of quote. If al-Zamakhshari means that the ʿayn is among the letters of augmentation, and likewise the rāʾ, which is the apparent sense of his words, then this is not correct, because the ʿayn and the rāʾ are not among the letters of augmentation. If he means that the word contains letters, and that what they mention as added to those letters, namely the ʿayn and the rāʾ, is like the root of farqaʿa and qamtara, then this is correct. But were it not for the implication of what al-Zamakhshari said about this word, I would not have mentioned this reading, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf).

They also said other things regarding God's saying, ﴿Until, when it is lifted﴾, besides what has preceded. Ka'b said: "When God, mighty and majestic, speaks, without how, the angels strike their wings and fall down in terror. They say to one another, ﴿'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'The truth.'﴾" It is also said: when Isra'fil calls them from their graves, they reply, saying "What?", and this is from the terror which is the calling and the seeking of help, as Zuhayr said:

*When they are terrified they fly to the one they seek refuge with,*
*tall spears, neither weak nor unarmed.*

(p-279)

It is also said: it is the terror of the angels of the lowest heaven at the descent of the arrangers (al-mudabbirat) to the earth. It is also said: when there was an interval (fatra) between Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ), and God sent Muhammad, God sent Gabriel with the revelation. The angels thought that something of the matter of the Hour had descended, and they were stunned by that. So Gabriel began passing by every heaven, lifting the terror from them and informing them that it was the revelation. This was said by Qatada, Muqatil, and Ibn al-Sa'ib. It is also said: the angels who follow one another (al-muʿaqqibat), who go among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when God sends them down, a loud sound is heard from them, so those below them among the angels think it is something of the matter of the Hour, and they fall prostrate, stunned. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud.

These sayings, and those preceding them, scarcely fit the words of the Qur'an. So I ask God to grant us understanding of His Book. The closest of them to me is that the pronoun in "their hearts" (qulubihim) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "they followed him" (ittaba'uhu) and "upon them" (ʿalayhim) refers, and to some of those who are in doubt about it. The sentence after that is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraD). And the saying "they said" (qalu), that is, the angels, to those followers who are doubtful, asking them a question of reproach: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾, on the tongue of the one who was sent to you after the veil was lifted from their hearts. Then they will acknowledge at that time that what He said, and what His prophets brought, is the truth, not the falsehood in which we were, following Iblis and doubting the resurrection.

"What" (mādhā) may be the object of "said" (qāla), meaning "what thing has your Lord said?" It may also be in the place of a nominative, with "dhā" as a relative pronoun, meaning "what is it that your Lord said?" and "dhā" is its predicate, and the object of "said" is an implied pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿qalu al-ḥaqqu﴾ with "al-ḥaqqu" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: its saying is the truth. ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence and glorification by them.

Then he returned to addressing the disbelievers and asked them about who provides for them, arguing against them that their provider is God, since they cannot say that their gods provide for them, and ask them whether they ﴿possess not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾. He commanded him to take on the task of answering and affirming on their behalf with his saying, ﴿"Say: God"﴾, because they may not answer out of love for obstinacy and preference for polytheism. It is known that there is no answer for them, or for anyone, except to say, "He is God."

﴿"And indeed we"﴾, that is, the monotheists who provide and worship, ﴿"or you"﴾, the polytheists who worship idols and inanimate things.

﴿"Surely we are upon guidance"﴾, that is, a straight path, ﴿"or in clear error"﴾, that is, in obvious and manifest confusion. The meaning is: one of the two parties, us or you, is surely upon one of the two states of guidance or misguidance, and the statement is put in the form of doubt and possibility. It is known that whoever worships God and affirms His oneness is upon guidance, and whoever worships other than Him, whether a stone or something else, is in error. This sentence includes fairness and gentleness in calling to God, and whoever hears it knows that it is a statement of attribution. Refutation by indirect allusion and implication is more eloquent than refutation by explicit statement. Similar to this is the saying of the Arabs: "May God disgrace the liar between me and you," which is said by one who is certain that his companion is the liar. A parallel to it is the saying of the poet:

*So whichever of us and you was the worse, he will be led to humiliation in disgrace.*

And Hassan said:

*Do you satirize him when you are not equal to him? So the worse of you two is the ransom for the better.*

This type is called in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan) istidrāj al-mukhāṭab (drawing the addressee along). One mentions to him a matter which he accepts, even if it is contrary to what is actually the case, until he listens to what is being put to him. For if he began with something he dislikes, he would not listen, and one keeps moving him from state to state until the truth becomes clear to him and he accepts it. Here, when they heard the alternation between him and them, it appeared to them that he was not certain that the truth was with him, so he said to them by way of reasoning: your gods do not possess an atom's weight, and they neither benefit nor harm, because they are inanimate, and you know this. Thus it became certain that the provider for them, and the one who benefits and harms, is God, glorified be He.

It is also said: the meaning of the sentence is to belittle the polytheists and to mock them. They have made clear that their gods provide them with nothing and neither benefit nor harm. So God wanted from His Prophet, and commanded him, to rebuke them, belittle them, and call them liars with a statement that is not explicit, if that is more forceful in belittling them, like your saying: "Surely one of us is a liar," while you know that the person you are addressing is the liar, but you rebuked him with a wording that is not explicit (p-280).

The "or" (aw) here is used in its proper function, to indicate one of two things or several things. The predicate of ﴿"Surely we or you"﴾ is ﴿"upon guidance or in clear error"﴾, and it does not need an omitted element to be posited, since the meaning is: one of us is in one of these two. Like your saying: "Zayd or ʿAmr is in the palace, or in the mosque." This does not need an omitted element to be posited, since its meaning is: one of these two is in one of these two. It is also said: the predicate is omitted. It is said the predicate of "lā" (wa-lahu, a grammatical term) is omitted, and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance or in clear error," so it was omitted because the predicate of what follows indicates it. Thus "upon guidance or in clear error", the affirmed predicate, is a predicate about it (inna), or "you", since it is in the estimate of "we". But because it was omitted, the pronoun was joined. It is also said: it is the predicate of the second, and the estimate is: "Or you, surely upon guidance or in clear error," and it was omitted because the predicate of the first indicates it. This affirmed one is ﴿"surely upon guidance or in clear error"﴾. There is no need for this estimate of omission if what follows "or" is not conjoined by it, as in: "Zayd or ʿAmr is standing." That would need this estimate. And "inna" with what may be a predicate, its subject is conjoined by "or", and the predicate is conjoined by "or", so it does not need it.

Abu ʿUbayda held that "or" has the meaning of "wa" (and), so it is of the category of wrapping and spreading (al-laff wa al-nashr), and the estimate is: "And surely we are upon guidance, and you in clear error," so he informs about each according to what fits it. There is no need to remove "or" from its proper function.

"Upon" (ʿalā) is used with guidance because its holder is one of elevation and firm establishment in what he is upon, acting as he wills. "From" (ʿan) is used with error because he is immersed in confusion, bewildered therein, not knowing where to turn.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 25–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "You will not be questioned about what we committed as sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do."﴾ This is more equitable and more eloquent than the first formulation, and gentler and more conciliatory. He called their action "a crime" (ijram), as they claim, although it is rewarded and thanked. He called their action "work" (amal), although it is forbidden and prohibited. It may also be intended that the attribution of this to the believers alone, not the Messenger, since the believer is hardly free of minor sins. And "what you do" refers to unbelief and what is below it of major sins. It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf, the verse that commands fighting).

﴿Say: "Our Lord will gather us together"﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿"Then He will judge (yaftah)"﴾, that is, He will decide, ﴿"with truth"﴾, with justice, so He will admit the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to the Fire.

﴿"And He is the Opener (al-Fattah), the Knower"﴾: the Judge who decides, ﴿"the All-Knowing"﴾ of the deeds of the servants. Al-Fattah and al-'Alim are intensive forms (sigat mubalagha, forms of emphasis), and this contains a threat and a rebuke. It is like saying to one whom you have advised and warned but who did not accept: "You will see the evil outcome of the matter." Isa read al-Fatih as an active participle (ism fa'il), while the majority read al-Fattah.

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined to Him as partners."﴾ The apparent meaning is that ara (show/see) here means a'lama (inform/make know), so it takes three objects: the pronoun of the speaker (the first), alladhina (the second), and shurakaa' (partners, the third). That is, "Show me, with proof and evidence, how the partnership is conceived, and whether they possess the weight of an atom or provide you with sustenance." It has also been said that it is visual sight (ru'yat basar), and shurakaa' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the omitted pronoun in alhaqtum, its meaning being: "you attached them to Him while thinking them partners to Him." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is weak, because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit (la ghina'a lahu)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying 'Show me,' when He sees them and knows them? I say: He intends by this to show them the great error in attaching partners to God, and to compare, before their eyes, between Him and their idols, in order to inform them of the state of comparing Him with them and associating them with Him." And "Nay (kalla)" is a deterrent for them from their doctrine after He broke it by refuting the comparison, as Abraham said: ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship besides God"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 67], after he had argued against them, and He drew attention to the gross enormity of their error, and that they should measure God by His true measure through His saying ﴿"He is God, the Mighty, the Wise"﴾, as if He said: "Which of those whom you joined to Him possess these attributes?" The pronoun refers to God alone, or it is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), as in His saying ﴿"Say: He is God, One"﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit," meaning it has no profit, is not good. Rather, in it there is a rebuke and reproach for them, and the intent is not the literal reality of the matter. The meaning is: those whom you claim to be God's partners are of the kind that, if you were to show them, you would be disgraced, because they are wood, stone, and other stones and inanimate things. Just as you say to a man of base origin: "Mention to me your father, with whom you compared So-and-so the noble," while you do not intend the literal mention, but you intend to rebuke him, and that if he mentioned his father he would be disgraced. (p-281)

"Kaffatan" is an active participle from kaffa (to restrain). It has been said that it is a verbal noun like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah, in which case there is an omitted modifier: "except as one restraining," that is, "one who restrains people," meaning one who prevents them from unbelief, or one who prevents them from straying from your conveyance. When it is an active participle, al-Zajjaj and others said it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the kaf in "We sent you," and the meaning is: "except as one gathering the people in the conveyance," and kaffa means "gathering," and the ha' in it is for emphasis, as in 'allamah (very learned) and rawiyah (great transmitter). Al-Zamakhshari said: "except as a comprehensive message for them, encompassing them, because when it includes them it restrains them from anyone of them leaving it." He said: "Whoever makes it a state of the genitive (majrur) placed before it has erred, because placing the state of the genitive before it, in its original position, is like placing the genitive before the preposition. How many are there who commit this error and are not content with it until they add to it making the lam mean ila (to). For the first error cannot be fixed except by the second error, so both errors must be committed." End of quotation.

As for kaffatan in the sense of 'ammatan (general, comprehensive), what is transmitted from the grammarians is that it is only a circumstantial state (hal), and it is not used in any other way. So making it an adjective of an omitted verbal noun departs from what they transmitted, and its use as an adjective of an omitted noun is also not known. As for al-Zajjaj's statement that kaffatan means jami'an (gathering), and that the ha' in it is for emphasis, the language does not support that, because kaffa is not known to mean "gathered." As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "Whoever makes it a state…" and so on, this is a matter of disagreement. Most scholars held that this is not permissible, while Abu 'Ali, Ibn Kaysan, Ibn Burhan, and among our contemporaries Ibn Malik held that it is permissible, and this is the correct view. Among Abu 'Ali's examples: "Zayd is the best of what he can be, better than you," the estimate being: "Zayd is better than you, the best of what he can be," so he made "ma yakun" (what he can be) a state of the kaf in "minka" (than you), and placed it before it. The poet said:

"When a man finds manliness difficult in youth, its pursuit in middle age is hard for him."

And another said:

"I consoled myself for you all after your separation, by remembrance of you, until it is as if you are with me."

That is: "I consoled myself for you, all of you," that is, all together. The placing of a state before its owner, the genitive, and before what it depends on, has come, and among that is the saying of the poet:

"Infatuated with you, she has been infatuated, but separation has been decreed, and there is no way to you."

And another said:

"Heedless, the death comes upon a man, and he is called, but it is no time for refusal."

That is: "She was infatuated with you, infatuated," and "death comes upon a man heedless." If it is permissible to place it before the genitive and the governing word, then placing it before the genitive without the governing word is more permissible. And on the basis that kaffatan is a state of the people (al-nas), Ibn 'Atiyya adopted this and said: "It was placed first for emphasis." What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas is his saying: "That is, to the Arabs and the non-Arabs and all the nations," and the estimate is "to the people, all of them." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "How many are there who commit this error," to the end of his words, is objectionable, because the one who says this does not need to interpret the lam as meaning ila, since arsala (send) takes ila and also takes lam, as in His saying ﴿"And We sent you to the people as a messenger"﴾ [al-Nisa: 79]. If he interpreted the lam as meaning ila, it would not be an error, because the lam has come with the meaning of ila, and ila has come with the meaning of the lam, and arsala is among the verbs that take both with the genitive.

Then He related their statement in mockery of the resurrection and their urging for it, by way of denial, and they were not answered with the specification of the time, since that is among what God alone knows. Rather they were answered that what they were promised must come to pass, and that is the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of a similar sentence has already preceded. It is also possible that their question about what they were promised of punishment in this world, and what they urged, was in mockery from them.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "al-wa'd, al-wa'id, and al-mi'ad have the same meaning." The majority said: "al-wa'd is for good, al-wa'id is for evil, and al-mi'ad applies to this." The apparent meaning is that al-mi'ad is a noun of the pattern mif'al, used in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: "Say to you: the occurrence of the promise of a day and its fulfilment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-mi'ad is the time or place of the promise, and here it is the time, and the evidence for it is the reading of whoever read mi'ad yawm, so that yawm is put in apposition to it." End of quotation. What he said is not required, since it could be an apposition (badal) with an omitted estimate, meaning: "Say to you: the appointed time of a day," and when it is omitted, what takes its place is given its case.

The majority read mi'adu yawmin with the genitive construction (idafah). When al-Zamakhshari made al-mi'ad an adverb of time, he said: "As for the idafah, its idafah is explanatory (tabyin), as you say: 'the crushing of a garment' and 'the camel of irrigation.'" Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yazidi read mi'adun yawman with tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As for the accusative of yawm, it is for glorification (ta'zim), by supposing a verb whose estimate is 'for you there is an appointed time,' meaning a day, and I intend a day of a description, meaning such and such. It is possible that its accusative is by omitting a modifier, and it is possible that the nominative on this basis is for glorification." End of quotation. When al-mi'ad is made an adverb of time, the nominative and accusative come out in that way. It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of a day whose description is such and such. Isa read mi'adun, with tanwin, and yawma in the accusative without tanwin, being a genitive construction to a clause, so the explanation of al-Zamakhshari allows for glorification, and it allows an explanation as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of the day of such and such.

This answer came in the manner of a threat, matching the question having come in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are watched for the Day of Resurrection, which will surprise them, so they cannot delay from it nor advance before it. "The day" is the Day of Resurrection, which is what comes first to mind, or the day of the arrival of their term at the presence of their death, or the Day of Badr. These are the opinions.

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ means: in what includes monotheism, the messengership, and the resurrection mentioned earlier in it.

﴿"Nor in what is before it"﴾ is what was sent down of God's books announcing the Messenger of God. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Mecca asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in their books, and that angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an what preceded it of God's books in unbelief. "Those who disbelieved" would then be the polytheists of Quraysh and those who went their way. The well-known view is that "what is before it" is the Torah and the Gospel and the books that came before, and this is related from Ibn Jurayj. A group said that "what is before it" is the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error; its speaker did not understand the meaning of 'before' (bayn al-yad) in the language, which is what is earlier in time, and we have explained it above." End of quotation.

﴿"If you could see when the wrongdoers"﴾: He informed about their state in the manner of wonder at it, and "tara" (you see) here means ra'ayta (you saw), because it is in the sense of governing the past time adverb, and the object of "tara" is omitted, meaning: the state of the wrongdoers, when they are ﴿"made to stand"﴾ (mawquufun). The answer of law (jawab law) is omitted, meaning: you would see for them a remarkable state of their humiliation, their abasement, and their mutual arguing, where nothing of that benefits them. Then He explained that returning and disputing: the followers, who are the ones who were weakened, said to their leaders, by way of blame, rebuke, and returning the reproach upon them: ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The pronoun after lawla came as a nominative pronoun, which is the most eloquent usage. The imams Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and others related its coming with a genitive pronoun, as in "lawlakum" (had it not been for you), and al-Mubarrad's denial of that is not to be heeded. Since this is a situation, the subordinate and the superior are equal in it.

(p. 283) The followers began by rebuking their misleaders, since the leaders had lost their authority, and they could not deny that no messenger had come to them. Rather, they acknowledge it. Do you not see the words of those who were followed, ﴿after it had come to you﴾? The plural acknowledges that the Reminder had come to them. So their leaders said to them, ﴿Did we turn you away?﴾ They used the noun after the interrogative particle (ism ba'da adāt al-istifhām) to deny it, meaning that they themselves were the ones who turned them away. ﴿You were turned away by your own doing and your own choice﴾ after the interrogative particle. It is as if they said: We informed you and stood between you and the Reminder after you had resolved to enter faith. Rather, you yourselves denied your own souls their share and preferred error over guidance. So you were criminals and disbelievers by your own choice, not because of our words or our enticement. When their leaders denied that they were the cause of their disbelief, and affirmed by their words ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾ that their disbelief came from themselves, the followers countered one retraction with another, saying ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾. That is, our criminality did not come from us; rather, your scheming against us was constant, and your deceiving us night and day, as you commanded us while we were followers unable to oppose you, obedient to you because you dominated us through disbelief in God and the taking of rivals. The scheming (makr) is attributed to the night and the day by extension (ittisā') of the two time-expressions. They are then either in the accusative position as an object by extension (ʿalā al-siʿa), or in the nominative position by metaphorical predication (al-isnād al-majāzī), as people say: "a sleeping night." However, in my view the better reading is that makr is nominative as the agent, meaning: "Rather, your scheming with the night and the day turned us away," and its parallel is the saying of one who says: "I struck Zayd, but rather ʿAmr struck him," and the reply: "Rather, your servant struck him." The better estimate is that the meaning is: "Your servant struck him." It was also said that it may be a subject and predicate, meaning: "the cause of our disbelief." Qatādah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read bal makrun with tanwīn, and al-layla wa-l-nahāru in the accusative as a time adverbial (ẓarf). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr ibn Muhammad, Abu Razin, and Ibn Yaʿmar also read it with a fatha on the kāf and a shadda on the rāʾ, in the nominative and in construct (muḍāfa), and its meaning is: like the revolving of the night and the day and their alternation. Its meaning is: the postponement caused by long hope and being deceived by the days, together with these leaders' command of disbelief in God. Ibn Jubayr also read, as did Ṭalḥah and Rāshid (who is one of the Successors, among those who corrected the codices (al-maṣāḥif) by the order of al-Ḥajjāj), kadhālika, except that they put the rāʾ in the accusative as a time adverbial, its governing verb being an implied verb, meaning: "You turned us away from the scheming of the night and the day," that is, in their scheming, and its meaning is constant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: it is permissible for it to be governed by ﴿idh tamurūnanā﴾ ("when you commanded us"), as the accusative makra al-layli wa-l-nahār. He concluded. This is a mistake, because what follows idh (ḍamīr-less "idh" clause) does not govern what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Rather, the incitement is a constant scheming from which they never cease." He concluded.

And ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ came without a conjunction (wāw), because it is an answer to the speech of the oppressed, so it is resumed as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). The phrase ﴿Those who were oppressed said﴾ is conjoined to what preceded of their speech. The pronoun in (wa-asarrū) refers to all of them, the arrogant and the oppressed, who are the wrongdoers held in place (al-ẓālimūn al-mawqūfūn). The discussion of ﴿and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment﴾ has already occurred in Surah Yunus. Regret (al-nadāma) is among the inner meanings, so it does not appear; only what indicates it appears, and something else indicates it. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this has never been established in any language, that asarra is among the words with opposite meanings. The regret of those who were arrogant is over their own error and their misleading of others, and the regret of those who were oppressed is over their own error and their following of the misleaders.

﴿And We placed the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. The apparent meaning is the generality of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, so it includes the arrogant and the oppressed, because among the disbelievers there is one who has no followers to dispute words with in the Hereafter, and is not a follower of a disbelieving leader, like the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed. It was said that ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ are those among whom the dialogue previously occurred, and that the shackles indicate the manner of the punishment; they were certain that they would undergo it, so they abandoned regret.

(Is it ﴿are they recompensed﴾?) Its meaning is negation, and for this reason illā ("except") entered after the negation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 25–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "You will not be questioned about what we committed as sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do."﴾ This is more equitable and more eloquent than the first formulation, and gentler and more conciliatory. He called their action "a crime" (ijram), as they claim, although it is rewarded and thanked. He called their action "work" (amal), although it is forbidden and prohibited. It may also be intended that the attribution of this to the believers alone, not the Messenger, since the believer is hardly free of minor sins. And "what you do" refers to unbelief and what is below it of major sins. It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf, the verse that commands fighting).

﴿Say: "Our Lord will gather us together"﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿"Then He will judge (yaftah)"﴾, that is, He will decide, ﴿"with truth"﴾, with justice, so He will admit the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to the Fire.

﴿"And He is the Opener (al-Fattah), the Knower"﴾: the Judge who decides, ﴿"the All-Knowing"﴾ of the deeds of the servants. Al-Fattah and al-'Alim are intensive forms (sigat mubalagha, forms of emphasis), and this contains a threat and a rebuke. It is like saying to one whom you have advised and warned but who did not accept: "You will see the evil outcome of the matter." Isa read al-Fatih as an active participle (ism fa'il), while the majority read al-Fattah.

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined to Him as partners."﴾ The apparent meaning is that ara (show/see) here means a'lama (inform/make know), so it takes three objects: the pronoun of the speaker (the first), alladhina (the second), and shurakaa' (partners, the third). That is, "Show me, with proof and evidence, how the partnership is conceived, and whether they possess the weight of an atom or provide you with sustenance." It has also been said that it is visual sight (ru'yat basar), and shurakaa' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the omitted pronoun in alhaqtum, its meaning being: "you attached them to Him while thinking them partners to Him." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is weak, because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit (la ghina'a lahu)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying 'Show me,' when He sees them and knows them? I say: He intends by this to show them the great error in attaching partners to God, and to compare, before their eyes, between Him and their idols, in order to inform them of the state of comparing Him with them and associating them with Him." And "Nay (kalla)" is a deterrent for them from their doctrine after He broke it by refuting the comparison, as Abraham said: ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship besides God"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 67], after he had argued against them, and He drew attention to the gross enormity of their error, and that they should measure God by His true measure through His saying ﴿"He is God, the Mighty, the Wise"﴾, as if He said: "Which of those whom you joined to Him possess these attributes?" The pronoun refers to God alone, or it is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), as in His saying ﴿"Say: He is God, One"﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit," meaning it has no profit, is not good. Rather, in it there is a rebuke and reproach for them, and the intent is not the literal reality of the matter. The meaning is: those whom you claim to be God's partners are of the kind that, if you were to show them, you would be disgraced, because they are wood, stone, and other stones and inanimate things. Just as you say to a man of base origin: "Mention to me your father, with whom you compared So-and-so the noble," while you do not intend the literal mention, but you intend to rebuke him, and that if he mentioned his father he would be disgraced. (p-281)

"Kaffatan" is an active participle from kaffa (to restrain). It has been said that it is a verbal noun like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah, in which case there is an omitted modifier: "except as one restraining," that is, "one who restrains people," meaning one who prevents them from unbelief, or one who prevents them from straying from your conveyance. When it is an active participle, al-Zajjaj and others said it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the kaf in "We sent you," and the meaning is: "except as one gathering the people in the conveyance," and kaffa means "gathering," and the ha' in it is for emphasis, as in 'allamah (very learned) and rawiyah (great transmitter). Al-Zamakhshari said: "except as a comprehensive message for them, encompassing them, because when it includes them it restrains them from anyone of them leaving it." He said: "Whoever makes it a state of the genitive (majrur) placed before it has erred, because placing the state of the genitive before it, in its original position, is like placing the genitive before the preposition. How many are there who commit this error and are not content with it until they add to it making the lam mean ila (to). For the first error cannot be fixed except by the second error, so both errors must be committed." End of quotation.

As for kaffatan in the sense of 'ammatan (general, comprehensive), what is transmitted from the grammarians is that it is only a circumstantial state (hal), and it is not used in any other way. So making it an adjective of an omitted verbal noun departs from what they transmitted, and its use as an adjective of an omitted noun is also not known. As for al-Zajjaj's statement that kaffatan means jami'an (gathering), and that the ha' in it is for emphasis, the language does not support that, because kaffa is not known to mean "gathered." As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "Whoever makes it a state…" and so on, this is a matter of disagreement. Most scholars held that this is not permissible, while Abu 'Ali, Ibn Kaysan, Ibn Burhan, and among our contemporaries Ibn Malik held that it is permissible, and this is the correct view. Among Abu 'Ali's examples: "Zayd is the best of what he can be, better than you," the estimate being: "Zayd is better than you, the best of what he can be," so he made "ma yakun" (what he can be) a state of the kaf in "minka" (than you), and placed it before it. The poet said:

"When a man finds manliness difficult in youth, its pursuit in middle age is hard for him."

And another said:

"I consoled myself for you all after your separation, by remembrance of you, until it is as if you are with me."

That is: "I consoled myself for you, all of you," that is, all together. The placing of a state before its owner, the genitive, and before what it depends on, has come, and among that is the saying of the poet:

"Infatuated with you, she has been infatuated, but separation has been decreed, and there is no way to you."

And another said:

"Heedless, the death comes upon a man, and he is called, but it is no time for refusal."

That is: "She was infatuated with you, infatuated," and "death comes upon a man heedless." If it is permissible to place it before the genitive and the governing word, then placing it before the genitive without the governing word is more permissible. And on the basis that kaffatan is a state of the people (al-nas), Ibn 'Atiyya adopted this and said: "It was placed first for emphasis." What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas is his saying: "That is, to the Arabs and the non-Arabs and all the nations," and the estimate is "to the people, all of them." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "How many are there who commit this error," to the end of his words, is objectionable, because the one who says this does not need to interpret the lam as meaning ila, since arsala (send) takes ila and also takes lam, as in His saying ﴿"And We sent you to the people as a messenger"﴾ [al-Nisa: 79]. If he interpreted the lam as meaning ila, it would not be an error, because the lam has come with the meaning of ila, and ila has come with the meaning of the lam, and arsala is among the verbs that take both with the genitive.

Then He related their statement in mockery of the resurrection and their urging for it, by way of denial, and they were not answered with the specification of the time, since that is among what God alone knows. Rather they were answered that what they were promised must come to pass, and that is the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of a similar sentence has already preceded. It is also possible that their question about what they were promised of punishment in this world, and what they urged, was in mockery from them.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "al-wa'd, al-wa'id, and al-mi'ad have the same meaning." The majority said: "al-wa'd is for good, al-wa'id is for evil, and al-mi'ad applies to this." The apparent meaning is that al-mi'ad is a noun of the pattern mif'al, used in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: "Say to you: the occurrence of the promise of a day and its fulfilment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-mi'ad is the time or place of the promise, and here it is the time, and the evidence for it is the reading of whoever read mi'ad yawm, so that yawm is put in apposition to it." End of quotation. What he said is not required, since it could be an apposition (badal) with an omitted estimate, meaning: "Say to you: the appointed time of a day," and when it is omitted, what takes its place is given its case.

The majority read mi'adu yawmin with the genitive construction (idafah). When al-Zamakhshari made al-mi'ad an adverb of time, he said: "As for the idafah, its idafah is explanatory (tabyin), as you say: 'the crushing of a garment' and 'the camel of irrigation.'" Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yazidi read mi'adun yawman with tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As for the accusative of yawm, it is for glorification (ta'zim), by supposing a verb whose estimate is 'for you there is an appointed time,' meaning a day, and I intend a day of a description, meaning such and such. It is possible that its accusative is by omitting a modifier, and it is possible that the nominative on this basis is for glorification." End of quotation. When al-mi'ad is made an adverb of time, the nominative and accusative come out in that way. It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of a day whose description is such and such. Isa read mi'adun, with tanwin, and yawma in the accusative without tanwin, being a genitive construction to a clause, so the explanation of al-Zamakhshari allows for glorification, and it allows an explanation as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of the day of such and such.

This answer came in the manner of a threat, matching the question having come in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are watched for the Day of Resurrection, which will surprise them, so they cannot delay from it nor advance before it. "The day" is the Day of Resurrection, which is what comes first to mind, or the day of the arrival of their term at the presence of their death, or the Day of Badr. These are the opinions.

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ means: in what includes monotheism, the messengership, and the resurrection mentioned earlier in it.

﴿"Nor in what is before it"﴾ is what was sent down of God's books announcing the Messenger of God. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Mecca asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in their books, and that angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an what preceded it of God's books in unbelief. "Those who disbelieved" would then be the polytheists of Quraysh and those who went their way. The well-known view is that "what is before it" is the Torah and the Gospel and the books that came before, and this is related from Ibn Jurayj. A group said that "what is before it" is the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error; its speaker did not understand the meaning of 'before' (bayn al-yad) in the language, which is what is earlier in time, and we have explained it above." End of quotation.

﴿"If you could see when the wrongdoers"﴾: He informed about their state in the manner of wonder at it, and "tara" (you see) here means ra'ayta (you saw), because it is in the sense of governing the past time adverb, and the object of "tara" is omitted, meaning: the state of the wrongdoers, when they are ﴿"made to stand"﴾ (mawquufun). The answer of law (jawab law) is omitted, meaning: you would see for them a remarkable state of their humiliation, their abasement, and their mutual arguing, where nothing of that benefits them. Then He explained that returning and disputing: the followers, who are the ones who were weakened, said to their leaders, by way of blame, rebuke, and returning the reproach upon them: ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The pronoun after lawla came as a nominative pronoun, which is the most eloquent usage. The imams Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and others related its coming with a genitive pronoun, as in "lawlakum" (had it not been for you), and al-Mubarrad's denial of that is not to be heeded. Since this is a situation, the subordinate and the superior are equal in it.

For the first error cannot be fixed except by the second error, so both errors must be committed." End of quotation.

As for kaffatan in the sense of 'ammatan (general, comprehensive), what is transmitted from the grammarians is that it is only a circumstantial state (hal), and it is not used in any other way. So making it an adjective of an omitted verbal noun departs from what they transmitted, and its use as an adjective of an omitted noun is also not known. As for al-Zajjaj's statement that kaffatan means jami'an (gathering), and that the ha' in it is for emphasis, the language does not support that, because kaffa is not known to mean "gathered." As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "Whoever makes it a state…" and so on, this is a matter of disagreement. Most scholars held that this is not permissible, while Abu 'Ali, Ibn Kaysan, Ibn Burhan, and among our contemporaries Ibn Malik held that it is permissible, and this is the correct view. Among Abu 'Ali's examples: "Zayd is the best of what he can be, better than you," the estimate being: "Zayd is better than you, the best of what he can be," so he made "ma yakun" (what he can be) a state of the kaf in "minka" (than you), and placed it before it. The poet said:

"When a man finds manliness difficult in youth, its pursuit in middle age is hard for him."

And another said:

"I consoled myself for you all after your separation, by remembrance of you, until it is as if you are with me."

That is: "I consoled myself for you, all of you," that is, all together. The placing of a state before its owner, the genitive, and before what it depends on, has come, and among that is the saying of the poet:

"Infatuated with you, she has been infatuated, but separation has been decreed, and there is no way to you."

And another said:

"Heedless, the death comes upon a man, and he is called, but it is no time for refusal."

That is: "She was infatuated with you, infatuated," and "death comes upon a man heedless." If it is permissible to place it before the genitive and the governing word, then placing it before the genitive without the governing word is more permissible. And on the basis that kaffatan is a state of the people (al-nas), Ibn 'Atiyya adopted this and said: "It was placed first for emphasis." What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas is his saying: "That is, to the Arabs and the non-Arabs and all the nations," and the estimate is "to the people, all of them." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "How many are there who commit this error," to the end of his words, is objectionable, because the one who says this does not need to interpret the lam as meaning ila, since arsala (send) takes ila and also takes lam, as in His saying ﴿"And We sent you to the people as a messenger"﴾ [al-Nisa: 79]. If he interpreted the lam as meaning ila, it would not be an error, because the lam has come with the meaning of ila, and ila has come with the meaning of the lam, and arsala is among the verbs that take both with the genitive.

Then He related their statement in mockery of the resurrection and their urging for it, by way of denial, and they were not answered with the specification of the time, since that is among what God alone knows. Rather they were answered that what they were promised must come to pass, and that is the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of a similar sentence has already preceded. It is also possible that their question about what they were promised of punishment in this world, and what they urged, was in mockery from them.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "al-wa'd, al-wa'id, and al-mi'ad have the same meaning." The majority said: "al-wa'd is for good, al-wa'id is for evil, and al-mi'ad applies to this." The apparent meaning is that al-mi'ad is a noun of the pattern mif'al, used in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: "Say to you: the occurrence of the promise of a day and its fulfilment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-mi'ad is the time or place of the promise, and here it is the time, and the evidence for it is the reading of whoever read mi'ad yawm, so that yawm is put in apposition to it." End of quotation. What he said is not required, since it could be an apposition (badal) with an omitted estimate, meaning: "Say to you: the appointed time of a day," and when it is omitted, what takes its place is given its case.

The majority read mi'adu yawmin with the genitive construction (idafah). When al-Zamakhshari made al-mi'ad an adverb of time, he said: "As for the idafah, its idafah is explanatory (tabyin), as you say: 'the crushing of a garment' and 'the camel of irrigation.'" Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yazidi read mi'adun yawman with tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As for the accusative of yawm, it is for glorification (ta'zim), by supposing a verb whose estimate is 'for you there is an appointed time,' meaning a day, and I intend a day of a description, meaning such and such. It is possible that its accusative is by omitting a modifier, and it is possible that the nominative on this basis is for glorification." End of quotation. When al-mi'ad is made an adverb of time, the nominative and accusative come out in that way. It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of a day whose description is such and such. Isa read mi'adun, with tanwin, and yawma in the accusative without tanwin, being a genitive construction to a clause, so the explanation of al-Zamakhshari allows for glorification, and it allows an explanation as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of the day of such and such.

This answer came in the manner of a threat, matching the question having come in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are watched for the Day of Resurrection, which will surprise them, so they cannot delay from it nor advance before it. "The day" is the Day of Resurrection, which is what comes first to mind, or the day of the arrival of their term at the presence of their death, or the Day of Badr. These are the opinions.

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ means: in what includes monotheism, the messengership, and the resurrection mentioned earlier in it.

﴿"Nor in what is before it"﴾ is what was sent down of God's books announcing the Messenger of God. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Mecca asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in their books, and that angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an what preceded it of God's books in unbelief. "Those who disbelieved" would then be the polytheists of Quraysh and those who went their way. The well-known view is that "what is before it" is the Torah and the Gospel and the books that came before, and this is related from Ibn Jurayj. A group said that "what is before it" is the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error; its speaker did not understand the meaning of 'before' (bayn al-yad) in the language, which is what is earlier in time, and we have explained it above." End of quotation.

﴿"If you could see when the wrongdoers"﴾: He informed about their state in the manner of wonder at it, and "tara" (you see) here means ra'ayta (you saw), because it is in the sense of governing the past time adverb, and the object of "tara" is omitted, meaning: the state of the wrongdoers, when they are ﴿"made to stand"﴾ (mawquufun). The answer of law (jawab law) is omitted, meaning: you would see for them a remarkable state of their humiliation, their abasement, and their mutual arguing, where nothing of that benefits them. Then He explained that returning and disputing: the followers, who are the ones who were weakened, said to their leaders, by way of blame, rebuke, and returning the reproach upon them: ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The pronoun after lawla came as a nominative pronoun, which is the most eloquent usage. The imams Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and others related its coming with a genitive pronoun, as in "lawlakum" (had it not been for you), and al-Mubarrad's denial of that is not to be heeded. Since this is a situation, the subordinate and the superior are equal in it.

(p. 283) The followers began by rebuking their misleaders, since the leaders had lost their authority, and they could not deny that no messenger had come to them. Rather, they acknowledge it. Do you not see the words of those who were followed, ﴿after it had come to you﴾? The plural acknowledges that the Reminder had come to them. So their leaders said to them, ﴿Did we turn you away?﴾ They used the noun after the interrogative particle (ism ba'da adāt al-istifhām) to deny it, meaning that they themselves were the ones who turned them away. ﴿You were turned away by your own doing and your own choice﴾ after the interrogative particle. It is as if they said: We informed you and stood between you and the Reminder after you had resolved to enter faith. Rather, you yourselves denied your own souls their share and preferred error over guidance. So you were criminals and disbelievers by your own choice, not because of our words or our enticement. When their leaders denied that they were the cause of their disbelief, and affirmed by their words ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾ that their disbelief came from themselves, the followers countered one retraction with another, saying ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾. That is, our criminality did not come from us; rather, your scheming against us was constant, and your deceiving us night and day, as you commanded us while we were followers unable to oppose you, obedient to you because you dominated us through disbelief in God and the taking of rivals. The scheming (makr) is attributed to the night and the day by extension (ittisā') of the two time-expressions. They are then either in the accusative position as an object by extension (ʿalā al-siʿa), or in the nominative position by metaphorical predication (al-isnād al-majāzī), as people say: "a sleeping night." However, in my view the better reading is that makr is nominative as the agent, meaning: "Rather, your scheming with the night and the day turned us away," and its parallel is the saying of one who says: "I struck Zayd, but rather ʿAmr struck him," and the reply: "Rather, your servant struck him." The better estimate is that the meaning is: "Your servant struck him." It was also said that it may be a subject and predicate, meaning: "the cause of our disbelief." Qatādah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read bal makrun with tanwīn, and al-layla wa-l-nahāru in the accusative as a time adverbial (ẓarf). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr ibn Muhammad, Abu Razin, and Ibn Yaʿmar also read it with a fatha on the kāf and a shadda on the rāʾ, in the nominative and in construct (muḍāfa), and its meaning is: like the revolving of the night and the day and their alternation. Its meaning is: the postponement caused by long hope and being deceived by the days, together with these leaders' command of disbelief in God. Ibn Jubayr also read, as did Ṭalḥah and Rāshid (who is one of the Successors, among those who corrected the codices (al-maṣāḥif) by the order of al-Ḥajjāj), kadhālika, except that they put the rāʾ in the accusative as a time adverbial, its governing verb being an implied verb, meaning: "You turned us away from the scheming of the night and the day," that is, in their scheming, and its meaning is constant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: it is permissible for it to be governed by ﴿idh tamurūnanā﴾ ("when you commanded us"), as the accusative makra al-layli wa-l-nahār. He concluded. This is a mistake, because what follows idh (ḍamīr-less "idh" clause) does not govern what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Rather, the incitement is a constant scheming from which they never cease." He concluded.

And ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ came without a conjunction (wāw), because it is an answer to the speech of the oppressed, so it is resumed as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). The phrase ﴿Those who were oppressed said﴾ is conjoined to what preceded of their speech. The pronoun in (wa-asarrū) refers to all of them, the arrogant and the oppressed, who are the wrongdoers held in place (al-ẓālimūn al-mawqūfūn). The discussion of ﴿and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment﴾ has already occurred in Surah Yunus. Regret (al-nadāma) is among the inner meanings, so it does not appear; only what indicates it appears, and something else indicates it. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this has never been established in any language, that asarra is among the words with opposite meanings. The regret of those who were arrogant is over their own error and their misleading of others, and the regret of those who were oppressed is over their own error and their following of the misleaders.

﴿And We placed the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. The apparent meaning is the generality of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, so it includes the arrogant and the oppressed, because among the disbelievers there is one who has no followers to dispute words with in the Hereafter, and is not a follower of a disbelieving leader, like the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed. It was said that ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ are those among whom the dialogue previously occurred, and that the shackles indicate the manner of the punishment; they were certain that they would undergo it, so they abandoned regret.

(Is it ﴿are they recompensed﴾?) Its meaning is negation, and for this reason illā ("except") entered after the negation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 25–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "You will not be questioned about what we committed as sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do."﴾ This is more equitable and more eloquent than the first formulation, and gentler and more conciliatory. He called their action "a crime" (ijram), as they claim, although it is rewarded and thanked. He called their action "work" (amal), although it is forbidden and prohibited. It may also be intended that the attribution of this to the believers alone, not the Messenger, since the believer is hardly free of minor sins. And "what you do" refers to unbelief and what is below it of major sins. It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf, the verse that commands fighting).

﴿Say: "Our Lord will gather us together"﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿"Then He will judge (yaftah)"﴾, that is, He will decide, ﴿"with truth"﴾, with justice, so He will admit the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to the Fire.

﴿"And He is the Opener (al-Fattah), the Knower"﴾: the Judge who decides, ﴿"the All-Knowing"﴾ of the deeds of the servants. Al-Fattah and al-'Alim are intensive forms (sigat mubalagha, forms of emphasis), and this contains a threat and a rebuke. It is like saying to one whom you have advised and warned but who did not accept: "You will see the evil outcome of the matter." Isa read al-Fatih as an active participle (ism fa'il), while the majority read al-Fattah.

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined to Him as partners."﴾ The apparent meaning is that ara (show/see) here means a'lama (inform/make know), so it takes three objects: the pronoun of the speaker (the first), alladhina (the second), and shurakaa' (partners, the third). That is, "Show me, with proof and evidence, how the partnership is conceived, and whether they possess the weight of an atom or provide you with sustenance." It has also been said that it is visual sight (ru'yat basar), and shurakaa' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the omitted pronoun in alhaqtum, its meaning being: "you attached them to Him while thinking them partners to Him." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is weak, because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit (la ghina'a lahu)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying 'Show me,' when He sees them and knows them? I say: He intends by this to show them the great error in attaching partners to God, and to compare, before their eyes, between Him and their idols, in order to inform them of the state of comparing Him with them and associating them with Him." And "Nay (kalla)" is a deterrent for them from their doctrine after He broke it by refuting the comparison, as Abraham said: ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship besides God"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 67], after he had argued against them, and He drew attention to the gross enormity of their error, and that they should measure God by His true measure through His saying ﴿"He is God, the Mighty, the Wise"﴾, as if He said: "Which of those whom you joined to Him possess these attributes?" The pronoun refers to God alone, or it is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), as in His saying ﴿"Say: He is God, One"﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit," meaning it has no profit, is not good. Rather, in it there is a rebuke and reproach for them, and the intent is not the literal reality of the matter. The meaning is: those whom you claim to be God's partners are of the kind that, if you were to show them, you would be disgraced, because they are wood, stone, and other stones and inanimate things. Just as you say to a man of base origin: "Mention to me your father, with whom you compared So-and-so the noble," while you do not intend the literal mention, but you intend to rebuke him, and that if he mentioned his father he would be disgraced. Qatādah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read bal makrun with tanwīn, and al-layla wa-l-nahāru in the accusative as a time adverbial (ẓarf). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr ibn Muhammad, Abu Razin, and Ibn Yaʿmar also read it with a fatha on the kāf and a shadda on the rāʾ, in the nominative and in construct (muḍāfa), and its meaning is: like the revolving of the night and the day and their alternation. Its meaning is: the postponement caused by long hope and being deceived by the days, together with these leaders' command of disbelief in God. Ibn Jubayr also read, as did Ṭalḥah and Rāshid (who is one of the Successors, among those who corrected the codices (al-maṣāḥif) by the order of al-Ḥajjāj), kadhālika, except that they put the rāʾ in the accusative as a time adverbial, its governing verb being an implied verb, meaning: "You turned us away from the scheming of the night and the day," that is, in their scheming, and its meaning is constant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: it is permissible for it to be governed by ﴿idh tamurūnanā﴾ ("when you commanded us"), as the accusative makra al-layli wa-l-nahār. He concluded. This is a mistake, because what follows idh (ḍamīr-less "idh" clause) does not govern what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Rather, the incitement is a constant scheming from which they never cease." He concluded.

And ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ came without a conjunction (wāw), because it is an answer to the speech of the oppressed, so it is resumed as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). The phrase ﴿Those who were oppressed said﴾ is conjoined to what preceded of their speech. The pronoun in (wa-asarrū) refers to all of them, the arrogant and the oppressed, who are the wrongdoers held in place (al-ẓālimūn al-mawqūfūn). The discussion of ﴿and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment﴾ has already occurred in Surah Yunus. Regret (al-nadāma) is among the inner meanings, so it does not appear; only what indicates it appears, and something else indicates it. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this has never been established in any language, that asarra is among the words with opposite meanings. The regret of those who were arrogant is over their own error and their misleading of others, and the regret of those who were oppressed is over their own error and their following of the misleaders.

﴿And We placed the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. The apparent meaning is the generality of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, so it includes the arrogant and the oppressed, because among the disbelievers there is one who has no followers to dispute words with in the Hereafter, and is not a follower of a disbelieving leader, like the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed. It was said that ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ are those among whom the dialogue previously occurred, and that the shackles indicate the manner of the punishment; they were certain that they would undergo it, so they abandoned regret.

(Is it ﴿are they recompensed﴾?) Its meaning is negation, and for this reason illā ("except") entered after the negation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 34, verses 25–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "You will not be questioned about what we committed as sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do."﴾ This is more equitable and more eloquent than the first formulation, and gentler and more conciliatory. He called their action "a crime" (ijram), as they claim, although it is rewarded and thanked. He called their action "work" (amal), although it is forbidden and prohibited. It may also be intended that the attribution of this to the believers alone, not the Messenger, since the believer is hardly free of minor sins. And "what you do" refers to unbelief and what is below it of major sins. It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf, the verse that commands fighting).

﴿Say: "Our Lord will gather us together"﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿"Then He will judge (yaftah)"﴾, that is, He will decide, ﴿"with truth"﴾, with justice, so He will admit the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to the Fire.

﴿"And He is the Opener (al-Fattah), the Knower"﴾: the Judge who decides, ﴿"the All-Knowing"﴾ of the deeds of the servants. Al-Fattah and al-'Alim are intensive forms (sigat mubalagha, forms of emphasis), and this contains a threat and a rebuke. It is like saying to one whom you have advised and warned but who did not accept: "You will see the evil outcome of the matter." Isa read al-Fatih as an active participle (ism fa'il), while the majority read al-Fattah.

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined to Him as partners."﴾ The apparent meaning is that ara (show/see) here means a'lama (inform/make know), so it takes three objects: the pronoun of the speaker (the first), alladhina (the second), and shurakaa' (partners, the third). That is, "Show me, with proof and evidence, how the partnership is conceived, and whether they possess the weight of an atom or provide you with sustenance." It has also been said that it is visual sight (ru'yat basar), and shurakaa' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the omitted pronoun in alhaqtum, its meaning being: "you attached them to Him while thinking them partners to Him." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is weak, because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit (la ghina'a lahu)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying 'Show me,' when He sees them and knows them? I say: He intends by this to show them the great error in attaching partners to God, and to compare, before their eyes, between Him and their idols, in order to inform them of the state of comparing Him with them and associating them with Him." And "Nay (kalla)" is a deterrent for them from their doctrine after He broke it by refuting the comparison, as Abraham said: ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship besides God"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 67], after he had argued against them, and He drew attention to the gross enormity of their error, and that they should measure God by His true measure through His saying ﴿"He is God, the Mighty, the Wise"﴾, as if He said: "Which of those whom you joined to Him possess these attributes?" The pronoun refers to God alone, or it is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), as in His saying ﴿"Say: He is God, One"﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "because demanding visual sight in this matter has no benefit," meaning it has no profit, is not good. Rather, in it there is a rebuke and reproach for them, and the intent is not the literal reality of the matter. The meaning is: those whom you claim to be God's partners are of the kind that, if you were to show them, you would be disgraced, because they are wood, stone, and other stones and inanimate things. Just as you say to a man of base origin: "Mention to me your father, with whom you compared So-and-so the noble," while you do not intend the literal mention, but you intend to rebuke him, and that if he mentioned his father he would be disgraced. (p-281)

"Kaffatan" is an active participle from kaffa (to restrain). It has been said that it is a verbal noun like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah, in which case there is an omitted modifier: "except as one restraining," that is, "one who restrains people," meaning one who prevents them from unbelief, or one who prevents them from straying from your conveyance. When it is an active participle, al-Zajjaj and others said it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the kaf in "We sent you," and the meaning is: "except as one gathering the people in the conveyance," and kaffa means "gathering," and the ha' in it is for emphasis, as in 'allamah (very learned) and rawiyah (great transmitter). Al-Zamakhshari said: "except as a comprehensive message for them, encompassing them, because when it includes them it restrains them from anyone of them leaving it." He said: "Whoever makes it a state of the genitive (majrur) placed before it has erred, because placing the state of the genitive before it, in its original position, is like placing the genitive before the preposition. How many are there who commit this error and are not content with it until they add to it making the lam mean ila (to). For the first error cannot be fixed except by the second error, so both errors must be committed." End of quotation.

As for kaffatan in the sense of 'ammatan (general, comprehensive), what is transmitted from the grammarians is that it is only a circumstantial state (hal), and it is not used in any other way. So making it an adjective of an omitted verbal noun departs from what they transmitted, and its use as an adjective of an omitted noun is also not known. As for al-Zajjaj's statement that kaffatan means jami'an (gathering), and that the ha' in it is for emphasis, the language does not support that, because kaffa is not known to mean "gathered." As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "Whoever makes it a state…" and so on, this is a matter of disagreement. Most scholars held that this is not permissible, while Abu 'Ali, Ibn Kaysan, Ibn Burhan, and among our contemporaries Ibn Malik held that it is permissible, and this is the correct view. Among Abu 'Ali's examples: "Zayd is the best of what he can be, better than you," the estimate being: "Zayd is better than you, the best of what he can be," so he made "ma yakun" (what he can be) a state of the kaf in "minka" (than you), and placed it before it. The poet said:

"When a man finds manliness difficult in youth, its pursuit in middle age is hard for him."

And another said:

"I consoled myself for you all after your separation, by remembrance of you, until it is as if you are with me."

That is: "I consoled myself for you, all of you," that is, all together. The placing of a state before its owner, the genitive, and before what it depends on, has come, and among that is the saying of the poet:

"Infatuated with you, she has been infatuated, but separation has been decreed, and there is no way to you."

And another said:

"Heedless, the death comes upon a man, and he is called, but it is no time for refusal."

That is: "She was infatuated with you, infatuated," and "death comes upon a man heedless." If it is permissible to place it before the genitive and the governing word, then placing it before the genitive without the governing word is more permissible. And on the basis that kaffatan is a state of the people (al-nas), Ibn 'Atiyya adopted this and said: "It was placed first for emphasis." What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas is his saying: "That is, to the Arabs and the non-Arabs and all the nations," and the estimate is "to the people, all of them." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "How many are there who commit this error," to the end of his words, is objectionable, because the one who says this does not need to interpret the lam as meaning ila, since arsala (send) takes ila and also takes lam, as in His saying ﴿"And We sent you to the people as a messenger"﴾ [al-Nisa: 79]. If he interpreted the lam as meaning ila, it would not be an error, because the lam has come with the meaning of ila, and ila has come with the meaning of the lam, and arsala is among the verbs that take both with the genitive.

Then He related their statement in mockery of the resurrection and their urging for it, by way of denial, and they were not answered with the specification of the time, since that is among what God alone knows. Rather they were answered that what they were promised must come to pass, and that is the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of a similar sentence has already preceded. It is also possible that their question about what they were promised of punishment in this world, and what they urged, was in mockery from them.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "al-wa'd, al-wa'id, and al-mi'ad have the same meaning." The majority said: "al-wa'd is for good, al-wa'id is for evil, and al-mi'ad applies to this." The apparent meaning is that al-mi'ad is a noun of the pattern mif'al, used in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: "Say to you: the occurrence of the promise of a day and its fulfilment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-mi'ad is the time or place of the promise, and here it is the time, and the evidence for it is the reading of whoever read mi'ad yawm, so that yawm is put in apposition to it." End of quotation. What he said is not required, since it could be an apposition (badal) with an omitted estimate, meaning: "Say to you: the appointed time of a day," and when it is omitted, what takes its place is given its case.

The majority read mi'adu yawmin with the genitive construction (idafah). When al-Zamakhshari made al-mi'ad an adverb of time, he said: "As for the idafah, its idafah is explanatory (tabyin), as you say: 'the crushing of a garment' and 'the camel of irrigation.'" Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yazidi read mi'adun yawman with tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As for the accusative of yawm, it is for glorification (ta'zim), by supposing a verb whose estimate is 'for you there is an appointed time,' meaning a day, and I intend a day of a description, meaning such and such. It is possible that its accusative is by omitting a modifier, and it is possible that the nominative on this basis is for glorification." End of quotation. When al-mi'ad is made an adverb of time, the nominative and accusative come out in that way. It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of a day whose description is such and such. Isa read mi'adun, with tanwin, and yawma in the accusative without tanwin, being a genitive construction to a clause, so the explanation of al-Zamakhshari allows for glorification, and it allows an explanation as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of the day of such and such.

This answer came in the manner of a threat, matching the question having come in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are watched for the Day of Resurrection, which will surprise them, so they cannot delay from it nor advance before it. "The day" is the Day of Resurrection, which is what comes first to mind, or the day of the arrival of their term at the presence of their death, or the Day of Badr. These are the opinions.

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ means: in what includes monotheism, the messengership, and the resurrection mentioned earlier in it.

﴿"Nor in what is before it"﴾ is what was sent down of God's books announcing the Messenger of God. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Mecca asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in their books, and that angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an what preceded it of God's books in unbelief. "Those who disbelieved" would then be the polytheists of Quraysh and those who went their way. The well-known view is that "what is before it" is the Torah and the Gospel and the books that came before, and this is related from Ibn Jurayj. A group said that "what is before it" is the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error; its speaker did not understand the meaning of 'before' (bayn al-yad) in the language, which is what is earlier in time, and we have explained it above." End of quotation.

﴿"If you could see when the wrongdoers"﴾: He informed about their state in the manner of wonder at it, and "tara" (you see) here means ra'ayta (you saw), because it is in the sense of governing the past time adverb, and the object of "tara" is omitted, meaning: the state of the wrongdoers, when they are ﴿"made to stand"﴾ (mawquufun). The answer of law (jawab law) is omitted, meaning: you would see for them a remarkable state of their humiliation, their abasement, and their mutual arguing, where nothing of that benefits them. Then He explained that returning and disputing: the followers, who are the ones who were weakened, said to their leaders, by way of blame, rebuke, and returning the reproach upon them: ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The pronoun after lawla came as a nominative pronoun, which is the most eloquent usage. The imams Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and others related its coming with a genitive pronoun, as in "lawlakum" (had it not been for you), and al-Mubarrad's denial of that is not to be heeded. Since this is a situation, the subordinate and the superior are equal in it.

Do you not see the words of those who were followed, ﴿after it had come to you﴾? The plural acknowledges that the Reminder had come to them. So their leaders said to them, ﴿Did we turn you away?﴾ They used the noun after the interrogative particle (ism ba'da adāt al-istifhām) to deny it, meaning that they themselves were the ones who turned them away. ﴿You were turned away by your own doing and your own choice﴾ after the interrogative particle. It is as if they said: We informed you and stood between you and the Reminder after you had resolved to enter faith. Rather, you yourselves denied your own souls their share and preferred error over guidance. So you were criminals and disbelievers by your own choice, not because of our words or our enticement.
