Abu 'Ubayd said: "al-wa'd, al-wa'id, and al-mi'ad have the same meaning." The majority said: "al-wa'd is for good, al-wa'id is for evil, and al-mi'ad applies to this." The apparent meaning is that al-mi'ad is a noun of the pattern mif'al, used in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: "Say to you: the occurrence of the promise of a day and its fulfilment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-mi'ad is the time or place of the promise, and here it is the time, and the evidence for it is the reading of whoever read mi'ad yawm, so that yawm is put in apposition to it." End of quotation. What he said is not required, since it could be an apposition (badal) with an omitted estimate, meaning: "Say to you: the appointed time of a day," and when it is omitted, what takes its place is given its case.

The majority read mi'adu yawmin with the genitive construction (idafah). When al-Zamakhshari made al-mi'ad an adverb of time, he said: "As for the idafah, its idafah is explanatory (tabyin), as you say: 'the crushing of a garment' and 'the camel of irrigation.'" Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yazidi read mi'adun yawman with tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As for the accusative of yawm, it is for glorification (ta'zim), by supposing a verb whose estimate is 'for you there is an appointed time,' meaning a day, and I intend a day of a description, meaning such and such. It is possible that its accusative is by omitting a modifier, and it is possible that the nominative on this basis is for glorification." End of quotation. When al-mi'ad is made an adverb of time, the nominative and accusative come out in that way. It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of a day whose description is such and such. Isa read mi'adun, with tanwin, and yawma in the accusative without tanwin, being a genitive construction to a clause, so the explanation of al-Zamakhshari allows for glorification, and it allows an explanation as an adverb of time by omitting a modifier, meaning: the fulfilment of the promise of the day of such and such.

This answer came in the manner of a threat, matching the question having come in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are watched for the Day of Resurrection, which will surprise them, so they cannot delay from it nor advance before it. "The day" is the Day of Resurrection, which is what comes first to mind, or the day of the arrival of their term at the presence of their death, or the Day of Badr. These are the opinions.

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ means: in what includes monotheism, the messengership, and the resurrection mentioned earlier in it.

﴿"Nor in what is before it"﴾ is what was sent down of God's books announcing the Messenger of God. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Mecca asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in their books, and that angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an what preceded it of God's books in unbelief. "Those who disbelieved" would then be the polytheists of Quraysh and those who went their way. The well-known view is that "what is before it" is the Torah and the Gospel and the books that came before, and this is related from Ibn Jurayj. A group said that "what is before it" is the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error; its speaker did not understand the meaning of 'before' (bayn al-yad) in the language, which is what is earlier in time, and we have explained it above." End of quotation.

﴿"If you could see when the wrongdoers"﴾: He informed about their state in the manner of wonder at it, and "tara" (you see) here means ra'ayta (you saw), because it is in the sense of governing the past time adverb, and the object of "tara" is omitted, meaning: the state of the wrongdoers, when they are ﴿"made to stand"﴾ (mawquufun). The answer of law (jawab law) is omitted, meaning: you would see for them a remarkable state of their humiliation, their abasement, and their mutual arguing, where nothing of that benefits them. Then He explained that returning and disputing: the followers, who are the ones who were weakened, said to their leaders, by way of blame, rebuke, and returning the reproach upon them: ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The pronoun after lawla came as a nominative pronoun, which is the most eloquent usage. The imams Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and others related its coming with a genitive pronoun, as in "lawlakum" (had it not been for you), and al-Mubarrad's denial of that is not to be heeded. Since this is a situation, the subordinate and the superior are equal in it.

(p. 283) The followers began by rebuking their misleaders, since the leaders had lost their authority, and they could not deny that no messenger had come to them. Rather, they acknowledge it. Do you not see the words of those who were followed, ﴿after it had come to you﴾? The plural acknowledges that the Reminder had come to them. So their leaders said to them, ﴿Did we turn you away?﴾ They used the noun after the interrogative particle (ism ba'da adāt al-istifhām) to deny it, meaning that they themselves were the ones who turned them away. ﴿You were turned away by your own doing and your own choice﴾ after the interrogative particle. It is as if they said: We informed you and stood between you and the Reminder after you had resolved to enter faith. Rather, you yourselves denied your own souls their share and preferred error over guidance. So you were criminals and disbelievers by your own choice, not because of our words or our enticement. When their leaders denied that they were the cause of their disbelief, and affirmed by their words ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾ that their disbelief came from themselves, the followers countered one retraction with another, saying ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾. That is, our criminality did not come from us; rather, your scheming against us was constant, and your deceiving us night and day, as you commanded us while we were followers unable to oppose you, obedient to you because you dominated us through disbelief in God and the taking of rivals. The scheming (makr) is attributed to the night and the day by extension (ittisā') of the two time-expressions. They are then either in the accusative position as an object by extension (ʿalā al-siʿa), or in the nominative position by metaphorical predication (al-isnād al-majāzī), as people say: "a sleeping night." However, in my view the better reading is that makr is nominative as the agent, meaning: "Rather, your scheming with the night and the day turned us away," and its parallel is the saying of one who says: "I struck Zayd, but rather ʿAmr struck him," and the reply: "Rather, your servant struck him." The better estimate is that the meaning is: "Your servant struck him." It was also said that it may be a subject and predicate, meaning: "the cause of our disbelief." Qatādah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read bal makrun with tanwīn, and al-layla wa-l-nahāru in the accusative as a time adverbial (ẓarf). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr ibn Muhammad, Abu Razin, and Ibn Yaʿmar also read it with a fatha on the kāf and a shadda on the rāʾ, in the nominative and in construct (muḍāfa), and its meaning is: like the revolving of the night and the day and their alternation. Its meaning is: the postponement caused by long hope and being deceived by the days, together with these leaders' command of disbelief in God. Ibn Jubayr also read, as did Ṭalḥah and Rāshid (who is one of the Successors, among those who corrected the codices (al-maṣāḥif) by the order of al-Ḥajjāj), kadhālika, except that they put the rāʾ in the accusative as a time adverbial, its governing verb being an implied verb, meaning: "You turned us away from the scheming of the night and the day," that is, in their scheming, and its meaning is constant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: it is permissible for it to be governed by ﴿idh tamurūnanā﴾ ("when you commanded us"), as the accusative makra al-layli wa-l-nahār. He concluded. This is a mistake, because what follows idh (ḍamīr-less "idh" clause) does not govern what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Rather, the incitement is a constant scheming from which they never cease." He concluded.

And ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ came without a conjunction (wāw), because it is an answer to the speech of the oppressed, so it is resumed as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). The phrase ﴿Those who were oppressed said﴾ is conjoined to what preceded of their speech. The pronoun in (wa-asarrū) refers to all of them, the arrogant and the oppressed, who are the wrongdoers held in place (al-ẓālimūn al-mawqūfūn). The discussion of ﴿and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment﴾ has already occurred in Surah Yunus. Regret (al-nadāma) is among the inner meanings, so it does not appear; only what indicates it appears, and something else indicates it. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this has never been established in any language, that asarra is among the words with opposite meanings. The regret of those who were arrogant is over their own error and their misleading of others, and the regret of those who were oppressed is over their own error and their following of the misleaders.

﴿And We placed the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. The apparent meaning is the generality of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, so it includes the arrogant and the oppressed, because among the disbelievers there is one who has no followers to dispute words with in the Hereafter, and is not a follower of a disbelieving leader, like the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed. It was said that ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ are those among whom the dialogue previously occurred, and that the shackles indicate the manner of the punishment; they were certain that they would undergo it, so they abandoned regret.

(Is it ﴿are they recompensed﴾?) Its meaning is negation, and for this reason illā ("except") entered after the negation.

(p-٢٨٤) ﴿Never did We send a warner to a town but its affluent ones said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ ﴿And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know."﴾ ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in nearness, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a double reward for what they did, and they will be safe in the upper chambers.﴾ ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, will be brought to the punishment.﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers."﴾ ﴿And the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ ﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm another, and We will say to those who wronged, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, they say, "This is only a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship," and they say, "This is only a fabricated lie," and those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is only evident magic."﴾.

(p-٢٨٥) (﴿Never did We send﴾) the verse. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people, the Quraysh, of disbelief and boasting in wealth and children. It also indicates that what they mentioned of this is the habit of the affluent (al-mutrafun) toward their prophets, so their matter should not concern you. The phrase ﴿warner﴾ (min nadhir) is general, meaning you warn them of the punishment of Allah if they do not affirm His oneness. The phrase ﴿its affluent ones said﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and He specified the affluent because they were the first to deny the messengers, due to their preoccupation with the glitter of this world and what dominated their minds of it, so their hearts are always occupied and absorbed, unlike the poor. The poor are free of the worldly pleasures, so their hearts are more receptive to good, and for this reason they are the followers of the prophets, as came in the hadith of Heraclius (Hiraql). The word ﴿with what﴾ (bima) is connected to ﴿disbelievers﴾ (kafirun), and the word ﴿with which﴾ (bihi) is connected to ﴿you have been sent﴾ (ursiltum), and ﴿what﴾ (ma) is general, covering what the warners brought: calling to belief in Allah, singling Him out in worship, informing that they are His messengers to them, and the resurrection and the recompense for deeds. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ (qalu) refers to the affluent; it has been said that it refers to the Quraysh, and what follows of address supports this in His saying ﴿Say﴾ (qul), because those affluent who came before and perished are not addressed, so only those present would speak. His saying ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children﴾ is addressed to them. They argued for Allah's pleasure with them by His bounty toward them: if He were not honoring them, He would not have expanded (provision) for us; as for you, because of your abasement before Him, He has deprived you, O followers of the messengers. Then they say, "They will not be punished," a general negation, because the prophets may warn of a punishment that is hasty in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, so they negated all of that. Either they were deniers of the Hereafter, in which case they negated their punishment there, because if it does not exist, there is no punishment in it; or they affirm it in reality or by way of supposition, and they say: just as He bestowed favor upon us in this world, He will bestow favor upon us in the Hereafter in the same condition as this world, by a corrupt analogy (qiyas fasid). Allah refuted this by saying that provision is a bounty from Him, distributed upon us in the Hereafter according to the condition of this world, as He wills. ﴿For whom He wills﴾: He may expand upon the disobedient and restrict upon the obedient, and He may expand upon both; existence bears witness to this, so expansion in this world should not be used as an analogy, because in the Hereafter it is only in accordance with righteous deeds. Al-A'mash read ﴿yuqaddiru﴾ (restricts) with a shadda in both places; the majority read it without shadda, and its meaning is "restricts," the opposite of ﴿yabsutu﴾ (extends).

﴿But most people﴾ like these disbelievers ﴿do not know﴾ that provision is distributed by will, and that it is not a proof of approval. Then He informed that their wealth and children, of which they boasted, do not bring them near to Allah; rather, belief and righteous deeds bring one near. The majority read ﴿bi-llati﴾ (with that which), and a broken plural (jam' taksir) of rational and non-rational beings may be treated as a feminine singular. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿that which﴾ refers to piety (taqwa), which alone brings one near to Allah in nearness, meaning your wealth is not that which is set for bringing near. End of his words. So he made ﴿alla﴾ a qualifier of an omitted noun, which is piety. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted noun. The apparent meaning is that ﴿alla﴾ refers to wealth and children, as al-Farra' said. He also said, along with al-Zajjaj: it was omitted from the first part due to the second part indicating it, and the estimate is ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which brings you near to Us in nearness﴾. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted element, since it is valid for ﴿alla﴾ to refer to the collective of wealth and children. Al-Hasan read ﴿bi-l-latī﴾ in the plural, which also refers to wealth and children. It is read ﴿bi-lladhi﴾, and ﴿zulfa﴾ (nearness) is a verbal noun like ﴿qurba﴾ (kinship/nearness), and its accusative case is as a verbal noun from the meaning, meaning "it brings you near." Al-Dahhak read ﴿zulafan﴾ with a fatha on the lam and tanwin on the fa', the plural of ﴿zulfa﴾, which is a degree of nearness.

﴿Except for those who believe﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not from the same category), and it is in the accusative as an exception, meaning "but rather whoever believes." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾: so his belief and his deed bring him near. (p-٢٨٦) Al-Zajjaj said: it is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in ﴿brings you near﴾. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because the kaf and mim are for the addressee, so substitution is not permissible; if this were permissible, it would be permissible to say: "I saw you Zayd." This statement of Abu Ishaq is the statement of al-Farra'. End. The school of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permissible to substitute from the pronoun of the addressee and the speaker, but substitution in this verse is not valid. Do you not see that it is not valid to make the verb that serves as the relative clause (silah) free for what follows ﴿illa﴾ (except)? If you say: "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Khalid," it would not be valid. Al-Zajjaj imagined that the relative clause, although it is negated in meaning, makes substitution valid, but it is not permissible except where the free element is valid. Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: ﴿except for those who believe﴾ is an exception from the ﴿you﴾ (kum) in ﴿brings you near﴾, and the meaning is: wealth does not bring anyone near except the believing righteous one who spends it in the way of Allah; and children do not bring anyone near except one who taught them good, and guided them in religion and prepared them for righteousness and obedience. End. And this is not permissible, as we mentioned: it is not permissible to say "Zayd is not the one who goes out except as a brother," nor "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Amr," nor "Zayd is not the one who passes except by Bakr." The construction that al-Zamakhshari formed from his saying "does not bring anyone near except the believer" does not agree with the Qur'an; in the form he constructed, what he said is permissible, but in the wording of the Qur'an it is not. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿man﴾ (who) be in the nominative position, and the meaning of the sentence according to him is: what is the one brought near? ﴿Except whoever believes﴾. End. This statement is one from which no meaning is obtained, as if he was asleep when he said that.

The majority read ﴿jaza'u al-di'f﴾ (the reward of double) with an idafa (construct), where the verbal noun is annexed to its object. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as a passive form, the verb whose subject is not named, and said: that they be recompensed double. The verbal noun in its being formed in the passive form of the unnamed subject is disputed, and the correct view is that it is prohibited. Here it is estimated that Allah makes them pass beyond the double, meaning He multiplies their good deeds for them: a good deed is multiplied tenfold, and up to seven hundred times for whom He wills. Qatada read ﴿jaza'un al-di'fu﴾ with both nominative: so ﴿al-di'f﴾ is a substitute (badal). Ya'qub in one narration read ﴿jaza'an﴾ with accusative and ﴿al-di'fu﴾ with nominative; al-Dani transmitted this reading from Qatada, and ﴿jaza'an﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), like your saying: "in the house, Zayd is standing." The majority read ﴿fi al-ghurufat﴾ in the plural with a damma on the ra'; al-Hasan and 'Asim (with a variant from him) read it with sukun on the ra'; al-A'mash and Muhammad ibn Ka'b read it with sukun; and some readers read it with fatha. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-A'mash, Talha, and Hamza, in his choice, read ﴿al-ghurfa﴾ in the singular with a sukun on the ra'; and Ibn Thabbat also read it with fatha in the singular.

When He mentioned the reward of those who believe, He mentioned the punishment of those who disbelieve, to make the contrast between the two recompenses clear. The explanation of a similar word has preceded. Since their boasting was in the abundance of wealth and children, they were informed that this is according to what Allah willed, and this meaning emphasizes that this operates according to what Allah willed, except that it is according to desert, not as honor nor as humiliation. The meaning of ﴿so He will replace it﴾ is that He will bring a replacement and a substitute for it. The phrase ﴿of His servants﴾ (min 'ibadihi) suggests the believers, and similarly the address in ﴿whatever you spend﴾ here intends the provision of the believers, so the context of ﴿Say, indeed my Lord extends﴾ is not the context of what was said to the disbelievers, but the context of admonition, of renunciation of this world, and of urging spending in obedience to Allah, and replacing what was spent, either immediately in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, and this is conditional upon seeking the face of Allah. Mujahid said: whoever has of this wealth what sustains him, let him aim (for moderation), and know that provision is apportioned, and perhaps what is apportioned to him is little, yet he spends as one who is wealthy, so he spends all that is in his hand, and then remains in poverty all his life and cannot manage.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾ in the Hereafter. The meaning of the verse: whatever there is of replacement, it is from Him. ﴿The best of providers﴾ came in the plural, although the provider in reality is Allah alone; because it is said: a man provides for his dependents, a commander for his army, a master for his slave, and "providers" is pluralized with this consideration, but those (human providers) are provided from what Allah has provided them, and He has made them free to dispose of it, whereas Allah the Exalted provides from treasuries that do not perish, and from bringing forth from non-existence into existence.

﴿And the Day He gathers them all﴾ — that is, the deniers, those who came before and those who came after. The majority read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ and ﴿naqulu﴾ with a nun in both, and Hafs read them with a ya', and this was mentioned in al-An'am. The address to the angels is a rebuke to the disbelievers, and Allah knows that the angels are (p-٢٨٧) exalted and free from what was directed at them of questioning; this is only by way of establishing the disbelievers' guilt, and the evil of what they committed of worshipping other than Allah is known, and that those whom they worshipped disown them. ﴿These﴾ (ha'ulā') is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿used to worship﴾ (kanu ya'budun), and ﴿you﴾ (iyyakum) is the object of ﴿worship﴾. Since it came first, it became detached; it was fronted because it is more emphatic in address, and because ﴿worship﴾ becomes a closing word (fasila, rhyme-end). If the pronoun had been used in its detached form, the structure would have been ya'budunakum, and it would not have been a closing word. The fronting of this element has been used as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of kana (was) over it when kana's predicate is a sentence; this is a matter of disagreement: Ibn al-Sarraj permitted it, and some grammarians prohibited it, and likewise they prohibited its placement in the middle when it is a sentence. Ibn al-Sarraj said: analogy permits it, but it has not been heard. The point of proof from the verse is that fronting the object indicates fronting the verb, so just as ﴿you﴾ may be fronted, ﴿worship﴾ may be fronted; but this rule is not consistent, and it is better to prohibit it until a proof from the Arabs confirms its permissibility.

When they answered Allah, they began by glorifying Him and declaring Him free of every evil, as Jesus, peace be upon him, said ﴿Glory be to You﴾ (subhanaka), then they affiliated themselves to His guardianship rather than those disbelievers, meaning ﴿You are our Protector﴾, since there is no alliance between us and them.

In their words ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ there is an indication of what they had worshipped, though it is not stated explicitly. The particle of retraction *bal* ("rather") points to it, because the one worshipped, if he is not pleased with the worship of his worshipper and does not desire it, is not truly worshipped by that worshipper. For this reason they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, since their vile deeds, arising from the whisperings, seduction and desires of the devils, truly worship them. Hence they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, for the devils are pleased with those deeds. It has been said: the devils made images of a people of the jinn appear to them, and said, "These are the images of the angels, so worship them." It has also been said: they (the devils) used to enter into the bellies of the idols when they were worshipped, and so they worshipped through their worship. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the angels did not deny that human beings worshipped them, but they affirmed that they had no share in that. The worship of the jinn by human beings consists in their acknowledging the jinn's authority over them and their listening to the jinn's whisperings and seduction, and this is a kind of worship. It is possible that among the disbelieving nations there were those who worshipped the jinn, and the Qur'an contains verses from which it appears that the jinn were worshipped, in Surat al-An'am and elsewhere. End of quotation. Now, if they had indeed worshipped the jinn, what is the meaning of their words ﴿most of them were believers﴾ (said of the jinn), instead of "all of them", when they themselves had reported that they used to worship the jinn? The answer is that they did not claim to encompass everything, for there may be among the unbelievers those whom the angels did not observe. Or they limited the statement to the majority because of their belief in the jinn, since faith is an act of the heart, and they did not claim knowledge of all the deeds of their hearts, for that belongs to God Most High alone. The meaning of "believers" (*mu'minun*) is "those who affirm" that they were the ones worshipped. It has also been said: "those who affirm" that they are the daughters of God and that they are angels, ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. As for the one who says that "most" here means "all", nothing objectionable arises for him, but this is not the established usage of the language.

﴿Today﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection. The address in "some of you" (*ba'dukum*) is said to be to the angels, since they are the ones addressed in His words ﴿Are these the ones who used to worship you?﴾. This would be a rebuke to the disbelievers, when it is made clear to them that those they worshipped neither benefit nor harm. This is supported by ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and because what follows is ﴿and We shall say to those who did wrong﴾. Had the address been to the disbelievers, the construction would have been "so taste". It has also been said that the address is to the disbelievers, because the mention of the Day implies their presence, and His words "and He says" would be an emphasis on the description of their state in wrongdoing. It has also been said that it is an address from God to those who were worshipped and to those who worshipped. As for His words "benefit" (*naf'an*), it is said that this means by intercession, and "harm" (*darran*) means by punishment. It is said here ﴿the Fire which you used to deny﴾, while in the Sajdah it is ﴿the punishment which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. Each of the two refers to the punishment and to the Fire respectively, because here they were not yet involved in the punishment; rather, this was the first time they saw the Fire, as it came directly after the gathering, so the Fire was described to them as the very thing you used to deny. As for the one in the Sajdah, they are involved in the punishment, hesitating about it, due to His words ﴿every time they wish to leave it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So the punishment that they are actually undergoing was described to them, namely the everlasting punishment which they had denied.

The demonstrative in His words "this is not but a man" refers to the reciter of the verses, which is implied by His words "and when they are recited", namely the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God Most High related their slanders made upon hearing the Qur'an recited to them. They began first by attacking the reciter, for he disparages your gods. Second, they attacked what the Messenger brought of the Qur'an, saying that it is a fabricated lie from himself and not from God. Third, they said that what he brought is clear magic, because it contains what brings about attraction, the influence of souls upon it, and their response to it. They attacked the Messenger, what he brought, and his description, and it is possible that this was said by them collectively, and it is also possible that each statement was made by a different group from those who made the other statements. In His words "when it came to them" there is evidence that when it came to them they did not reflect upon it, but rushed to deny it and attribute it to magic. They did not suffice with saying "it is magic", but went on to describe it as clear to anyone who reflects upon it. It has been said that the denial of the Qur'an and of the miracle was agreed upon among the polytheists and the People of the Book, and so God Most High said ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth﴾, in a general sense.

(p-٢٨٤) ﴿Never did We send a warner to a town but its affluent ones said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ ﴿And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know."﴾ ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in nearness, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a double reward for what they did, and they will be safe in the upper chambers.﴾ ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, will be brought to the punishment.﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers."﴾ ﴿And the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ ﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm another, and We will say to those who wronged, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, they say, "This is only a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship," and they say, "This is only a fabricated lie," and those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is only evident magic."﴾.

(p-٢٨٥) (﴿Never did We send﴾) the verse. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people, the Quraysh, of disbelief and boasting in wealth and children. It also indicates that what they mentioned of this is the habit of the affluent (al-mutrafun) toward their prophets, so their matter should not concern you. The phrase ﴿warner﴾ (min nadhir) is general, meaning you warn them of the punishment of Allah if they do not affirm His oneness. The phrase ﴿its affluent ones said﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and He specified the affluent because they were the first to deny the messengers, due to their preoccupation with the glitter of this world and what dominated their minds of it, so their hearts are always occupied and absorbed, unlike the poor. The poor are free of the worldly pleasures, so their hearts are more receptive to good, and for this reason they are the followers of the prophets, as came in the hadith of Heraclius (Hiraql). The word ﴿with what﴾ (bima) is connected to ﴿disbelievers﴾ (kafirun), and the word ﴿with which﴾ (bihi) is connected to ﴿you have been sent﴾ (ursiltum), and ﴿what﴾ (ma) is general, covering what the warners brought: calling to belief in Allah, singling Him out in worship, informing that they are His messengers to them, and the resurrection and the recompense for deeds. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ (qalu) refers to the affluent; it has been said that it refers to the Quraysh, and what follows of address supports this in His saying ﴿Say﴾ (qul), because those affluent who came before and perished are not addressed, so only those present would speak. His saying ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children﴾ is addressed to them. They argued for Allah's pleasure with them by His bounty toward them: if He were not honoring them, He would not have expanded (provision) for us; as for you, because of your abasement before Him, He has deprived you, O followers of the messengers. Then they say, "They will not be punished," a general negation, because the prophets may warn of a punishment that is hasty in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, so they negated all of that. Either they were deniers of the Hereafter, in which case they negated their punishment there, because if it does not exist, there is no punishment in it; or they affirm it in reality or by way of supposition, and they say: just as He bestowed favor upon us in this world, He will bestow favor upon us in the Hereafter in the same condition as this world, by a corrupt analogy (qiyas fasid). Allah refuted this by saying that provision is a bounty from Him, distributed upon us in the Hereafter according to the condition of this world, as He wills. ﴿For whom He wills﴾: He may expand upon the disobedient and restrict upon the obedient, and He may expand upon both; existence bears witness to this, so expansion in this world should not be used as an analogy, because in the Hereafter it is only in accordance with righteous deeds. Al-A'mash read ﴿yuqaddiru﴾ (restricts) with a shadda in both places; the majority read it without shadda, and its meaning is "restricts," the opposite of ﴿yabsutu﴾ (extends).

﴿But most people﴾ like these disbelievers ﴿do not know﴾ that provision is distributed by will, and that it is not a proof of approval. Then He informed that their wealth and children, of which they boasted, do not bring them near to Allah; rather, belief and righteous deeds bring one near. The majority read ﴿bi-llati﴾ (with that which), and a broken plural (jam' taksir) of rational and non-rational beings may be treated as a feminine singular. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿that which﴾ refers to piety (taqwa), which alone brings one near to Allah in nearness, meaning your wealth is not that which is set for bringing near. End of his words. So he made ﴿alla﴾ a qualifier of an omitted noun, which is piety. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted noun. The apparent meaning is that ﴿alla﴾ refers to wealth and children, as al-Farra' said. He also said, along with al-Zajjaj: it was omitted from the first part due to the second part indicating it, and the estimate is ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which brings you near to Us in nearness﴾. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted element, since it is valid for ﴿alla﴾ to refer to the collective of wealth and children. Al-Hasan read ﴿bi-l-latī﴾ in the plural, which also refers to wealth and children. It is read ﴿bi-lladhi﴾, and ﴿zulfa﴾ (nearness) is a verbal noun like ﴿qurba﴾ (kinship/nearness), and its accusative case is as a verbal noun from the meaning, meaning "it brings you near." Al-Dahhak read ﴿zulafan﴾ with a fatha on the lam and tanwin on the fa', the plural of ﴿zulfa﴾, which is a degree of nearness.

﴿Except for those who believe﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not from the same category), and it is in the accusative as an exception, meaning "but rather whoever believes." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾: so his belief and his deed bring him near. (p-٢٨٦) Al-Zajjaj said: it is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in ﴿brings you near﴾. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because the kaf and mim are for the addressee, so substitution is not permissible; if this were permissible, it would be permissible to say: "I saw you Zayd." This statement of Abu Ishaq is the statement of al-Farra'. End. The school of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permissible to substitute from the pronoun of the addressee and the speaker, but substitution in this verse is not valid. Do you not see that it is not valid to make the verb that serves as the relative clause (silah) free for what follows ﴿illa﴾ (except)? If you say: "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Khalid," it would not be valid. Al-Zajjaj imagined that the relative clause, although it is negated in meaning, makes substitution valid, but it is not permissible except where the free element is valid. Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: ﴿except for those who believe﴾ is an exception from the ﴿you﴾ (kum) in ﴿brings you near﴾, and the meaning is: wealth does not bring anyone near except the believing righteous one who spends it in the way of Allah; and children do not bring anyone near except one who taught them good, and guided them in religion and prepared them for righteousness and obedience. End. And this is not permissible, as we mentioned: it is not permissible to say "Zayd is not the one who goes out except as a brother," nor "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Amr," nor "Zayd is not the one who passes except by Bakr." The construction that al-Zamakhshari formed from his saying "does not bring anyone near except the believer" does not agree with the Qur'an; in the form he constructed, what he said is permissible, but in the wording of the Qur'an it is not. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿man﴾ (who) be in the nominative position, and the meaning of the sentence according to him is: what is the one brought near? ﴿Except whoever believes﴾. End. This statement is one from which no meaning is obtained, as if he was asleep when he said that.

The majority read ﴿jaza'u al-di'f﴾ (the reward of double) with an idafa (construct), where the verbal noun is annexed to its object. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as a passive form, the verb whose subject is not named, and said: that they be recompensed double. The verbal noun in its being formed in the passive form of the unnamed subject is disputed, and the correct view is that it is prohibited. Here it is estimated that Allah makes them pass beyond the double, meaning He multiplies their good deeds for them: a good deed is multiplied tenfold, and up to seven hundred times for whom He wills. Qatada read ﴿jaza'un al-di'fu﴾ with both nominative: so ﴿al-di'f﴾ is a substitute (badal). Ya'qub in one narration read ﴿jaza'an﴾ with accusative and ﴿al-di'fu﴾ with nominative; al-Dani transmitted this reading from Qatada, and ﴿jaza'an﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), like your saying: "in the house, Zayd is standing." The majority read ﴿fi al-ghurufat﴾ in the plural with a damma on the ra'; al-Hasan and 'Asim (with a variant from him) read it with sukun on the ra'; al-A'mash and Muhammad ibn Ka'b read it with sukun; and some readers read it with fatha. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-A'mash, Talha, and Hamza, in his choice, read ﴿al-ghurfa﴾ in the singular with a sukun on the ra'; and Ibn Thabbat also read it with fatha in the singular.

When He mentioned the reward of those who believe, He mentioned the punishment of those who disbelieve, to make the contrast between the two recompenses clear. The explanation of a similar word has preceded. Since their boasting was in the abundance of wealth and children, they were informed that this is according to what Allah willed, and this meaning emphasizes that this operates according to what Allah willed, except that it is according to desert, not as honor nor as humiliation. The meaning of ﴿so He will replace it﴾ is that He will bring a replacement and a substitute for it. The phrase ﴿of His servants﴾ (min 'ibadihi) suggests the believers, and similarly the address in ﴿whatever you spend﴾ here intends the provision of the believers, so the context of ﴿Say, indeed my Lord extends﴾ is not the context of what was said to the disbelievers, but the context of admonition, of renunciation of this world, and of urging spending in obedience to Allah, and replacing what was spent, either immediately in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, and this is conditional upon seeking the face of Allah. Mujahid said: whoever has of this wealth what sustains him, let him aim (for moderation), and know that provision is apportioned, and perhaps what is apportioned to him is little, yet he spends as one who is wealthy, so he spends all that is in his hand, and then remains in poverty all his life and cannot manage.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾ in the Hereafter. The meaning of the verse: whatever there is of replacement, it is from Him. ﴿The best of providers﴾ came in the plural, although the provider in reality is Allah alone; because it is said: a man provides for his dependents, a commander for his army, a master for his slave, and "providers" is pluralized with this consideration, but those (human providers) are provided from what Allah has provided them, and He has made them free to dispose of it, whereas Allah the Exalted provides from treasuries that do not perish, and from bringing forth from non-existence into existence.

﴿And the Day He gathers them all﴾ — that is, the deniers, those who came before and those who came after. The majority read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ and ﴿naqulu﴾ with a nun in both, and Hafs read them with a ya', and this was mentioned in al-An'am. The address to the angels is a rebuke to the disbelievers, and Allah knows that the angels are (p-٢٨٧) exalted and free from what was directed at them of questioning; this is only by way of establishing the disbelievers' guilt, and the evil of what they committed of worshipping other than Allah is known, and that those whom they worshipped disown them. ﴿These﴾ (ha'ulā') is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿used to worship﴾ (kanu ya'budun), and ﴿you﴾ (iyyakum) is the object of ﴿worship﴾. Since it came first, it became detached; it was fronted because it is more emphatic in address, and because ﴿worship﴾ becomes a closing word (fasila, rhyme-end). If the pronoun had been used in its detached form, the structure would have been ya'budunakum, and it would not have been a closing word. The fronting of this element has been used as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of kana (was) over it when kana's predicate is a sentence; this is a matter of disagreement: Ibn al-Sarraj permitted it, and some grammarians prohibited it, and likewise they prohibited its placement in the middle when it is a sentence. Ibn al-Sarraj said: analogy permits it, but it has not been heard. The point of proof from the verse is that fronting the object indicates fronting the verb, so just as ﴿you﴾ may be fronted, ﴿worship﴾ may be fronted; but this rule is not consistent, and it is better to prohibit it until a proof from the Arabs confirms its permissibility.

When they answered Allah, they began by glorifying Him and declaring Him free of every evil, as Jesus, peace be upon him, said ﴿Glory be to You﴾ (subhanaka), then they affiliated themselves to His guardianship rather than those disbelievers, meaning ﴿You are our Protector﴾, since there is no alliance between us and them.

In their words ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ there is an indication of what they had worshipped, though it is not stated explicitly. The particle of retraction *bal* ("rather") points to it, because the one worshipped, if he is not pleased with the worship of his worshipper and does not desire it, is not truly worshipped by that worshipper. For this reason they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, since their vile deeds, arising from the whisperings, seduction and desires of the devils, truly worship them. Hence they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, for the devils are pleased with those deeds. It has been said: the devils made images of a people of the jinn appear to them, and said, "These are the images of the angels, so worship them." It has also been said: they (the devils) used to enter into the bellies of the idols when they were worshipped, and so they worshipped through their worship. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the angels did not deny that human beings worshipped them, but they affirmed that they had no share in that. The worship of the jinn by human beings consists in their acknowledging the jinn's authority over them and their listening to the jinn's whisperings and seduction, and this is a kind of worship. It is possible that among the disbelieving nations there were those who worshipped the jinn, and the Qur'an contains verses from which it appears that the jinn were worshipped, in Surat al-An'am and elsewhere. End of quotation. Now, if they had indeed worshipped the jinn, what is the meaning of their words ﴿most of them were believers﴾ (said of the jinn), instead of "all of them", when they themselves had reported that they used to worship the jinn? The answer is that they did not claim to encompass everything, for there may be among the unbelievers those whom the angels did not observe. Or they limited the statement to the majority because of their belief in the jinn, since faith is an act of the heart, and they did not claim knowledge of all the deeds of their hearts, for that belongs to God Most High alone. The meaning of "believers" (*mu'minun*) is "those who affirm" that they were the ones worshipped. It has also been said: "those who affirm" that they are the daughters of God and that they are angels, ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. As for the one who says that "most" here means "all", nothing objectionable arises for him, but this is not the established usage of the language.

﴿Today﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection. The address in "some of you" (*ba'dukum*) is said to be to the angels, since they are the ones addressed in His words ﴿Are these the ones who used to worship you?﴾. This would be a rebuke to the disbelievers, when it is made clear to them that those they worshipped neither benefit nor harm. This is supported by ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and because what follows is ﴿and We shall say to those who did wrong﴾. Had the address been to the disbelievers, the construction would have been "so taste". It has also been said that the address is to the disbelievers, because the mention of the Day implies their presence, and His words "and He says" would be an emphasis on the description of their state in wrongdoing. It has also been said that it is an address from God to those who were worshipped and to those who worshipped. As for His words "benefit" (*naf'an*), it is said that this means by intercession, and "harm" (*darran*) means by punishment. It is said here ﴿the Fire which you used to deny﴾, while in the Sajdah it is ﴿the punishment which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. Each of the two refers to the punishment and to the Fire respectively, because here they were not yet involved in the punishment; rather, this was the first time they saw the Fire, as it came directly after the gathering, so the Fire was described to them as the very thing you used to deny. As for the one in the Sajdah, they are involved in the punishment, hesitating about it, due to His words ﴿every time they wish to leave it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So the punishment that they are actually undergoing was described to them, namely the everlasting punishment which they had denied.

The demonstrative in His words "this is not but a man" refers to the reciter of the verses, which is implied by His words "and when they are recited", namely the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God Most High related their slanders made upon hearing the Qur'an recited to them. They began first by attacking the reciter, for he disparages your gods. Second, they attacked what the Messenger brought of the Qur'an, saying that it is a fabricated lie from himself and not from God. Third, they said that what he brought is clear magic, because it contains what brings about attraction, the influence of souls upon it, and their response to it. They attacked the Messenger, what he brought, and his description, and it is possible that this was said by them collectively, and it is also possible that each statement was made by a different group from those who made the other statements. In His words "when it came to them" there is evidence that when it came to them they did not reflect upon it, but rushed to deny it and attribute it to magic. The verbal noun in its being formed in the passive form of the unnamed subject is disputed, and the correct view is that it is prohibited. Here it is estimated that Allah makes them pass beyond the double, meaning He multiplies their good deeds for them: a good deed is multiplied tenfold, and up to seven hundred times for whom He wills. Qatada read ﴿jaza'un al-di'fu﴾ with both nominative: so ﴿al-di'f﴾ is a substitute (badal). Ya'qub in one narration read ﴿jaza'an﴾ with accusative and ﴿al-di'fu﴾ with nominative; al-Dani transmitted this reading from Qatada, and ﴿jaza'an﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), like your saying: "in the house, Zayd is standing." The majority read ﴿fi al-ghurufat﴾ in the plural with a damma on the ra'; al-Hasan and 'Asim (with a variant from him) read it with sukun on the ra'; al-A'mash and Muhammad ibn Ka'b read it with sukun; and some readers read it with fatha. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-A'mash, Talha, and Hamza, in his choice, read ﴿al-ghurfa﴾ in the singular with a sukun on the ra'; and Ibn Thabbat also read it with fatha in the singular.

When He mentioned the reward of those who believe, He mentioned the punishment of those who disbelieve, to make the contrast between the two recompenses clear. The explanation of a similar word has preceded. Since their boasting was in the abundance of wealth and children, they were informed that this is according to what Allah willed, and this meaning emphasizes that this operates according to what Allah willed, except that it is according to desert, not as honor nor as humiliation. The meaning of ﴿so He will replace it﴾ is that He will bring a replacement and a substitute for it. The phrase ﴿of His servants﴾ (min 'ibadihi) suggests the believers, and similarly the address in ﴿whatever you spend﴾ here intends the provision of the believers, so the context of ﴿Say, indeed my Lord extends﴾ is not the context of what was said to the disbelievers, but the context of admonition, of renunciation of this world, and of urging spending in obedience to Allah, and replacing what was spent, either immediately in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, and this is conditional upon seeking the face of Allah. Mujahid said: whoever has of this wealth what sustains him, let him aim (for moderation), and know that provision is apportioned, and perhaps what is apportioned to him is little, yet he spends as one who is wealthy, so he spends all that is in his hand, and then remains in poverty all his life and cannot manage.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾ in the Hereafter. The meaning of the verse: whatever there is of replacement, it is from Him. ﴿The best of providers﴾ came in the plural, although the provider in reality is Allah alone; because it is said: a man provides for his dependents, a commander for his army, a master for his slave, and "providers" is pluralized with this consideration, but those (human providers) are provided from what Allah has provided them, and He has made them free to dispose of it, whereas Allah the Exalted provides from treasuries that do not perish, and from bringing forth from non-existence into existence.

﴿And the Day He gathers them all﴾ — that is, the deniers, those who came before and those who came after. The majority read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ and ﴿naqulu﴾ with a nun in both, and Hafs read them with a ya', and this was mentioned in al-An'am. The address to the angels is a rebuke to the disbelievers, and Allah knows that the angels are (p-٢٨٧) exalted and free from what was directed at them of questioning; this is only by way of establishing the disbelievers' guilt, and the evil of what they committed of worshipping other than Allah is known, and that those whom they worshipped disown them. ﴿These﴾ (ha'ulā') is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿used to worship﴾ (kanu ya'budun), and ﴿you﴾ (iyyakum) is the object of ﴿worship﴾. Since it came first, it became detached; it was fronted because it is more emphatic in address, and because ﴿worship﴾ becomes a closing word (fasila, rhyme-end). If the pronoun had been used in its detached form, the structure would have been ya'budunakum, and it would not have been a closing word. The fronting of this element has been used as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of kana (was) over it when kana's predicate is a sentence; this is a matter of disagreement: Ibn al-Sarraj permitted it, and some grammarians prohibited it, and likewise they prohibited its placement in the middle when it is a sentence. Ibn al-Sarraj said: analogy permits it, but it has not been heard. The point of proof from the verse is that fronting the object indicates fronting the verb, so just as ﴿you﴾ may be fronted, ﴿worship﴾ may be fronted; but this rule is not consistent, and it is better to prohibit it until a proof from the Arabs confirms its permissibility.

When they answered Allah, they began by glorifying Him and declaring Him free of every evil, as Jesus, peace be upon him, said ﴿Glory be to You﴾ (subhanaka), then they affiliated themselves to His guardianship rather than those disbelievers, meaning ﴿You are our Protector﴾, since there is no alliance between us and them.

In their words ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ there is an indication of what they had worshipped, though it is not stated explicitly. The particle of retraction *bal* ("rather") points to it, because the one worshipped, if he is not pleased with the worship of his worshipper and does not desire it, is not truly worshipped by that worshipper. For this reason they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, since their vile deeds, arising from the whisperings, seduction and desires of the devils, truly worship them. Hence they said ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, for the devils are pleased with those deeds. It has been said: the devils made images of a people of the jinn appear to them, and said, "These are the images of the angels, so worship them." It has also been said: they (the devils) used to enter into the bellies of the idols when they were worshipped, and so they worshipped through their worship. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the angels did not deny that human beings worshipped them, but they affirmed that they had no share in that. The worship of the jinn by human beings consists in their acknowledging the jinn's authority over them and their listening to the jinn's whisperings and seduction, and this is a kind of worship. It is possible that among the disbelieving nations there were those who worshipped the jinn, and the Qur'an contains verses from which it appears that the jinn were worshipped, in Surat al-An'am and elsewhere. End of quotation. Now, if they had indeed worshipped the jinn, what is the meaning of their words ﴿most of them were believers﴾ (said of the jinn), instead of "all of them", when they themselves had reported that they used to worship the jinn? The answer is that they did not claim to encompass everything, for there may be among the unbelievers those whom the angels did not observe. Or they limited the statement to the majority because of their belief in the jinn, since faith is an act of the heart, and they did not claim knowledge of all the deeds of their hearts, for that belongs to God Most High alone. The meaning of "believers" (*mu'minun*) is "those who affirm" that they were the ones worshipped. It has also been said: "those who affirm" that they are the daughters of God and that they are angels, ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. As for the one who says that "most" here means "all", nothing objectionable arises for him, but this is not the established usage of the language.

﴿Today﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection. The address in "some of you" (*ba'dukum*) is said to be to the angels, since they are the ones addressed in His words ﴿Are these the ones who used to worship you?﴾. This would be a rebuke to the disbelievers, when it is made clear to them that those they worshipped neither benefit nor harm. This is supported by ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and because what follows is ﴿and We shall say to those who did wrong﴾. Had the address been to the disbelievers, the construction would have been "so taste". It has also been said that the address is to the disbelievers, because the mention of the Day implies their presence, and His words "and He says" would be an emphasis on the description of their state in wrongdoing. It has also been said that it is an address from God to those who were worshipped and to those who worshipped. As for His words "benefit" (*naf'an*), it is said that this means by intercession, and "harm" (*darran*) means by punishment. It is said here ﴿the Fire which you used to deny﴾, while in the Sajdah it is ﴿the punishment which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. Each of the two refers to the punishment and to the Fire respectively, because here they were not yet involved in the punishment; rather, this was the first time they saw the Fire, as it came directly after the gathering, so the Fire was described to them as the very thing you used to deny. As for the one in the Sajdah, they are involved in the punishment, hesitating about it, due to His words ﴿every time they wish to leave it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So the punishment that they are actually undergoing was described to them, namely the everlasting punishment which they had denied.

The demonstrative in His words "this is not but a man" refers to the reciter of the verses, which is implied by His words "and when they are recited", namely the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God Most High related their slanders made upon hearing the Qur'an recited to them. They began first by attacking the reciter, for he disparages your gods. Second, they attacked what the Messenger brought of the Qur'an, saying that it is a fabricated lie from himself and not from God. Third, they said that what he brought is clear magic, because it contains what brings about attraction, the influence of souls upon it, and their response to it. They attacked the Messenger, what he brought, and his description, and it is possible that this was said by them collectively, and it is also possible that each statement was made by a different group from those who made the other statements. In His words "when it came to them" there is evidence that when it came to them they did not reflect upon it, but rushed to deny it and attribute it to magic. They did not suffice with saying "it is magic", but went on to describe it as clear to anyone who reflects upon it. It has been said that the denial of the Qur'an and of the miracle was agreed upon among the polytheists and the People of the Book, and so God Most High said ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth﴾, in a general sense.

(p-٢٨٤) ﴿Never did We send a warner to a town but its affluent ones said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ ﴿And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know."﴾ ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in nearness, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a double reward for what they did, and they will be safe in the upper chambers.﴾ ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, will be brought to the punishment.﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers."﴾ ﴿And the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ ﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm another, and We will say to those who wronged, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, they say, "This is only a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship," and they say, "This is only a fabricated lie," and those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is only evident magic."﴾.

(p-٢٨٥) (﴿Never did We send﴾) the verse. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people, the Quraysh, of disbelief and boasting in wealth and children. It also indicates that what they mentioned of this is the habit of the affluent (al-mutrafun) toward their prophets, so their matter should not concern you. The phrase ﴿warner﴾ (min nadhir) is general, meaning you warn them of the punishment of Allah if they do not affirm His oneness. The phrase ﴿its affluent ones said﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and He specified the affluent because they were the first to deny the messengers, due to their preoccupation with the glitter of this world and what dominated their minds of it, so their hearts are always occupied and absorbed, unlike the poor. The poor are free of the worldly pleasures, so their hearts are more receptive to good, and for this reason they are the followers of the prophets, as came in the hadith of Heraclius (Hiraql). The word ﴿with what﴾ (bima) is connected to ﴿disbelievers﴾ (kafirun), and the word ﴿with which﴾ (bihi) is connected to ﴿you have been sent﴾ (ursiltum), and ﴿what﴾ (ma) is general, covering what the warners brought: calling to belief in Allah, singling Him out in worship, informing that they are His messengers to them, and the resurrection and the recompense for deeds. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ (qalu) refers to the affluent; it has been said that it refers to the Quraysh, and what follows of address supports this in His saying ﴿Say﴾ (qul), because those affluent who came before and perished are not addressed, so only those present would speak. His saying ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children﴾ is addressed to them. They argued for Allah's pleasure with them by His bounty toward them: if He were not honoring them, He would not have expanded (provision) for us; as for you, because of your abasement before Him, He has deprived you, O followers of the messengers. Then they say, "They will not be punished," a general negation, because the prophets may warn of a punishment that is hasty in this world or deferred in the Hereafter, so they negated all of that. Either they were deniers of the Hereafter, in which case they negated their punishment there, because if it does not exist, there is no punishment in it; or they affirm it in reality or by way of supposition, and they say: just as He bestowed favor upon us in this world, He will bestow favor upon us in the Hereafter in the same condition as this world, by a corrupt analogy (qiyas fasid). Allah refuted this by saying that provision is a bounty from Him, distributed upon us in the Hereafter according to the condition of this world, as He wills. ﴿For whom He wills﴾: He may expand upon the disobedient and restrict upon the obedient, and He may expand upon both; existence bears witness to this, so expansion in this world should not be used as an analogy, because in the Hereafter it is only in accordance with righteous deeds. Al-A'mash read ﴿yuqaddiru﴾ (restricts) with a shadda in both places; the majority read it without shadda, and its meaning is "restricts," the opposite of ﴿yabsutu﴾ (extends).

﴿But most people﴾ like these disbelievers ﴿do not know﴾ that provision is distributed by will, and that it is not a proof of approval. Then He informed that their wealth and children, of which they boasted, do not bring them near to Allah; rather, belief and righteous deeds bring one near. The majority read ﴿bi-llati﴾ (with that which), and a broken plural (jam' taksir) of rational and non-rational beings may be treated as a feminine singular. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿that which﴾ refers to piety (taqwa), which alone brings one near to Allah in nearness, meaning your wealth is not that which is set for bringing near. End of his words. So he made ﴿alla﴾ a qualifier of an omitted noun, which is piety. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted noun. The apparent meaning is that ﴿alla﴾ refers to wealth and children, as al-Farra' said. He also said, along with al-Zajjaj: it was omitted from the first part due to the second part indicating it, and the estimate is ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children are that which brings you near to Us in nearness﴾. End. But there is no need to estimate this omitted element, since it is valid for ﴿alla﴾ to refer to the collective of wealth and children. Al-Hasan read ﴿bi-l-latī﴾ in the plural, which also refers to wealth and children. It is read ﴿bi-lladhi﴾, and ﴿zulfa﴾ (nearness) is a verbal noun like ﴿qurba﴾ (kinship/nearness), and its accusative case is as a verbal noun from the meaning, meaning "it brings you near." Al-Dahhak read ﴿zulafan﴾ with a fatha on the lam and tanwin on the fa', the plural of ﴿zulfa﴾, which is a degree of nearness.

﴿Except for those who believe﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not from the same category), and it is in the accusative as an exception, meaning "but rather whoever believes." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾: so his belief and his deed bring him near. (p-٢٨٦) Al-Zajjaj said: it is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in ﴿brings you near﴾. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because the kaf and mim are for the addressee, so substitution is not permissible; if this were permissible, it would be permissible to say: "I saw you Zayd." This statement of Abu Ishaq is the statement of al-Farra'. End. The school of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permissible to substitute from the pronoun of the addressee and the speaker, but substitution in this verse is not valid. Do you not see that it is not valid to make the verb that serves as the relative clause (silah) free for what follows ﴿illa﴾ (except)? If you say: "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Khalid," it would not be valid. Al-Zajjaj imagined that the relative clause, although it is negated in meaning, makes substitution valid, but it is not permissible except where the free element is valid. Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: ﴿except for those who believe﴾ is an exception from the ﴿you﴾ (kum) in ﴿brings you near﴾, and the meaning is: wealth does not bring anyone near except the believing righteous one who spends it in the way of Allah; and children do not bring anyone near except one who taught them good, and guided them in religion and prepared them for righteousness and obedience. End. And this is not permissible, as we mentioned: it is not permissible to say "Zayd is not the one who goes out except as a brother," nor "Zayd is not the one who strikes except Amr," nor "Zayd is not the one who passes except by Bakr." The construction that al-Zamakhshari formed from his saying "does not bring anyone near except the believer" does not agree with the Qur'an; in the form he constructed, what he said is permissible, but in the wording of the Qur'an it is not. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿man﴾ (who) be in the nominative position, and the meaning of the sentence according to him is: what is the one brought near? ﴿Except whoever believes﴾. End. This statement is one from which no meaning is obtained, as if he was asleep when he said that.
