Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ means "with one trait," and he explained it with His saying ﴿that you stand,﴾ taking it as an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to it. End quote. This is not permissible, because (بِواحِدَةٍ) [with one thing] is indefinite, while (أنْ تَقُومُوا) [that you stand] is definite, since its estimate is "your standing for God." Explicative apposition has two views: the first is that it requires the appositive to be definite from a definite, which is the view of the Kufans. As for the mismatch in definiteness, no one has held this view; it is only an error on the part of its speaker. The grammarians have refuted al-Zamakhshari for his saying that ﴿مَقامُ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ [the station of Ibrahim] is an explicative apposition to ﴿آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾ [clear signs], for the same reason of mismatch; so this is likewise.

The apparent meaning of standing (القِيامُ) here is taking a stand in the matter and rising to it with resolve, not the standing that is meant literally, according to the two views. It is unlikely that it means what al-Zamakhshari allowed: standing up from the gathering of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and dispersing from their assembly before him. The meaning: "I admonish you with only one thing in which lies your attaining the truth and your salvation: that you stand for the sake of God in groups of two and singly, and then reflect on the matter of Muhammad and what he brought." He said ﴿in pairs and singly﴾ because a group, when assembled, has confusion of thought, obstruction to reflection, mixing of speech, partisanship for schools of thought, and little fairness, as is witnessed in the lessons where groups gather, so no truth is established there. As for two people, if they look with fairness and each presents to the other what has become clear to him, the truth hardly escapes them both. As for one person, if he has good understanding, sound judgment, is free of partisanship, and seeks the truth, it is unlikely that he will miss it. (مَثْنى وفُرادى) [in pairs and singly] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and (مَثْنى) [in pairs] is placed first because seeking realities from two who support each other in consideration is more beneficial than one thought alone: when the truth flashes between the two, each of them then turns back to it, and thereby gains more insight. The poet said:

When they gather, they bring every rare thing, so that some of the people increase in knowledge from others.

﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا﴾ [and then reflect] is a conjunction to ﴿أنْ تَقُومُوا﴾ [that you stand]; the reflection here concerns the condition of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what they attributed to him. Reflection generally leads to the right course when its holder is free of what disturbs judgment. The pause at ﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا ما بِصاحِبِكم مِن جِنَّةٍ﴾ [and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion] according to Abu Hatim is a new negation. Ibn Atiyyah said: according to Sibawayh, it is the answer to what functions as an oath, because (تَفَكَّرَ) [reflect] is among the verbs that give a specification, like (تَبَيَّنَ) [become clear]; and on this view it refers to the signs of God and belief in Him. End quote. It is also possible that (تَتَفَكَّرُوا) is suspended (mu'allaq), and the negated clause is in the position of the accusative, being the object of the reflection; that is: "then reflect on the absence of madness in Muhammad." For attributing it to him cannot be valid for one who was the most intelligent of Quraysh, the most stable of mind, the most truthful of speech, the most pure of soul, and upon whose hands this inimitable Qur'an appeared. By reflection they will know that attributing madness to him is impossible, that no sane person would go to it, and that whoever attributes it to him is a liar and a fabricator. The apparent meaning is that (ما) is for negation, as we have explained. It was also said: (ما) is interrogative, and it is an interrogative not meant in its literal sense, but its meaning reverts to negation; the estimate: "What is there in your companion of madness?" that is, there is nothing of that in him. When He, the Exalted, negated madness from him, He affirmed that he is (نَذِيرٌ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ عَذابٍ شَدِيدٍ) [a warner before a severe punishment]: that is, he precedes in time the punishment with which they were threatened. And (بَيْنَ يَدَيْ) [before] indicates the nearness of the punishment.

﴿قُلْ ما سَألْتُكم مِن أجْرٍ﴾ [Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you] verse concerns disavowing the pursuit of worldly gain, the seeking of payment for the light he brought, and reliance upon God in it. (ما) may be a relative pronoun as subject, with the returning pronoun of the relative clause omitted, its estimate being: "what I asked you for," and ﴿فَهُوَ لَكُمْ﴾ [it is yours] is the predicate. The (فَ) entered because the subject carries the meaning of a condition. It is also possible that (ما) is a conditional, object of (سَألْتُكم) [I asked you], and (فَهُوَ لَكُمْ) [it is yours] is the clause that is the answer of the condition. His saying ﴿Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ has two meanings. The first: negation of asking for a reward, as a man says to his companion: "If you give me something, take it," while he knows that he has not given him anything, but he intends to make certain by making the taking conditional on what has not occurred. This is supported by ﴿My reward is only from God﴾. The second: that by "reward" he means what is in His saying ﴿Say: I ask you no reward for it, except for whoever wills to take a path to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 57], and in His saying ﴿I ask you for no reward for it, except love for kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23]; because taking a path to God benefits them, and likewise love in kinship, since kinship has bound them together with him. So said al-Zamakhshari, though there is some addition in it. Ibn Abbas said: the reward is love in kinship. Qatadah said: ﴿it is yours﴾, that is, its fruit and its reward, because I asked you to maintain the ties of kinship. Muqatil said: "I have left it to you."

﴿And He is over all things a witness.﴾ He is the Observer and Guardian. He knows that I do not seek any reward for my counsel and my call to Him except from Him, and that I do not hope for anything from you.

Al-qadhf is throwing with force and reliance. It is used figuratively for the sense of casting, as in His words ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ [Taha: 39] and ﴿and He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. Qatadah said: ﴿He casts the truth﴾ means He makes the proof clear and manifest. Ibn al-Qushayri said: He makes the proof clear such that there is no objection to it, because He is ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, and I hold fast to what truth is cast to me. The original sense of al-qadhf is throwing an arrow, or pebbles, or speech. Ibn Abbas said: He casts falsehood with the truth. The apparent reading is that "bi-l-haqq" (with the truth) is the object, so al-haqq is the thing cast, deleted, meaning: He casts, that is, He casts what He casts to His prophets of revelation and law, with the truth and not with falsehood. Then the bāʾ (the preposition "bi-") is either for accompaniment or for causation. This possibility is supported by the fact that qadhafa is transitive by itself. If you make bi-l-haqq the object, then the bāʾ is an extra particle in a position where its extra use is not regular.

The majority read ʿallāmu (Knower) in the nominative case. The apparent reading is that it is a second predicate, which is the apparent view of al-Zajjaj, who said: it is nominative because the implied sense is "Say: My Lord is the Knower of the unseen." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is nominative, agreeing with the position of inna and its subject (its grammatical locus), or with the pronoun hidden in yaqdhifu, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quotation. As for agreement with the locus of inna and its subject, this is not the view of Sibawayh, and it is not correct according to our scholars, as we have established in the books of grammar. As for his saying "with the hidden pronoun in yaqdhifu," he did not explain the reason for this agreement, and it seems he means that it is a substitute for the pronoun in yaqdhifu. Al-Kisa'i said: it is an attributive adjective for that pronoun, because his view is that it is permissible to make an attribute of an implicit third-person pronoun.

ʿIsa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, and Harb from Talha read ʿallāma in the accusative case. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an attribute of my Lord. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi and Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is a substitute. Al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute or an attribute. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a form of praise. It was read al-ghuyūbi in the genitive. As for the ḍamma (u-vowel), it is the plural of ghayb. As for the kasra (i-vowel), it is likewise, as they found two ḍammas and a waw heavy, so it was made kasra, and the harmony is kasra with the yāʾ, and the ḍamma that is on the yāʾ with the wāw. As for the fatḥa, it is an object form for intensification, like al-ṣabūr, and it is the thing that is absent and very hidden.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He casts with the truth in the present tense, He informed that the truth has come, and that is the Qur'an and the revelation, and what is other than it of religions has been nullified. Thus nothing remains of stability for any religion except Islam, neither at the beginning nor at the end. So Islam is not to be feared for what would nullify it, as He said ﴿Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42]. Qatadah said: al-batil is Satan, who creates nothing and does not bring anything back. Al-Dahhak said: the idols do not do that. Abu Sulayman said: the idol does not begin speech from itself so as to be answered, nor does it refute what has come of the truth with any proof. It was said: al-batil is that which opposes the truth. So the meaning is: falsehood has departed with the coming of the truth, so no remnant of it is left. This is because when the one who comes (the originator) perishes, nothing remains of him in beginning or return, so their saying "he neither begins nor returns" became a proverb for destruction. From this is the saying of the poet:

"More impoverished than his people are the slaves; today he neither begins nor returns."

The apparent view is that mā is a negation. It was also said that it is an interrogative whose ultimate meaning is negation, as if he said: what thing begins falsehood, that is Iblis, and returns it? This was said by al-Zajjaj and a group with him. From al-Hasan: he does not begin, that is Iblis, good for his people, nor does he return it, that is, he does not benefit them in this world or the hereafter. It was also said: al-Shaytan (Satan) is al-batil, because he is the companion of falsehood, because he is destroyed, just as he is called al-Shaytan from shāṭa, meaning he perished. It was said: al-haqq is the sword. From Ibn Masʿud: The Messenger of Allah entered Makkah, and around the Kaʿba were three hundred and sixty idols, and he began to strike them with a stick of a jujube tree and say: "﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra: 81], ﴿The truth has come, and falsehood neither begins nor returns﴾."

The majority read ﴿Say: If I go astray﴾ with a fatḥa on the lām, ﴿then I only go astray﴾ with a kasra on the ḍād. Al-Hasan, Ibn Wththab, and ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Muqri read with a kasra on the lām and a fatḥa on the ḍād, and this is the dialect of Tamim. ʿAbd al-Rahman made the hamza of (aḍillu) kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: there are two dialects, like ḍalaltu aḍillu and ẓalaltu aẓillu.

﴿And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾. The bi- here may be masdariyya (verbal-noun forming), meaning: by the revelation of my Lord. The verbal correspondence is: "and if I am guided, then I am guided only for my own benefit," corresponding to ﴿Whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾ [Fussilat: 46], which corresponds to ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and ﴿Whoever goes astray, he goes astray only against himself﴾ [Yunus: 108], which corresponds to ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for himself﴾ [al-Zumar: 41]. Or it is said: "then I only go astray to my own detriment." As for the verse itself, the correspondence is semantic, because the self is everything that is against it, is for it, meaning every harm against it is by its cause.

﴿Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53], and what is beneficial for it is by the guidance and success of its Lord. This is a general ruling for every person responsible. He commanded His Messenger to attribute it to himself, because when he enters under it along with the greatness of his position and the secret of his way, like others he is more worthy of it. End of quotation, and it is from the words of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Indeed He is Hearing, Near﴾, He perceives the speech and deed of every one who goes astray and every one who is guided.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified﴾ refers to the time of resurrection and the establishment of the Hour. Frequently it came: (p. 293) ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27], ﴿And if you could see when the criminals bow their heads before their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12], and all of that is on the Day of Resurrection. He expressed it with fazaʿū (they were terrified), uhhidhū (they were seized), and qālū (they said), and the past tense was used for them to indicate the certainty of their occurrence by the true report. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: this is in the punishment of this world. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the disbelievers at their emergence from the graves. Mujahid said: on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: it refers to the people of Badr when their necks were struck, so they could not flee from the punishment, nor return to repentance. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Abza said: it refers to an army going to attack the Kaʿba, and they will be swallowed up by the earth in a desert, and no one will escape except a man from Juhayna, who will inform the people of what befell him. They said: for him it was said:

"And with Juhayna is the certain news."

A lengthy hadith about this meaning was narrated from Hudhayfa. al-Tabari mentioned that its chain is weak, and it is falsely attributed in the narration of Ibn al-Jarrah. Al-Zamakhshari said, and from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning the sinking in the desert, because eighty thousand men will march to the Kaʿba to destroy it, and when they enter the desert they will be swallowed up. It is mentioned in the hadith of Hudhayfa that "There will be a turmoil between the people of the east and the west. While they are in that state, al-Sufyani will come out from the dry valley immediately, at the time he descends to Damascus, and he sends an army to Madina, and they plunder it for three days. Then they go out to Makkah, and Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them and strikes it, that is the earth, with his foot a single blow, and Allah sinks them into a desert of the earth. No one will escape except a man from Juhayna, who will inform the people of what befell him. That is His saying ﴿so there is no escape﴾." Only two men from Juhayna will escape from them, and for this the proverb became current: "And with Juhayna is the certain news." The name of one of them is Bashir, who gives glad tidings to the people of Makkah, and the other is Nadhir, who returns with the report of al-Sufyani. It was also said: only one man will return, named Najiya from Juhayna, whose face will be turned to the back of his neck.

The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, meaning: and if you could see the disbelievers when they are terrified, so there is no escape, that is, they cannot escape Allah, and there is no flight for them from what He intends for them. Al-Hasan said: "so there is no escape" means from the blast of resurrection, and they are seized from the belly of the earth to its surface. End of quotation. Or from the place of standing to the Fire when they are raised; or from the surface of the earth to its belly when they die; or from the desert of Badr to the well; or from beneath their feet when they are swallowed up. These are sayings built upon those earlier sayings concerning the return of the pronoun in fazaʿū. Describing the place as near, from where Allah's power is over them, so wherever they are, it is near.

The majority read ﴿so there is no escape﴾ as a fatḥa-built form (fala fawta), ﴿and they are seized﴾ as a past-tense verb. The apparent view is that it is conjoined to ﴿they were terrified﴾. It was also said: it is conjoined to ﴿so there is no escape﴾, because its meaning is "they will not be made to escape, and they are seized." ʿAbd al-Rahman, mawla of Banu Hashim, from his father, and Talha read: ﴿fa-la fawtun, wa-akhdhun﴾ as two nominal masdars with tanwin. Ubayy read: ﴿fa-la fawta﴾ built, and (wa-akhdhun) as a tanwin masdar. Whoever reads (wa-akhdhun) with a ḍamma (raf'), it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: and their state is seizure; or it is a subject, meaning: and there is seizure there. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was read: wa-akhdhun, and it is conjoined to the locus of fala fawta, and its meaning: there is no escape there, and there is seizure there. End of quotation. It is as if he says: "no escape" is a collective negation, and the built form with it is in the position of a subject, and its predicate is "there." So likewise "wa-akhdhun" is a subject and its predicate is "there," so it is conjunction of sentences, even if one of them contains negation and the other contains affirmation.

The pronoun in bihi refers to Allah, said by Mujahid, meaning: they say that when they see the punishment. Al-Hasan said: it refers to resurrection. Muqatil said: it refers to the Qur'an. It was also said: it refers to the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: it refers to the Messenger, because his mention passed in the verse ﴿Your companion is not possessed﴾.

﴿And how can they reach from a place far away?﴾ Ibn Abbas said: al-tanawush is returning to the world. Ibn al-Anbari recited:

"Mayy wishes that she would return to me, but there is no path to reaching her."

That is: she desires. This is an image of their seeking what cannot happen, which is that their faith would benefit them at that time, as their faith benefits the believers in this world. Their state is likened to the state of one who wants to take a thing from afar, as another takes it from near. The majority read al-tanawush with a waw. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu ʿAmr, and Abu Bakr read it with a hamza. It is permissible that (p. 294) both are roots, one of which is n-w-sh-, and the other is ʾ-w-sh- with a hamza... and their explanation was already given in the lexicon sections. It is permissible that the origin of the hamza is a waw, as said by al-Zajjaj, and followed by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa. al-Zajjaj said: every waw with a permanent ḍamma, you have the choice: if you wish you keep its hamza, and if you wish you leave its hamza. You say: thalāth adwur without a hamza, and adʾur with a hamza. He said: the meaning: from where is it for them to reach what they sought of repentance after the passing of its time, because it is only accepted in this world, and this world has gone, so they are far from the hereafter. That is His saying ﴿from a place far away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: the waw with a permanent ḍamma was hamzated, as it was hamzated in ujūh and udur. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: As for al-tanā'ush with a hamza, it may be from al-tanawush, and the waw was hamzated since it was a permanent ḍamma, as they said: afteytu. Al-Hawfi said: whoever reads with a hamza may have two possibilities: one, that it is from al-nāsh, which is movement in slowness, or it may be from nāsha yanūshu, the waw was hamzated because of its being ḍammed, as afteytu and adūru were hamzated. Abu al-Baqa said: it is read with a hamza because of the waw, and it was also said: it is an original root from nāshahu. End of quotation. What they mention, that a waw with a permanent ḍamma may be replaced by a hamza, is not absolute; rather that is not permitted in the medial position when it is assimilated into it, like ya'ūdu and ta'ūdu as verbal nouns; nor when it is sound in the verb, like tarhawka tarhūkan, and taʿāwana taʿāwunan, and two hamzas are not heard from that, so it is not permitted. Al-tanawush is like al-taʿāwun, so its hamzation is not permitted, because its waw is sound in the verb, as he says: tanāwasha.

﴿وقَدْ كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ The pronoun in *bihi* refers to what the phrase *(āmannā bihi,* "we believe in it") refers to, according to the opinions. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāliyyah*, a clause describing the state of the subject), and *(min qablu)* means before the descent of the punishment. Most readers recite *(wa-yaqdhifūna)* in the active voice, as a narration of a past state (*ḥikāyat ḥāl*, a report of a state that had already occurred). Al-Ḥasan said: "Their saying: there is no Paradise and no Fire." Qatādah added: "Nor resurrection, nor Fire." Ibn Zayd said: "Attacking the Qur'an with their saying: ﴿fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'ām: 25]." Mujāhid said: "Attacking the Messenger (ﷺ) with their saying: poet, sorcerer, and soothsayer."

﴿مِن مَكانٍ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means from a distant direction, because attributing any of those things to him is among the most remote of things. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is speech about the unseen and a hidden matter, because they had not witnessed from him any sorcery, poetry, or lying. They have brought this unseen matter from a distant position relative to his condition, because the thing furthest from what he brought is poetry and sorcery, and the thing furthest from his habit, which was known among them and tested, is lying and falsehood." End of quote. It was also said: this is a resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnaf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), meaning: they utter the word of faith at a time when faith itself will not benefit them. Their state is thus likened to their seeking to obtain, in the Hereafter, what they had neglected of faith in this world by saying: "We believe in the Hereafter." That is a remote aim for one who throws something from a distant place where there is no room to reach it, since he wants to hit it while it is absent from him and far away. *Al-ghayb* means the absent thing.

Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywa, and Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr recited *(wa-yuqadhūna)* in the passive voice. Mujāhid said: "He will pelt them with what they dislike from the sky." Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: "They will be struck with the unseen from where they do not know. Its meaning: they will be repaid for their evil deeds, and they will have no knowledge of what has come to them, either at the time when repentance is impossible at the sight of death, or in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is, their devils bring it to them, meaning the unseen, and teach it to them." It was also said: they are pelted into the Fire. It was said: this is a parable (*mathal*, an illustrative comparison), because one who is called from a distant place does not hear, meaning they do not understand and do not hear.

﴿وحِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: "The adverbial of place (*al-ẓarf*) stands in place of the subject of the passive verb." End of quote. But if it were as he stated, it would be in the nominative, *baynahum*, as in the reading of the one who recited ﴿لَقَدْ تَّقَطَّعَ بَيْنَكم﴾ [Indeed, your bond has been severed] in one of its two meanings. One does not say that a noun that is attached to an indeclinable word, which is the pronoun, is indeclinable and therefore in the position of the nominative, even though it is indeclinable. Just as one of them said concerning the line: *wa-idh mā mathhalahum*, pointing out that it is in the nominative position because it is attached to the pronoun, even though it is vowelled with fatḥa. That is a corrupt statement. One may say: "I passed by your boy," and "Your boy stood" with fatḥa, and no one says this. Building (*binā'*, becoming indeclinable) because of attachment to an indeclinable word is not absolute, but has particular positions that are established in grammar. No one says that, and the poet says: *wa-qad ḥīla bayna al-ʿīr wa-l-nazawān* [And indeed a barrier was placed between al-ʿĪr and al-Nazawān], for he put *bayna* in the accusative, though it is attached to a declinable noun. What occurs of this kind is only explained by saying that the element standing in for the subject is the pronoun of the verbal noun indicated by it, and *ḥīla* is that, i.e. the barrier (*al-ḥawl*). Because it is a pronoun, it is not an emphatic verbal noun, so it may stand in place of the subject. On this basis the saying of the poet is explained: *wa-qālat matā yubkhal ʿalayka wa-yuʿtalal bisūʾin wa-in yukshaf gharāmuka tadrub* [She said: "When you are withheld from and an excuse is made against you with ill, and if your passion is revealed, you will be harried."], meaning: and he is excused, i.e. the excusing.

Those they desire to return to the world: this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Or it is the family, wealth, and children, said by al-Suddī. Or the barrier is between the army and the destruction of the Kaʿba, or between the believers, or between salvation from the punishment, or between the delights of this world and its pleasures, said by Mujāhid as well. ﴿as was done to their likes﴾, from the disbelieving nations, meaning that a barrier was placed between them and their desires. *Min qablu* may be connected to *(ashyāʿihim)*, meaning whoever was characterized by their attribute from among those before, that is, in the earlier time. This is preferred, because what is done to all of them occurs at one time. It may also be connected to a verb if the barrier is in this world. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Their likes are the people of the Elephant," meaning the likes of Quraysh, and he seems to have presented it as an example. As for specifying them, there is no evidence for it. ﴿Indeed they were in a disquieting doubt﴾, meaning in this world. *Murīb* is an active participle from *arāba al-rajul*, meaning he committed a suspicious act and entered into it, and *arabtu al-rajul* means I caused him to fall into suspicion. Attributing causing suspicion to doubt is a metaphor (*majāz*, a figurative usage). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Except that there is a difference between them: the *murīb* from the transitive verb is transferred from that which can be suspicious among concrete things to the meaning, and from the intransitive verb is transferred from the doubter to the doubt, as you say: *shiʿru shāʿir* [the poetry of a poet]." End of quote, and there is some lack of clarity in it. It was said: it is possible that he followed it with doubt, and both have the same meaning, for the end of the verse harmonizes with the preceding one from a near place, as you say: *ʿajabun ʿajīb*, *shitāʾun shātin*, *laylatun laylāʾ*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The disquieting doubt is the strongest and most intense form of doubt in darkening."

[p. 295]

(p. 289) ﴿We did not give them books to study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ ﴿Those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My rejection!﴾ ﴿Say: I admonish you with only one thing: that you stand up before God, in pairs and singly, and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only from God, and He is a witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Say: My Lord hurls down the truth; He is the Knower of the unseen.﴾ ﴿Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore.﴾ ﴿Say: If I go astray, I go astray only to my own loss; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near.﴾ ﴿If you could see when they are terrified, with no escape, and they are seized from a near place.﴾ ﴿And they say: We believe in Him. But how can they reach [it] from a far place?﴾ ﴿And they had disbelieved in it before, and cast [doubts] about the unseen from a far place.﴾ ﴿And between them and what they desire is a barrier, as was done with their like before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾

﴿وما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ [We did not give them]: the people of Makkah. ﴿مِن كُتُبٍ﴾ [books]. al-Suddi said: "From Us," so that they would know by studying them that what you brought is false. Ibn Zayd said: "So they would confirm that polytheism is permissible." This is like His saying: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum: 35]. Qatadah said: God did not send down to the Arabs any book before the Qur'an, nor did He send them any prophet before Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: From where did they deny, when no book or warner had come to them concerning this? It was also said: He described them as an unlettered people, people of ignorance, who have no religion and no prior knowledge of the revelation of a book or the sending of a messenger. As He said: ﴿Or have We given them a book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21]. So there is no established basis for their denial, nor any semblance of a claim to it. Likewise, the People of the Book say, though they are falsifiers: "We are the People of the Book and the laws, and we rely upon messengers from among the messengers of God." It was also said: The meaning is that they speak about the Book of God by their own opinions: some say it is magic, and some say it is fabrication, and they do not rely on any trace of knowledge or on the report of anyone whose report is accepted. "For We have given them books which they study, and We did not send them any messenger or warner, so they could claim that their statements are based on His command."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿يَدْرُسُونَها﴾ as the imperfect of darasa (to study), unstressed. Abu Haywah read it with a fatha on the dal, a shadda, and a kasra on the ra, as the imperfect of iddaraса (ittafala from al-dars), meaning: "you study them together." Also from Abu Haywah: yudarrisuna-ha, from al-tadris (repeated study), or from duris al-kitab (unstressed), and durrisa al-kitab (stressed); the doubling is by consideration of plurality. As for the meaning of (قَبْلَكَ) [before you], Ibn Atiyyah said: That is, We did not send any warner who would address them directly with something, nor who would be in contact with the people of their era, nor from close to their forefathers. Yet warning existed in the world and among the Arabs with Shu'ayb, Salih, and Hud. The call to God and His Oneness is established; the earth has never been without someone calling to Him. The meaning is only: no warner who is specifically sent to these people to whom he was sent. Among the Arabs there was much of the warning of Isma'il, and God the Exalted says: ﴿He was true to his promise, and he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54]. But none dedicated himself to warning and fought for it except Muhammad (ﷺ). End quote.

﴿وكَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Those before them denied]: a warning to them from the nations that preceded them, and what their affair came to; and consolation to His messenger that their habit of denial is the habit of the earlier nations, and what befell those will befall them. The two pronouns in (بَلَغُوا) [they reached] and in ﴿ما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ [what We gave them] refer to (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ) [those before them], to be consistent with His saying (فَكَذَّبُوا) [so they denied], meaning: they did not reach, in thanking for the blessing and in repaying the favour, a tenth of the blessings and kindness We had given them. (p. 290) Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun in (بَلَغُوا) refers to Quraysh, and in ﴿ما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ to the nations (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ). The meaning: these did not reach even some of what We gave those [earlier nations] of long lives, strength of bodies, and abundance of wealth; and when they denied My messengers, My rejection came upon them through destruction and annihilation. The strength they had did not avail them. So how will the state of these be when punishment and destruction come to them? It was also said: the pronoun in (بَلَغُوا) refers to (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ), and in (آتَيْناهم) to Quraysh: the earlier nations did not reach a tenth of what We gave Quraysh of signs, clear proofs, and the light which you brought them. Ibn Atiyyah presented these statements as possibilities. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned the second, and Abu Abdullah al-Razi preferred the third, saying: that is, (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ) did not reach a tenth of what We gave the people of Muhammad of proof, because the Book of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is more complete and clearer than all other books, and Muhammad (peace be upon him) is better than all the messengers and more eloquent; his proof is more sufficient and his explanation more healing. This supports what we mentioned: ﴿and We did not give them books which they study﴾ [which would make the Qur'an unnecessary]. Since the one given in the first verse is the Book, the giving in the second verse is taken to mean the giving of the Book, and this is preferable. End quote.

It is related from Ibn Abbas: "There is no one more knowledgeable than his community, and no book clearer than his book." (al-mi'shar) is a form of (al-'ashr) [tenth], and no other numeral has been formed on this pattern except (al-mirba') [quarter]; their meanings are: a tenth and a quarter. Some said: al-mi'shar is a tenth of a tenth. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is nothing. End quote. It was also said: in this view, "a tenth" means a tenth of tenths, so it is a part of a thousand parts. Al-Mawardi said: this is the most apparent, because the intention is extreme exaggeration in minimizing. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾, when it is dispensed with by His saying ﴿and those before them denied﴾? I say: since the meaning of His saying ﴿and those before them denied﴾ is that those before them committed denial and undertook it, the denial of the messengers is made a consequence of it. An example of this is when someone says: "So-and-so undertook disbelief, so he disbelieved in Muhammad." It is also permissible that it be connected to His saying (ما بَلَغُوا) [they did not reach], as when you say: "Zayd did not reach a tenth of the virtue of 'Amr," so that he is favoured over him.

﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ نَكِيرِ﴾ [So how was My rejection!] is for the earlier deniers, so that they would beware of the like of it. End quote. (فَكَيْفَ) [so how] is an expression of the magnitude of the matter, and it is not a plain interrogative. In it is a threat to Quraysh: that they are exposed to the like of that rejection. (النَّكِيرُ) [rejection] is a verbal noun like (al-inkar) [denial], and it is among the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'il, while the verb is on the pattern af'al, like (al-nadhir) and (al-'adhir) from (anhara) and (a'dhara). The ya' is deleted from (نَكِيرِ) [rejection] for lightness, since it is sufficient without it.

﴿قُلْ إنَّما أعِظُكم بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ [Say: I admonish you with only one thing]: he said: it is obedience to God and His Oneness. Al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but God." Qatadah said: it is "that you stand." Abu Ali said: ﴿أنْ تَقُومُوا﴾ [that you stand] is in the position of the genitive by substitution (badal) from (واحِدَةٍ) [one thing]. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ means "with one trait," and he explained it with His saying ﴿that you stand,﴾ taking it as an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to it. End quote. This is not permissible, because (بِواحِدَةٍ) [with one thing] is indefinite, while (أنْ تَقُومُوا) [that you stand] is definite, since its estimate is "your standing for God." Explicative apposition has two views: the first is that it requires the appositive to be definite from a definite, which is the view of the Kufans. As for the mismatch in definiteness, no one has held this view; it is only an error on the part of its speaker. The grammarians have refuted al-Zamakhshari for his saying that ﴿مَقامُ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ [the station of Ibrahim] is an explicative apposition to ﴿آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾ [clear signs], for the same reason of mismatch; so this is likewise.

The apparent meaning of standing (القِيامُ) here is taking a stand in the matter and rising to it with resolve, not the standing that is meant literally, according to the two views. It is unlikely that it means what al-Zamakhshari allowed: standing up from the gathering of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and dispersing from their assembly before him. The meaning: "I admonish you with only one thing in which lies your attaining the truth and your salvation: that you stand for the sake of God in groups of two and singly, and then reflect on the matter of Muhammad and what he brought." He said ﴿in pairs and singly﴾ because a group, when assembled, has confusion of thought, obstruction to reflection, mixing of speech, partisanship for schools of thought, and little fairness, as is witnessed in the lessons where groups gather, so no truth is established there. As for two people, if they look with fairness and each presents to the other what has become clear to him, the truth hardly escapes them both. As for one person, if he has good understanding, sound judgment, is free of partisanship, and seeks the truth, it is unlikely that he will miss it. (مَثْنى وفُرادى) [in pairs and singly] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and (مَثْنى) [in pairs] is placed first because seeking realities from two who support each other in consideration is more beneficial than one thought alone: when the truth flashes between the two, each of them then turns back to it, and thereby gains more insight. The poet said:

When they gather, they bring every rare thing, so that some of the people increase in knowledge from others.

﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا﴾ [and then reflect] is a conjunction to ﴿أنْ تَقُومُوا﴾ [that you stand]; the reflection here concerns the condition of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what they attributed to him. Reflection generally leads to the right course when its holder is free of what disturbs judgment. The pause at ﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا ما بِصاحِبِكم مِن جِنَّةٍ﴾ [and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion] according to Abu Hatim is a new negation. Ibn Atiyyah said: according to Sibawayh, it is the answer to what functions as an oath, because (تَفَكَّرَ) [reflect] is among the verbs that give a specification, like (تَبَيَّنَ) [become clear]; and on this view it refers to the signs of God and belief in Him. End quote. It is also possible that (تَتَفَكَّرُوا) is suspended (mu'allaq), and the negated clause is in the position of the accusative, being the object of the reflection; that is: "then reflect on the absence of madness in Muhammad." For attributing it to him cannot be valid for one who was the most intelligent of Quraysh, the most stable of mind, the most truthful of speech, the most pure of soul, and upon whose hands this inimitable Qur'an appeared. By reflection they will know that attributing madness to him is impossible, that no sane person would go to it, and that whoever attributes it to him is a liar and a fabricator. The apparent meaning is that (ما) is for negation, as we have explained. It was also said: (ما) is interrogative, and it is an interrogative not meant in its literal sense, but its meaning reverts to negation; the estimate: "What is there in your companion of madness?" that is, there is nothing of that in him. When He, the Exalted, negated madness from him, He affirmed that he is (نَذِيرٌ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ عَذابٍ شَدِيدٍ) [a warner before a severe punishment]: that is, he precedes in time the punishment with which they were threatened. And (بَيْنَ يَدَيْ) [before] indicates the nearness of the punishment.

﴿قُلْ ما سَألْتُكم مِن أجْرٍ﴾ [Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you] verse concerns disavowing the pursuit of worldly gain, the seeking of payment for the light he brought, and reliance upon God in it. (ما) may be a relative pronoun as subject, with the returning pronoun of the relative clause omitted, its estimate being: "what I asked you for," and ﴿فَهُوَ لَكُمْ﴾ [it is yours] is the predicate. The (فَ) entered because the subject carries the meaning of a condition. It is also possible that (ما) is a conditional, object of (سَألْتُكم) [I asked you], and (فَهُوَ لَكُمْ) [it is yours] is the clause that is the answer of the condition. His saying ﴿Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ has two meanings. The first: negation of asking for a reward, as a man says to his companion: "If you give me something, take it," while he knows that he has not given him anything, but he intends to make certain by making the taking conditional on what has not occurred. This is supported by ﴿My reward is only from God﴾. The second: that by "reward" he means what is in His saying ﴿Say: I ask you no reward for it, except for whoever wills to take a path to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 57], and in His saying ﴿I ask you for no reward for it, except love for kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23]; because taking a path to God benefits them, and likewise love in kinship, since kinship has bound them together with him. So said al-Zamakhshari, though there is some addition in it. Ibn Abbas said: the reward is love in kinship. Qatadah said: ﴿it is yours﴾, that is, its fruit and its reward, because I asked you to maintain the ties of kinship. Muqatil said: "I have left it to you."

﴿And He is over all things a witness.﴾ He is the Observer and Guardian. He knows that I do not seek any reward for my counsel and my call to Him except from Him, and that I do not hope for anything from you.

Al-qadhf is throwing with force and reliance. It is used figuratively for the sense of casting, as in His words ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ [Taha: 39] and ﴿and He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. Qatadah said: ﴿He casts the truth﴾ means He makes the proof clear and manifest. Ibn al-Qushayri said: He makes the proof clear such that there is no objection to it, because He is ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, and I hold fast to what truth is cast to me. The original sense of al-qadhf is throwing an arrow, or pebbles, or speech. Ibn Abbas said: He casts falsehood with the truth. The apparent reading is that "bi-l-haqq" (with the truth) is the object, so al-haqq is the thing cast, deleted, meaning: He casts, that is, He casts what He casts to His prophets of revelation and law, with the truth and not with falsehood. Then the bāʾ (the preposition "bi-") is either for accompaniment or for causation. This possibility is supported by the fact that qadhafa is transitive by itself. If you make bi-l-haqq the object, then the bāʾ is an extra particle in a position where its extra use is not regular.

The majority read ʿallāmu (Knower) in the nominative case. The apparent reading is that it is a second predicate, which is the apparent view of al-Zajjaj, who said: it is nominative because the implied sense is "Say: My Lord is the Knower of the unseen." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is nominative, agreeing with the position of inna and its subject (its grammatical locus), or with the pronoun hidden in yaqdhifu, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quotation. As for agreement with the locus of inna and its subject, this is not the view of Sibawayh, and it is not correct according to our scholars, as we have established in the books of grammar. As for his saying "with the hidden pronoun in yaqdhifu," he did not explain the reason for this agreement, and it seems he means that it is a substitute for the pronoun in yaqdhifu. Al-Kisa'i said: it is an attributive adjective for that pronoun, because his view is that it is permissible to make an attribute of an implicit third-person pronoun.

ʿIsa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, and Harb from Talha read ʿallāma in the accusative case. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an attribute of my Lord. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi and Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is a substitute. Al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute or an attribute. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a form of praise. It was read al-ghuyūbi in the genitive. As for the ḍamma (u-vowel), it is the plural of ghayb. As for the kasra (i-vowel), it is likewise, as they found two ḍammas and a waw heavy, so it was made kasra, and the harmony is kasra with the yāʾ, and the ḍamma that is on the yāʾ with the wāw. As for the fatḥa, it is an object form for intensification, like al-ṣabūr, and it is the thing that is absent and very hidden.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He casts with the truth in the present tense, He informed that the truth has come, and that is the Qur'an and the revelation, and what is other than it of religions has been nullified. Thus nothing remains of stability for any religion except Islam, neither at the beginning nor at the end. So Islam is not to be feared for what would nullify it, as He said ﴿Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42]. Qatadah said: al-batil is Satan, who creates nothing and does not bring anything back. Al-Dahhak said: the idols do not do that. Abu Sulayman said: the idol does not begin speech from itself so as to be answered, nor does it refute what has come of the truth with any proof. It was said: al-batil is that which opposes the truth. So the meaning is: falsehood has departed with the coming of the truth, so no remnant of it is left. This is because when the one who comes (the originator) perishes, nothing remains of him in beginning or return, so their saying "he neither begins nor returns" became a proverb for destruction. From this is the saying of the poet:

"More impoverished than his people are the slaves; today he neither begins nor returns."

The apparent view is that mā is a negation. It was also said that it is an interrogative whose ultimate meaning is negation, as if he said: what thing begins falsehood, that is Iblis, and returns it? This was said by al-Zajjaj and a group with him. From al-Hasan: he does not begin, that is Iblis, good for his people, nor does he return it, that is, he does not benefit them in this world or the hereafter. It was also said: al-Shaytan (Satan) is al-batil, because he is the companion of falsehood, because he is destroyed, just as he is called al-Shaytan from shāṭa, meaning he perished. It was said: al-haqq is the sword. From Ibn Masʿud: The Messenger of Allah entered Makkah, and around the Kaʿba were three hundred and sixty idols, and he began to strike them with a stick of a jujube tree and say: "﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra: 81], ﴿The truth has come, and falsehood neither begins nor returns﴾."

The majority read ﴿Say: If I go astray﴾ with a fatḥa on the lām, ﴿then I only go astray﴾ with a kasra on the ḍād. Al-Hasan, Ibn Wththab, and ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Muqri read with a kasra on the lām and a fatḥa on the ḍād, and this is the dialect of Tamim. ʿAbd al-Rahman made the hamza of (aḍillu) kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: there are two dialects, like ḍalaltu aḍillu and ẓalaltu aẓillu.

﴿And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾. The bi- here may be masdariyya (verbal-noun forming), meaning: by the revelation of my Lord. The verbal correspondence is: "and if I am guided, then I am guided only for my own benefit," corresponding to ﴿Whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾ [Fussilat: 46], which corresponds to ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and ﴿Whoever goes astray, he goes astray only against himself﴾ [Yunus: 108], which corresponds to ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for himself﴾ [al-Zumar: 41]. Or it is said: "then I only go astray to my own detriment." As for the verse itself, the correspondence is semantic, because the self is everything that is against it, is for it, meaning every harm against it is by its cause.

﴿Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53], and what is beneficial for it is by the guidance and success of its Lord. This is a general ruling for every person responsible. He commanded His Messenger to attribute it to himself, because when he enters under it along with the greatness of his position and the secret of his way, like others he is more worthy of it. End of quotation, and it is from the words of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Indeed He is Hearing, Near﴾, He perceives the speech and deed of every one who goes astray and every one who is guided.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified﴾ refers to the time of resurrection and the establishment of the Hour. Frequently it came: (p. 293) ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27], ﴿And if you could see when the criminals bow their heads before their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12], and all of that is on the Day of Resurrection. He expressed it with fazaʿū (they were terrified), uhhidhū (they were seized), and qālū (they said), and the past tense was used for them to indicate the certainty of their occurrence by the true report. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: this is in the punishment of this world. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the disbelievers at their emergence from the graves. Mujahid said: on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: it refers to the people of Badr when their necks were struck, so they could not flee from the punishment, nor return to repentance. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Abza said: it refers to an army going to attack the Kaʿba, and they will be swallowed up by the earth in a desert, and no one will escape except a man from Juhayna, who will inform the people of what befell him. They said: for him it was said:

"And with Juhayna is the certain news."

A lengthy hadith about this meaning was narrated from Hudhayfa. al-Tabari mentioned that its chain is weak, and it is falsely attributed in the narration of Ibn al-Jarrah. Al-Zamakhshari said, and from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning the sinking in the desert, because eighty thousand men will march to the Kaʿba to destroy it, and when they enter the desert they will be swallowed up. It is mentioned in the hadith of Hudhayfa that "There will be a turmoil between the people of the east and the west. While they are in that state, al-Sufyani will come out from the dry valley immediately, at the time he descends to Damascus, and he sends an army to Madina, and they plunder it for three days. Then they go out to Makkah, and Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them and strikes it, that is the earth, with his foot a single blow, and Allah sinks them into a desert of the earth. No one will escape except a man from Juhayna, who will inform the people of what befell him. That is His saying ﴿so there is no escape﴾." Only two men from Juhayna will escape from them, and for this the proverb became current: "And with Juhayna is the certain news." The name of one of them is Bashir, who gives glad tidings to the people of Makkah, and the other is Nadhir, who returns with the report of al-Sufyani. It was also said: only one man will return, named Najiya from Juhayna, whose face will be turned to the back of his neck.

The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, meaning: and if you could see the disbelievers when they are terrified, so there is no escape, that is, they cannot escape Allah, and there is no flight for them from what He intends for them. Al-Hasan said: "so there is no escape" means from the blast of resurrection, and they are seized from the belly of the earth to its surface. End of quotation. Or from the place of standing to the Fire when they are raised; or from the surface of the earth to its belly when they die; or from the desert of Badr to the well; or from beneath their feet when they are swallowed up. These are sayings built upon those earlier sayings concerning the return of the pronoun in fazaʿū. Describing the place as near, from where Allah's power is over them, so wherever they are, it is near.

The majority read ﴿so there is no escape﴾ as a fatḥa-built form (fala fawta), ﴿and they are seized﴾ as a past-tense verb. The apparent view is that it is conjoined to ﴿they were terrified﴾. It was also said: it is conjoined to ﴿so there is no escape﴾, because its meaning is "they will not be made to escape, and they are seized." ʿAbd al-Rahman, mawla of Banu Hashim, from his father, and Talha read: ﴿fa-la fawtun, wa-akhdhun﴾ as two nominal masdars with tanwin. Ubayy read: ﴿fa-la fawta﴾ built, and (wa-akhdhun) as a tanwin masdar. Whoever reads (wa-akhdhun) with a ḍamma (raf'), it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: and their state is seizure; or it is a subject, meaning: and there is seizure there. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was read: wa-akhdhun, and it is conjoined to the locus of fala fawta, and its meaning: there is no escape there, and there is seizure there. End of quotation. It is as if he says: "no escape" is a collective negation, and the built form with it is in the position of a subject, and its predicate is "there." So likewise "wa-akhdhun" is a subject and its predicate is "there," so it is conjunction of sentences, even if one of them contains negation and the other contains affirmation.

The pronoun in bihi refers to Allah, said by Mujahid, meaning: they say that when they see the punishment. Al-Hasan said: it refers to resurrection. Muqatil said: it refers to the Qur'an. It was also said: it refers to the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: it refers to the Messenger, because his mention passed in the verse ﴿Your companion is not possessed﴾.

﴿And how can they reach from a place far away?﴾ Ibn Abbas said: al-tanawush is returning to the world. Ibn al-Anbari recited:

"Mayy wishes that she would return to me, but there is no path to reaching her."

That is: she desires. This is an image of their seeking what cannot happen, which is that their faith would benefit them at that time, as their faith benefits the believers in this world. Their state is likened to the state of one who wants to take a thing from afar, as another takes it from near. The majority read al-tanawush with a waw. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu ʿAmr, and Abu Bakr read it with a hamza. It is permissible that (p. 294) both are roots, one of which is n-w-sh-, and the other is ʾ-w-sh- with a hamza... and their explanation was already given in the lexicon sections. It is permissible that the origin of the hamza is a waw, as said by al-Zajjaj, and followed by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa. al-Zajjaj said: every waw with a permanent ḍamma, you have the choice: if you wish you keep its hamza, and if you wish you leave its hamza. You say: thalāth adwur without a hamza, and adʾur with a hamza. He said: the meaning: from where is it for them to reach what they sought of repentance after the passing of its time, because it is only accepted in this world, and this world has gone, so they are far from the hereafter. That is His saying ﴿from a place far away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: the waw with a permanent ḍamma was hamzated, as it was hamzated in ujūh and udur. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: As for al-tanā'ush with a hamza, it may be from al-tanawush, and the waw was hamzated since it was a permanent ḍamma, as they said: afteytu. Al-Hawfi said: whoever reads with a hamza may have two possibilities: one, that it is from al-nāsh, which is movement in slowness, or it may be from nāsha yanūshu, the waw was hamzated because of its being ḍammed, as afteytu and adūru were hamzated. Abu al-Baqa said: it is read with a hamza because of the waw, and it was also said: it is an original root from nāshahu. End of quotation. What they mention, that a waw with a permanent ḍamma may be replaced by a hamza, is not absolute; rather that is not permitted in the medial position when it is assimilated into it, like ya'ūdu and ta'ūdu as verbal nouns; nor when it is sound in the verb, like tarhawka tarhūkan, and taʿāwana taʿāwunan, and two hamzas are not heard from that, so it is not permitted. Al-tanawush is like al-taʿāwun, so its hamzation is not permitted, because its waw is sound in the verb, as he says: tanāwasha.

﴿وقَدْ كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ The pronoun in *bihi* refers to what the phrase *(āmannā bihi,* "we believe in it") refers to, according to the opinions. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāliyyah*, a clause describing the state of the subject), and *(min qablu)* means before the descent of the punishment. Most readers recite *(wa-yaqdhifūna)* in the active voice, as a narration of a past state (*ḥikāyat ḥāl*, a report of a state that had already occurred). Al-Ḥasan said: "Their saying: there is no Paradise and no Fire." Qatādah added: "Nor resurrection, nor Fire." Ibn Zayd said: "Attacking the Qur'an with their saying: ﴿fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'ām: 25]." Mujāhid said: "Attacking the Messenger (ﷺ) with their saying: poet, sorcerer, and soothsayer."

﴿مِن مَكانٍ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means from a distant direction, because attributing any of those things to him is among the most remote of things. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is speech about the unseen and a hidden matter, because they had not witnessed from him any sorcery, poetry, or lying. They have brought this unseen matter from a distant position relative to his condition, because the thing furthest from what he brought is poetry and sorcery, and the thing furthest from his habit, which was known among them and tested, is lying and falsehood." End of quote. It was also said: this is a resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnaf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), meaning: they utter the word of faith at a time when faith itself will not benefit them. Their state is thus likened to their seeking to obtain, in the Hereafter, what they had neglected of faith in this world by saying: "We believe in the Hereafter." That is a remote aim for one who throws something from a distant place where there is no room to reach it, since he wants to hit it while it is absent from him and far away. *Al-ghayb* means the absent thing.

Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywa, and Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr recited *(wa-yuqadhūna)* in the passive voice. Mujāhid said: "He will pelt them with what they dislike from the sky." Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: "They will be struck with the unseen from where they do not know. Its meaning: they will be repaid for their evil deeds, and they will have no knowledge of what has come to them, either at the time when repentance is impossible at the sight of death, or in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is, their devils bring it to them, meaning the unseen, and teach it to them." It was also said: they are pelted into the Fire. It was said: this is a parable (*mathal*, an illustrative comparison), because one who is called from a distant place does not hear, meaning they do not understand and do not hear.

﴿وحِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: "The adverbial of place (*al-ẓarf*) stands in place of the subject of the passive verb." End of quote. But if it were as he stated, it would be in the nominative, *baynahum*, as in the reading of the one who recited ﴿لَقَدْ تَّقَطَّعَ بَيْنَكم﴾ [Indeed, your bond has been severed] in one of its two meanings. One does not say that a noun that is attached to an indeclinable word, which is the pronoun, is indeclinable and therefore in the position of the nominative, even though it is indeclinable. Just as one of them said concerning the line: *wa-idh mā mathhalahum*, pointing out that it is in the nominative position because it is attached to the pronoun, even though it is vowelled with fatḥa. That is a corrupt statement. One may say: "I passed by your boy," and "Your boy stood" with fatḥa, and no one says this. Building (*binā'*, becoming indeclinable) because of attachment to an indeclinable word is not absolute, but has particular positions that are established in grammar. No one says that, and the poet says: *wa-qad ḥīla bayna al-ʿīr wa-l-nazawān* [And indeed a barrier was placed between al-ʿĪr and al-Nazawān], for he put *bayna* in the accusative, though it is attached to a declinable noun. What occurs of this kind is only explained by saying that the element standing in for the subject is the pronoun of the verbal noun indicated by it, and *ḥīla* is that, i.e. the barrier (*al-ḥawl*). Because it is a pronoun, it is not an emphatic verbal noun, so it may stand in place of the subject. On this basis the saying of the poet is explained: *wa-qālat matā yubkhal ʿalayka wa-yuʿtalal bisūʾin wa-in yukshaf gharāmuka tadrub* [She said: "When you are withheld from and an excuse is made against you with ill, and if your passion is revealed, you will be harried."], meaning: and he is excused, i.e. the excusing.

Those they desire to return to the world: this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Or it is the family, wealth, and children, said by al-Suddī. Or the barrier is between the army and the destruction of the Kaʿba, or between the believers, or between salvation from the punishment, or between the delights of this world and its pleasures, said by Mujāhid as well. ﴿as was done to their likes﴾, from the disbelieving nations, meaning that a barrier was placed between them and their desires. *Min qablu* may be connected to *(ashyāʿihim)*, meaning whoever was characterized by their attribute from among those before, that is, in the earlier time. This is preferred, because what is done to all of them occurs at one time. It may also be connected to a verb if the barrier is in this world. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Their likes are the people of the Elephant," meaning the likes of Quraysh, and he seems to have presented it as an example. As for specifying them, there is no evidence for it. ﴿Indeed they were in a disquieting doubt﴾, meaning in this world. *Murīb* is an active participle from *arāba al-rajul*, meaning he committed a suspicious act and entered into it, and *arabtu al-rajul* means I caused him to fall into suspicion. Attributing causing suspicion to doubt is a metaphor (*majāz*, a figurative usage). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Except that there is a difference between them: the *murīb* from the transitive verb is transferred from that which can be suspicious among concrete things to the meaning, and from the intransitive verb is transferred from the doubter to the doubt, as you say: *shiʿru shāʿir* [the poetry of a poet]." End of quote, and there is some lack of clarity in it. It was said: it is possible that he followed it with doubt, and both have the same meaning, for the end of the verse harmonizes with the preceding one from a near place, as you say: *ʿajabun ʿajīb*, *shitāʾun shātin*, *laylatun laylāʾ*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The disquieting doubt is the strongest and most intense form of doubt in darkening."

[p. 295]

(p. 289) ﴿We did not give them books to study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ ﴿Those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My rejection!﴾ ﴿Say: I admonish you with only one thing: that you stand up before God, in pairs and singly, and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only from God, and He is a witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Say: My Lord hurls down the truth; He is the Knower of the unseen.﴾ ﴿Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore.﴾ ﴿Say: If I go astray, I go astray only to my own loss; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near.﴾ ﴿If you could see when they are terrified, with no escape, and they are seized from a near place.﴾ ﴿And they say: We believe in Him. But how can they reach [it] from a far place?﴾ ﴿And they had disbelieved in it before, and cast [doubts] about the unseen from a far place.﴾ ﴿And between them and what they desire is a barrier, as was done with their like before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾

﴿وما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ [We did not give them]: the people of Makkah. ﴿مِن كُتُبٍ﴾ [books]. al-Suddi said: "From Us," so that they would know by studying them that what you brought is false. Ibn Zayd said: "So they would confirm that polytheism is permissible." This is like His saying: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum: 35]. Qatadah said: God did not send down to the Arabs any book before the Qur'an, nor did He send them any prophet before Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: From where did they deny, when no book or warner had come to them concerning this? It was also said: He described them as an unlettered people, people of ignorance, who have no religion and no prior knowledge of the revelation of a book or the sending of a messenger. As He said: ﴿Or have We given them a book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21]. So there is no established basis for their denial, nor any semblance of a claim to it. Likewise, the People of the Book say, though they are falsifiers: "We are the People of the Book and the laws, and we rely upon messengers from among the messengers of God." It was also said: The meaning is that they speak about the Book of God by their own opinions: some say it is magic, and some say it is fabrication, and they do not rely on any trace of knowledge or on the report of anyone whose report is accepted. "For We have given them books which they study, and We did not send them any messenger or warner, so they could claim that their statements are based on His command."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿يَدْرُسُونَها﴾ as the imperfect of darasa (to study), unstressed. Abu Haywah read it with a fatha on the dal, a shadda, and a kasra on the ra, as the imperfect of iddaraса (ittafala from al-dars), meaning: "you study them together." Also from Abu Haywah: yudarrisuna-ha, from al-tadris (repeated study), or from duris al-kitab (unstressed), and durrisa al-kitab (stressed); the doubling is by consideration of plurality. As for the meaning of (قَبْلَكَ) [before you], Ibn Atiyyah said: That is, We did not send any warner who would address them directly with something, nor who would be in contact with the people of their era, nor from close to their forefathers. Yet warning existed in the world and among the Arabs with Shu'ayb, Salih, and Hud. The call to God and His Oneness is established; the earth has never been without someone calling to Him. The meaning is only: no warner who is specifically sent to these people to whom he was sent. Among the Arabs there was much of the warning of Isma'il, and God the Exalted says: ﴿He was true to his promise, and he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54]. But none dedicated himself to warning and fought for it except Muhammad (ﷺ). End quote.

﴿وكَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Those before them denied]: a warning to them from the nations that preceded them, and what their affair came to; and consolation to His messenger that their habit of denial is the habit of the earlier nations, and what befell those will befall them. The two pronouns in (بَلَغُوا) [they reached] and in ﴿ما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ [what We gave them] refer to (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ) [those before them], to be consistent with His saying (فَكَذَّبُوا) [so they denied], meaning: they did not reach, in thanking for the blessing and in repaying the favour, a tenth of the blessings and kindness We had given them. (p. 290) Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun in (بَلَغُوا) refers to Quraysh, and in ﴿ما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ to the nations (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ). The meaning: these did not reach even some of what We gave those [earlier nations] of long lives, strength of bodies, and abundance of wealth; and when they denied My messengers, My rejection came upon them through destruction and annihilation. The strength they had did not avail them. So how will the state of these be when punishment and destruction come to them? It was also said: the pronoun in (بَلَغُوا) refers to (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ), and in (آتَيْناهم) to Quraysh: the earlier nations did not reach a tenth of what We gave Quraysh of signs, clear proofs, and the light which you brought them. Ibn Atiyyah presented these statements as possibilities. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned the second, and Abu Abdullah al-Razi preferred the third, saying: that is, (الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ) did not reach a tenth of what We gave the people of Muhammad of proof, because the Book of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is more complete and clearer than all other books, and Muhammad (peace be upon him) is better than all the messengers and more eloquent; his proof is more sufficient and his explanation more healing. This supports what we mentioned: ﴿and We did not give them books which they study﴾ [which would make the Qur'an unnecessary]. Since the one given in the first verse is the Book, the giving in the second verse is taken to mean the giving of the Book, and this is preferable. End quote.

It is related from Ibn Abbas: "There is no one more knowledgeable than his community, and no book clearer than his book." (al-mi'shar) is a form of (al-'ashr) [tenth], and no other numeral has been formed on this pattern except (al-mirba') [quarter]; their meanings are: a tenth and a quarter. Some said: al-mi'shar is a tenth of a tenth. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is nothing. End quote. It was also said: in this view, "a tenth" means a tenth of tenths, so it is a part of a thousand parts. Al-Mawardi said: this is the most apparent, because the intention is extreme exaggeration in minimizing. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾, when it is dispensed with by His saying ﴿and those before them denied﴾? I say: since the meaning of His saying ﴿and those before them denied﴾ is that those before them committed denial and undertook it, the denial of the messengers is made a consequence of it. An example of this is when someone says: "So-and-so undertook disbelief, so he disbelieved in Muhammad." It is also permissible that it be connected to His saying (ما بَلَغُوا) [they did not reach], as when you say: "Zayd did not reach a tenth of the virtue of 'Amr," so that he is favoured over him.

﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ نَكِيرِ﴾ [So how was My rejection!] is for the earlier deniers, so that they would beware of the like of it. End quote. (فَكَيْفَ) [so how] is an expression of the magnitude of the matter, and it is not a plain interrogative. In it is a threat to Quraysh: that they are exposed to the like of that rejection. (النَّكِيرُ) [rejection] is a verbal noun like (al-inkar) [denial], and it is among the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'il, while the verb is on the pattern af'al, like (al-nadhir) and (al-'adhir) from (anhara) and (a'dhara). The ya' is deleted from (نَكِيرِ) [rejection] for lightness, since it is sufficient without it.

﴿قُلْ إنَّما أعِظُكم بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ [Say: I admonish you with only one thing]: he said: it is obedience to God and His Oneness. Al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but God." Qatadah said: it is "that you stand." Abu Ali said: ﴿أنْ تَقُومُوا﴾ [that you stand] is in the position of the genitive by substitution (badal) from (واحِدَةٍ) [one thing]. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ means "with one trait," and he explained it with His saying ﴿that you stand,﴾ taking it as an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to it. End quote. This is not permissible, because (بِواحِدَةٍ) [with one thing] is indefinite, while (أنْ تَقُومُوا) [that you stand] is definite, since its estimate is "your standing for God." Explicative apposition has two views: the first is that it requires the appositive to be definite from a definite, which is the view of the Kufans. As for the mismatch in definiteness, no one has held this view; it is only an error on the part of its speaker. The grammarians have refuted al-Zamakhshari for his saying that ﴿مَقامُ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ [the station of Ibrahim] is an explicative apposition to ﴿آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾ [clear signs], for the same reason of mismatch; so this is likewise.

The apparent meaning of standing (القِيامُ) here is taking a stand in the matter and rising to it with resolve, not the standing that is meant literally, according to the two views. It is unlikely that it means what al-Zamakhshari allowed: standing up from the gathering of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and dispersing from their assembly before him. The meaning: "I admonish you with only one thing in which lies your attaining the truth and your salvation: that you stand for the sake of God in groups of two and singly, and then reflect on the matter of Muhammad and what he brought." He said ﴿in pairs and singly﴾ because a group, when assembled, has confusion of thought, obstruction to reflection, mixing of speech, partisanship for schools of thought, and little fairness, as is witnessed in the lessons where groups gather, so no truth is established there. As for two people, if they look with fairness and each presents to the other what has become clear to him, the truth hardly escapes them both. As for one person, if he has good understanding, sound judgment, is free of partisanship, and seeks the truth, it is unlikely that he will miss it. (مَثْنى وفُرادى) [in pairs and singly] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and (مَثْنى) [in pairs] is placed first because seeking realities from two who support each other in consideration is more beneficial than one thought alone: when the truth flashes between the two, each of them then turns back to it, and thereby gains more insight. The poet said:

When they gather, they bring every rare thing, so that some of the people increase in knowledge from others.

﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا﴾ [and then reflect] is a conjunction to ﴿أنْ تَقُومُوا﴾ [that you stand]; the reflection here concerns the condition of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what they attributed to him. Reflection generally leads to the right course when its holder is free of what disturbs judgment. The pause at ﴿ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُوا ما بِصاحِبِكم مِن جِنَّةٍ﴾ [and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion] according to Abu Hatim is a new negation. Ibn Atiyyah said: according to Sibawayh, it is the answer to what functions as an oath, because (تَفَكَّرَ) [reflect] is among the verbs that give a specification, like (تَبَيَّنَ) [become clear]; and on this view it refers to the signs of God and belief in Him. End quote. It is also possible that (تَتَفَكَّرُوا) is suspended (mu'allaq), and the negated clause is in the position of the accusative, being the object of the reflection; that is: "then reflect on the absence of madness in Muhammad." For attributing it to him cannot be valid for one who was the most intelligent of Quraysh, the most stable of mind, the most truthful of speech, the most pure of soul, and upon whose hands this inimitable Qur'an appeared. By reflection they will know that attributing madness to him is impossible, that no sane person would go to it, and that whoever attributes it to him is a liar and a fabricator. The apparent meaning is that (ما) is for negation, as we have explained. It was also said: (ما) is interrogative, and it is an interrogative not meant in its literal sense, but its meaning reverts to negation; the estimate: "What is there in your companion of madness?" that is, there is nothing of that in him. When He, the Exalted, negated madness from him, He affirmed that he is (نَذِيرٌ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ عَذابٍ شَدِيدٍ) [a warner before a severe punishment]: that is, he precedes in time the punishment with which they were threatened. And (بَيْنَ يَدَيْ) [before] indicates the nearness of the punishment.

﴿قُلْ ما سَألْتُكم مِن أجْرٍ﴾ [Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you] verse concerns disavowing the pursuit of worldly gain, the seeking of payment for the light he brought, and reliance upon God in it. (ما) may be a relative pronoun as subject, with the returning pronoun of the relative clause omitted, its estimate being: "what I asked you for," and ﴿فَهُوَ لَكُمْ﴾ [it is yours] is the predicate. The (فَ) entered because the subject carries the meaning of a condition. It is also possible that (ما) is a conditional, object of (سَألْتُكم) [I asked you], and (فَهُوَ لَكُمْ) [it is yours] is the clause that is the answer of the condition. His saying ﴿Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ has two meanings. The first: negation of asking for a reward, as a man says to his companion: "If you give me something, take it," while he knows that he has not given him anything, but he intends to make certain by making the taking conditional on what has not occurred. This is supported by ﴿My reward is only from God﴾. The second: that by "reward" he means what is in His saying ﴿Say: I ask you no reward for it, except for whoever wills to take a path to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 57], and in His saying ﴿I ask you for no reward for it, except love for kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23]; because taking a path to God benefits them, and likewise love in kinship, since kinship has bound them together with him. So said al-Zamakhshari, though there is some addition in it. Ibn Abbas said: the reward is love in kinship. Qatadah said: ﴿it is yours﴾, that is, its fruit and its reward, because I asked you to maintain the ties of kinship. Muqatil said: "I have left it to you."

﴿And He is over all things a witness.﴾ He is the Observer and Guardian. He knows that I do not seek any reward for my counsel and my call to Him except from Him, and that I do not hope for anything from you.

Al-qadhf is throwing with force and reliance. It is used figuratively for the sense of casting, as in His words ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ [Taha: 39] and ﴿and He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. Qatadah said: ﴿He casts the truth﴾ means He makes the proof clear and manifest. Ibn al-Qushayri said: He makes the proof clear such that there is no objection to it, because He is ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, and I hold fast to what truth is cast to me. The original sense of al-qadhf is throwing an arrow, or pebbles, or speech. Ibn Abbas said: He casts falsehood with the truth. The apparent reading is that "bi-l-haqq" (with the truth) is the object, so al-haqq is the thing cast, deleted, meaning: He casts, that is, He casts what He casts to His prophets of revelation and law, with the truth and not with falsehood. Then the bāʾ (the preposition "bi-") is either for accompaniment or for causation. This possibility is supported by the fact that qadhafa is transitive by itself. If you make bi-l-haqq the object, then the bāʾ is an extra particle in a position where its extra use is not regular.

The majority read ʿallāmu (Knower) in the nominative case. The apparent reading is that it is a second predicate, which is the apparent view of al-Zajjaj, who said: it is nominative because the implied sense is "Say: My Lord is the Knower of the unseen." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is nominative, agreeing with the position of inna and its subject (its grammatical locus), or with the pronoun hidden in yaqdhifu, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quotation.
